  copy still on the host rebuilds when it next launches, as the first
  launch of a version always has. A version is compared as dot-separated
  numbers; a tag that is not one (and every tag, when the launch's own
  version is not one) is never removed. A version newer than the launch's
  stays until a launch newer still removes it.
  *The base's copies where BuildKit reads.* Leerie also copies its base,
  under the same name, into each namespace BuildKit's workers read
  (`ensure_base_in_worker_ns`; `buildkit` on Colima, `default` on the
  standard rootless setup), so a repository's `FROM $BASE_IMAGE` resolves.
  Those copies are leerie's too, 2.4 GB each, and piled up the same way
  (one host's `buildkit` held `leerie:` 0.44.0 to 0.44.10). So the same
  reaper, under the same per-version holds and with the same unforced
  `image rm`, removes from each such namespace every `leerie:<v>` whose
  `<v>` is an older version, and nothing else there: not the pinned
  frontend, not the operator's images, not an image with no name. It runs
  where those namespaces are already known and the copy is made: on a
  launch that builds a repository image, under the host's image lock,
  after the sweep of an earlier leerie's repository images and before the
  base's copy. Asking BuildKit for its workers on every launch would cost
  a daemon query a launch with nothing to build never needs, and a copy is
  only ever added there, so each new version's copy removes the older
  ones. A version held by a launch of it keeps its copy too: that launch
  may be about to build `FROM` it.
  *Local only.* Fly and EC2 keep their images in their own registries, on
  their own lifetimes; a remote launch takes no hold and removes nothing.
  *Rootless and rootful.* The reaper and the holds run in the launcher,
  as the host user, before any container exists, and touch no container's
  files: the hold files live in the host-wide directory the launcher
  creates, never chowned (the rootful entry guard chowns that directory
  itself, not its contents). `nerdctl image rm` refuses an image in use on
  rootless containerd and on Colima's rootful one in its VM alike, where
  the launcher's `nerdctl` is a shim into the VM and the holds are files on
  the macOS host shared by every launch there.
  *Residuals.* A launcher from before this change takes no hold, so a
  launch of such a version can lose its images to a newer launch between
  its check and its run; it fails at `nerdctl run` and builds them again on
  its next launch. The holds are as wide as the host-wide directory, as
  the image lock is: launches given different `LEERIE_HOST_DIR`s on one
  containerd do not see each other's holds. An older base's copy where
  BuildKit reads stays until the next launch on the host that builds a
  repository image. `leerie prune` does not remove images: its scope is one
  repository's state, chosen by age, and the images are host-wide and need
  no age; a launch reaps them before the disk is needed, while the disk
  check that stops a launch on a full disk would stop it before any prune.
  *Designed 2026-11-04 (the operator's host):* the disk filled (191 of
  193 GB), a repository image build died with `no space left on device`
  and a run was stopped by leerie's own disk check (`only 2.0% free`).
  `leerie` held every version's images, and nothing removed any:
  `leerie:` 0.44.0, .1, .3, .6, .7 and .8 at 2.4 GB each, one repository's
  image per version at 4.76 GB each, another's at 5.9 GB for two
  versions; about 10-13 GB more per release per host. Removing the stale
  ones by hand freed 24 GB.
- *A command line is refused before any image step.* The orchestrator's
  parser, in the container, is the one authority on its command line, and
  the launcher reaches it only after the image steps, which take minutes
  when an image is built or copied. So before any of them the launcher
  runs that same parser on the host (`check_command_line`, through
  `python3 -I -S` on the launch's snapshot of `orchestrator/leerie.py`, as
  its other host helpers run), over the argv it will give the container,
  and a line the parser refuses ends the launch there with the parser's
  own message and status. The check builds the parser and parses; it
  reads no state and starts nothing, and a module the host's Python cannot
  load leaves the line to the container, as before. The module is
  compiled once per content, not once per launch: its code object is
  kept under `~/.cache/leerie/bytecode`, named by the sha256 of the
  interpreter's bytecode magic and the source, so the parser that runs is
  always the source's own, an edit is a new entry, and the four most
  recently used are kept. *Measured 2026-11-04 (review round 39,
  execution E4):* compiling the 3.5 MB module took 3.1 s of every launch,
  and a refused line took 4-7 s in all, not the "about a second" first
  claimed; loading the kept code object takes 0.3 s. The alternative, the
  parser in a module of its own, was rejected: its options read the
  orchestrator's constants, so the one parser would have to move out of
  the one file. *Designed 2026-11-03 (the
  operator's live 0.44.0 launches):* `leerie promptresume <run-id>
  --max-workers 2000 …`, a mistyped `resume`, spent about 10 minutes on
  the image steps before the container printed `leerie: error:
  unrecognized arguments: <run-id>`. A second copy of the orchestrator's
  options in the launcher was rejected: it would drift from the parser.
  A `resume` that names a run is checked the same way, for the same
  reason. On the local runtime the container mounts the host's state root.
  The launcher therefore gives the check that root, and the check resolves
  the named run there with the orchestrator's own `resolve_run_id`, which
  reads the runs' state files and nothing else. So a run ID that names no
  run ends the launch before any image step, with the message the
  container would print. That run list is the only state the check reads,
  and only for a local `resume`. A remote runtime's runs are resolved
  where they live, as before. *Designed 2026-11-04 (the operator's live
  0.44.7 launch):* `leerie resume <run-id less its last character> …`
  waited 16 minutes on two image builds before the container printed
  `run-id … does not match any known run`.
- *Fail closed, on every entry.* Where the image has a worker root, the
  confinement check every entry runs (`_require_confinement`) runs `test
  -e /.leerie-worker-env` confined and stops the run when it does not find
  the worker stage's mark (`_require_worker_view`): leerie never runs the
  repository's commands in its own root instead, nor its own in theirs.

**Runtimes.** *Rootless:* the worker root is the image's, owned as the
image built it (root's files appear as the running user, the image's
`leerie` files as `nobody`, exactly as in leerie's own root); the view's
binds of it are read-only, so no ownership question arises. *Rootful:* the
same files are root's and the worker reads them through their mode bits,
as it reads leerie's root today; `container-entry.sh`'s ownership fixes
touch only leerie's root. Both run the same two `nerdctl build`s; the
named OCI-layout context and the OCI export are BuildKit features nerdctl
passes through (measured on rootless nerdctl 2.3.5 with BuildKit 0.31.2).
*Fly:* `ensure_image` runs the same two builds through `build-push.sh`:
the repository's file as committed, from the committed tree, pushed under
its own tag, then leerie's, whose worker stage is that image's digest in
the registry (`FROM registry.fly.io/<app>@<digest>`), checked as
`_check_repo_image` checks it (`--layout-base`). The repository's image
is never started as a container there (`--no-run`, where a local build
would smoke-test it); the machine's root is the base. Each image is pushed
under its own tag and a machine starts from the digest leerie pushed
(§6½ *Per-repo container image*). *EC2:* the AMI is baked
from leerie's base Dockerfile only, and no repository image is built
there, so every process runs in leerie's root; a repository's image layers
reach no EC2 machine. The machine's `/work/.leerie/Dockerfile` is not
streamed back to the host on Fly or EC2 any more: a file a machine wrote
never becomes a build input.

**Cost.** `COPY --from=<worker stage> /` copies the whole worker root, which
is the base's filesystem plus the repository's layers: about 2.4 GB more
unpacked per repository image (one per checkout and leerie version), and
the copy's time on each rebuild. Locally the first build's image is also
written out once as an OCI layout in the build directory, about 1 GB and
49 s for an image on leerie's base (measured 2026-11-03), removed with the
directory; on Fly it is pushed under its own tag. A rebuild happens only when the
Dockerfile, what it reads from the committed tree, leerie's version or the
base image change (`.dockerfile-hash` records all four and
`REPO_IMAGE_LAYOUT`). A Dockerfile that copies the whole tree (`COPY .`)
is rebuilt on every commit. A rebuild runs every step of the repository's
file, since no build reuses BuildKit's cache (*No build consumes what
another build left in BuildKit*). An `apt-get install` step took 3.8 s
from the cache and 25.8 s with `--no-cache` (measured 2026-11-03). On
every rebuild the second build's copy of the whole root takes minutes
anyway. A checkout that switches between two branches whose copied files
differ rebuilds from nothing on each switch. Each launch exports, dates
and hashes the context, which for a whole-tree copy is the size of the
tree. A launch that needs no rebuild runs no build at all, whatever wrote
the Dockerfile. Leerie's generated file is tested only by its own build:
when its language-dep layer does not build, the launch builds the same
file without that layer (*Language deps*, §6½), and records the image
under the key of the file it generated, so the next launch, which
generates the same file, reuses it, and warns that it does. *Revised
2026-11-03 (review round 35, execution R35E-1).* A separate probe build of the generated file ran on
every launch, before the rebuild check; once every build was given
`--no-cache`, it reinstalled every language dependency on each launch and
threw the result away (32 s instead of 11 s for a one-package bake,
measured; minutes for a real lockfile), and each launch needed apt and the
package registry. On a rebuild it doubled the build.

**Residuals.** A worker's CLI reads with its `Read`, `Grep` and `Glob`
tools in leerie's root: a path only the worker root has (`/opt/venv/…`)
is found by a command, not by those tools. A worker stage whose last
stage has no `/bin/sh` cannot record its environment, so its build fails.
The pinned frontend image is a network pull (about 14 MB), as a
`# syntax=` frontend was. The launcher pulls it into the containerd
namespace BuildKit's worker reads before its first build
(`ensure_frontend_in_worker_ns`, as `ensure_base_in_worker_ns` copies the
base there) and keeps it there.
BuildKit's own pull of a frontend lives only in BuildKit's cache: after a
prune, a build on a host without the network failed to resolve it, while
one whose namespace held the pulled image built (measured 2026-11-03,
BuildKit 0.31.2, with the daemon's registry access cut). A host that has
never had the network has no base image either, so the frontend adds no
first-install case. On Fly the remote builder resolves the pin itself
(not measured there), and the cache-mount namespace holds there only if
the remote builder passes `--build-arg` through to the frontend (not
measured there). With a namespace per build no build reuses another's
cache mount, so the records a build leaves are dead once it ends, and
BuildKit's collection did not reclaim them: 13 builds each filling a
60 MB mount left 838 MB, above the default policy's 512 MB for cache
mounts, with nothing removed after 90 s idle (measured 2026-11-03,
BuildKit 0.31.2; the policy's 48-hour keep duration is the likely reason,
not proven), leaving only the disk-wide rules (10 GB reserved, 39 GB
kept free) as the bound. So after each build leerie removes the records
its own namespace names (`leerie_prune_cache_mounts`: `buildctl prune
--filter 'type==exec.cachemount,description~="<ns>/"'`, whose description
names the mount's id, which the frontend prefixes with the namespace; it
removed that build's record and no other's, measured): the base build,
both of `build_repo_image`'s, and `build-push.sh --local-build`'s with
nerdctl, whatever the build's status. A failed prune warns. Left to
BuildKit's collection: the records of a build its launch was killed
during, and every record on Fly's remote builder, which leerie cannot
prune. *Revised 2026-11-03 (review round 37, execution E4).* This said a
record is kept "until BuildKit's garbage collection removes it", one per
build; the collection did not.

### Leerie names its own Python by path

*Designed 2026-11-04.*

**Root cause.** A repository chose the interpreter that ran leerie's own
Python in leerie's root. `container-entry.sh` changes to `/work`, the
repository, and then ran the cgroup broker and the orchestrator as
`python3 …`. In the image `python3` is not the system's: PATH holds mise's
user shims ahead of `/usr/bin`, and a shim picks the program it runs from
the version files (`.python-version`, `.tool-versions`, `mise.toml`) of its
working directory and every directory above it. Measured 2026-11-04 in
`leerie:0.44.1`, rootless, through the real entrypoint with a checkout at
`/work`: with `.python-version` holding `3.11`, PID 1, still root in the
container, ran `mise`, which downloaded CPython 3.11.18 from GitHub and
installed it. The broker (root), the orchestrator, the Landlock shim and
the sandbox probe then all ran on that interpreter (`/proc/<pid>/exe`
`…/mise/installs/python/3.11.18/bin/python3.11`). With `3.12` they ran on
the mise-installed 3.12.16. With no pin, PID 1 still ran `mise` first, as
root, reading the repository's configuration, before falling through to
`/usr/bin/python3`. Every helper the orchestrator starts as
`sys.executable` inherited the choice. The orchestrator's working directory
has to be `/work`, so leaving the repository first, as the host launcher
does (§6 *The host never runs a program the checkout chose*), cannot apply
here. The Fly and EC2 launch wrapper started the orchestrator the same
way, as `python3` with `cwd="/work"`, and Fly's subtree collection ran
its Python from inside `/work/.leerie/runs/<id>/repo`, below the same
version files.

**Invariant.** Inside leerie's root (the container, a Fly machine, an EC2
instance), leerie's own Python started from a directory a repository's
files reach is named by its path, `/usr/bin/python3`, the image's
interpreter. It is never found through PATH. What leerie starts from it as
`sys.executable` follows. A repository's commands keep resolving through
the shims, which is what lets them run the version the repository pins
(§6½).

**Mechanism.** `container-entry.sh` execs `/usr/bin/python3` for the
broker and for the orchestrator after the privilege drop. The launch
wrapper (`_render_launch_suffix`) starts the orchestrator as
`/usr/bin/python3`. `collect-subtrees.sh`'s machine payload runs its three
Python steps the same way, and `worktree-lib.sh`'s `leerie_repo_lock` takes
the worktree lock the same way: its callers run with a working directory
under the run's own repository, where a repository's version files would
otherwise choose the interpreter that holds leerie's lock. A static rule checks these sites, and every
subprocess or `exec` call in leerie's own Python, for an interpreter named
by a bare name (`tests/test_leerie_python_is_named.py`).

**Scope.** Measured at the same time in the same image, from a directory
holding `.python-version`, `.nvmrc` and `.tool-versions`: only `python3` and
`python` resolve to a shim. `node` and `claude` resolve to the baked LTS
Node's `bin`, which is ahead of the user shims on PATH. `git`, `bash`,
`env`, `unshare` and `runuser` resolve to `/usr/bin` or `/usr/sbin`. So the
names leerie starts bare there are not a repository's to choose today. A
reordering of PATH would make them so, and would have to name them by path
too. Commands the host sends to a machine with no working directory of
their own (`flyctl ssh console -C`, the EC2 session) start in the session's
own directory, not in `/work` (not measured on Fly), and are
unchanged.

### A worker's commands cannot reach its CLI

*Designed 2026-11-01 (review round 21, isolation R4).*

**Root cause.** What a worker ran is read from its own transcript (§8),
and the transcript is the CLI's stdout: a pipe to the orchestrator. The
CLI and every process it starts shared one uid and one Landlock domain, and
`/proc` is readable to every grant, so any command the worker runs — a
test file, a build script, code under measurement — could open
`/proc/<cli pid>/fd/1` (a ptrace-mode read: allowed within one domain, and
Yama does not restrict reads) and write stream-json into the pipe. The
round-12 and round-14 fixes attribute events by *file* (the registry); the
stream itself was reachable by the code the worker runs. Measured (review
round 21; again 2026-11-01 with the real CLI 2.1.312 in both local
runtimes, isolated): a Bash-tool command wrote a forged `tool_use` into
the stream, and it reached the transcript. The same route injects a
`result` event or a `session_id`, which steers the re-ask's resume.

**Invariant.** Nothing the worker's CLI starts on the worker's behalf runs
in the CLI's own Landlock domain: each command and hook runs in a domain
nested inside it, so no process the worker's code can be may open, attach
to or read the memory of the CLI, and the CLI's stream carries only the
CLI's events.

**Mechanism.** The CLI runs every Bash-tool command and every hook as
`$CLAUDE_CODE_SHELL_PREFIX <command>` (measured, CLI 2.1.312: the prefix is
the CLI's direct child for a Bash command, and run under `/bin/sh -c` for a
hook; it gets the command as one argument). Every confined worker's CLI is
given `scripts/worker-shell.py` there (`_invoke`; and in its settings,
below). It enters a Landlock domain nested in the worker's
(`landlock_exec.nest`) and `exec`s `bash -c <command>`. The nested ruleset
handles every right the worker's does and allows all of it beneath `/`, so
the command reaches exactly what the worker's grants allow — an access
passes only when every layer of the domain allows it. But Landlock refuses
a process ptrace-class access to any process outside its domain and its
nested ones: `/proc/<cli>/fd`, `/proc/<cli>/mem`, `ptrace`, `pidfd_getfd`.
No scope is set in the nested domain, so a command may still signal, or
connect to an abstract socket of, what an earlier command of the same
worker left running. It fails closed: when the domain cannot be made, the
command does not run (126). The shell is named absolutely with `-I -S`: it
runs in the CLI's domain until it nests, so nothing a worker can write (a
`python3` earlier on `PATH`, a `site` directory) runs there. Measured
2026-11-01, real CLI, rootless and rootful, isolated: without the prefix a
command opened the CLI's `fd/1` and a forged line reached the stream; with
it both were refused, and `git`, `node` and `pnpm` ran unchanged; about
40 ms more per command on the host.

*The CLI reads no settings file.* A settings file runs code in the CLI's
own domain: `apiKeyHelper` runs under `/bin/sh -c` without the prefix
(measured), and a settings `env` can unset the prefix. Every file the CLI
would read is one a worker can write — its own configuration directory's
`settings.json`, and its tree's `.claude/settings.json` and
`.claude/settings.local.json`, which reach every later worker in that tree
(the gap §6 *Each worker's own configuration and temporary directories*
left to the write grant). So a confined worker's CLI gets
`--setting-sources ""` and its whole settings in `--settings`
(`_confined_cli_settings`): the operator's settings from the run's
read-only configuration template, the checkout's project and local
settings that git does not track (no worker writes the checkout, and a
tracked one is the repository's, which adds nothing: §6 *A repository
chooses no operator authority*), then leerie's
own — the PreToolUse hook and the shell prefix, which nothing below them
overrides (settings given on the command line win over every file scope,
measured). Merged as the CLI merges scopes: objects key by key, arrays
concatenated. The Fly recovery integrator gets the same from
`worker-guard.py`. A layer below leerie's own contributes only what is
listed, and every other key of it is dropped: `permissions.deny` and
`permissions.ask`, which only narrow; and the operator's endpoint and
credentials, which an untracked settings file may choose (*The names an
untracked settings file may still set*). That list is three things the
CLI names, none of which widens a worker's tools: the endpoint (the
provider switches, the API's, Bedrock's, Vertex's and Foundry's base URLs,
Foundry's resource, and the skip-auth switches a gateway uses), the
credentials (the CLI's credential helpers `apiKeyHelper`,
`awsCredentialExport`, `awsAuthRefresh` and `gcpAuthRefresh`; the API key
and token; the headers a gateway authenticates by; `AWS_*`; Vertex's
project and regions; Foundry's key) and the model mapping (`ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_*_MODEL` and
`ANTHROPIC_SMALL_FAST_MODEL`, which say what the alias leerie passes
resolves to on that endpoint, where it can lag the API's by a
generation). Review round 31 found the first list short: it kept
`CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX` but not Vertex's project and region, so Vertex
from settings always failed; `apiKeyHelper` but not its Bedrock
siblings; and no model mapping, which IMPLEMENTATION §0.5 documents for
Bedrock. Review round 32 found it short again: it kept
`ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` but not `ANTHROPIC_CUSTOM_HEADERS`, so a gateway's
requests went out without the header that authenticates them; and it
kept no name of Foundry, a provider the CLI documents beside Bedrock and
Vertex. A name that holds a path on the operator's host (a client
certificate and key, a Google credentials file, a unix socket) stays
out: the path names nothing in the container. So does
`CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`: the subscription credential is the one leerie
seeds, and a settings layer does not replace it. So do the CLI's
provider switches that no documented setup sets: the list holds only
names a documented setup reads. A worker's tool scope is leerie's argv alone (§12 *L1*), and no other key
can be trusted not to widen it: a permission mode (`defaultMode:
bypassPermissions` approves every tool), an allow list,
`additionalDirectories` (the directories the CLI's tools may reach), a
hook (a PreToolUse hook that answers "allow" approves the call), an `env`
name the CLI reads. A list of what to drop would miss the next such key,
as the first one did (review round 30: it dropped `defaultMode` and
`allow` and passed `additionalDirectories` and the hooks through).
*Designed 2026-11-03 (the live 0.43.0 barnacle runs).*
The operator's own `settings.json` on the host carried `defaultMode:
bypassPermissions` and `allow: [Bash, Read, Edit, Write, …]`; merged into
every confined worker's settings, it put every judgment worker in
`bypassPermissions` (every transcript checked — the classifier, the three
planners, five satisfied-probe logs — reports it), so its `--allowedTools`
scope approved nothing it would not have approved anyway. A satisfied
probe, read-only by its tools, ran `npx vitest` over twelve test files in
its read-only tree; eleven failed on `mkdirSync`, which Landlock refused,
and it answered `cannot_verify`, settling a subtask `unconverged` whose
work a sibling had delivered.

**Residuals.** The CLI's own spawns that are not commands: its `git`
calls are on leerie's terms (§6 *The CLI's own git runs on leerie's
terms*; the earlier claim here that they "run no code a worker chose" was
false — review round 22 isolation H1); `rg` for Grep and Glob runs in its
domain and runs no code a worker chose through settings, which it no
longer reads. A worker's configuration directory is writable whole, so a worker can replace
its links to the template's `plugins/` with its own; a plugin is loaded only
when the operator's settings enable it, and then at the next start of that
configuration — the worker's own re-ask. Closing that needs the
configuration's code-bearing directories out of the worker's reach, which
this design does not do. A nested command can still signal the CLI, at
every Landlock ABI: `nest()` sets no scope, deliberately, so a later
command can still stop or reach what an earlier command of the same worker
left running (sibling nested domains would otherwise refuse each other),
and the worker's own signal scope (ABI 6 and later) admits every process of
its own domain, the CLI included. That is a stop, not a forgery, and it
breaks no isolation invariant: the CLI is the worker's own process, which
any process of the worker could already signal, and the missing nested
scope adds no reach beyond the worker's domain — what a worker can signal
outside it is the worker's scope alone (*A worker writes only where it is
granted (I5)*, Residuals), so no worker reaches another worker or leerie
through it.

### The CLI's own git runs on leerie's terms

*Designed 2026-11-01 (review round 22, isolation H1).*

**Root cause.** The nest (§6 *A worker's commands cannot reach its CLI*)
was aimed at the commands the CLI runs for the worker; the CLI also runs git
for itself, in its own domain. At the start of every session it runs
`status`, `log`, `ls-files`, `config` and `remote` in its working directory
(measured, CLI 2.1.312; it passes `core.hooksPath=/dev/null` and
`core.fsmonitor=` but not `filter.*`). git found the repository through the
tree's `.git` file, and a committing worker writes that file and its whole
tree repository. So an implementer pointed `.git` at a git dir of its own
with a clean filter and `info/attributes`, the next worker's CLI ran the
filter in its session-start `git status`, and the filter wrote a forged
`tool_use` into `/proc/<cli>/fd/1`: the transcript. Leerie's clean-tree
checker never follows that `.git` (§6 *Leerie's git never takes a tree's
repository from the tree*), so it read the tree clean. The same holds for
the Fly recovery integrator. The CLI strips `GIT_DIR` and `GIT_WORK_TREE`
and sets its own `GIT_CONFIG_*` for these calls (measured), so no
environment pin reaches them.

**Invariant.** Every git process that runs on a worker's tree outside that
worker's own nested command domain addresses the repository from leerie's
layout, never the tree's `.git`, and runs in a domain nested away from the
CLI; and every worker starts on its tree's repository with leerie's
settings and a `.git` that names it, so nothing a worker before it chose
there reaches it or its CLI.

**Mechanism.**

- *The CLI's `git`.* A confined worker's CLI finds git on its `PATH`, and
  `scripts/cli-bin/` (holding only `git`) is first there (`_cli_git_env`,
  set by `_invoke` for every spawn with a grant, and by `worker-guard.py`
  for the Fly integrator). A call from one of the worker's own commands —
  marked by `worker-shell.py`, so inside the nested domain — gets the real
  git untouched. Any other call is the CLI's own: `scripts/cli-git.py`
  enters a nested Landlock domain (`landlock_exec.nest`) and runs the real
  git with the arguments leerie's own git on that tree takes
  (`_tree_git_args`: `--git-dir` of the tree's administrative directory,
  found from the repository's side, `--work-tree` the tree, leerie's pins).
  The tree's `.git` is never followed, and a driver it does run (one the
  same worker defined in its own repository's settings during its session)
  cannot open the CLI's `/proc` entries. It fails closed (126). A ref-less
  clone's CLI reads the clone through leerie's git directory for it, which
  its grant now reads. Not `_git_view`'s copies of the outside settings:
  they are outside every worker's grant, and the settings they copy (system,
  global) are ones no worker writes.
- *No settings layer below leerie's steers it.* The CLI applies its
  settings' `env` over its process environment, so an operator's or a
  repository's `env.PATH` sent one of its git calls (`ls-files`) past
  `scripts/cli-bin` (review round 23, measured on the host; the other five
  had resolved git earlier). Every variable the confinement reads — `PATH`,
  `CLAUDE_CODE_SHELL_PREFIX`, `LEERIE_WORKER_COMMAND`, `LEERIE_CLI_GIT`,
  `LEERIE_REAL_GIT` — is set in leerie's own layer, the top one: no lower
  layer's `env` keeps any of them or any other `LEERIE_*` variable
  (`_confined_cli_settings`), and `_invoke` lays the worker's own values of
  them over the `env` of the settings it passes (`_pin_cli_settings`), the
  marker empty, so leerie's guarantee depends on no other layer.
- *Every start.* Before each confined worker starts, leerie puts back its
  settings over the tree's repository (`_restore_settings`) and the tree's
  `.git` file naming the administrative directory leerie's layout gives it
  (`_restore_git_pointer`; a `.git` directory or link in its place is
  removed first, nothing is written through a link) —
  `_ready_tree_for_worker`. A rewritten pointer is not a violation to type:
  it is made irrelevant. Leerie's own git never reads it, the CLI's own git
  never reads it, and the next worker starts with it put back. A worker's
  own git — in its commands, nested — follows its tree's `.git` as git
  does, so what it chooses there reaches only itself.

Measured 2026-11-01, real CLI 2.1.312 (haiku), confined like a worker, in
both local runtimes (rootless and rootful): with the tree's `.git` pointed at
a planted git dir with a clean filter, without the shim the filter ran in
the session-start `git status` and a forged line reached the stream (the
round's finding reproduced); with the shim and the pointer put back the
filter never ran, nothing was forged, the CLI's git answered from the
tree's repository, and the worker's own `git add`/`commit` landed on the
tree's branch. On the host, the shim alone with no addressing let the
filter run but refused its write to the CLI's `fd/1` (the nest), and the
shim with addressing ran nothing.

### Leerie's runs of the repository's commands are confined too (I5, measurements)

*Designed 2026-10-31 (review round 18, H1).*

**Root cause.** I5 confined the worker's session, but a worker's output
is code, and leerie runs that code whenever it measures or installs: the
repository's build, lint and test commands, its install recipe, the
held-out acceptance runs, CI parity, coverage, the settle-by-execution
`verify` commands, and leerie's own AST scripts, which load the tree's
`typescript`. Each ran as the orchestrator, with the orchestrator's
access to the run directory. So the confinement boundary stopped one step
short of the code the worker wrote: the project's `conftest.py`, a
`postinstall`, a `Makefile` target. A worker could get through leerie's
commands what I5 refuses its session.

**Invariant (I5, measurement kind): a command leerie runs on a
repository's code writes only beneath its measurement grant, and reads
nothing of the state root but that grant.** The kernel enforces it the
way it enforces a worker's: the command is started through the same shim
(`scripts/landlock_exec.py`) with the grants `_measurement_grants(st,
tree, kind)` derives. `_run_streaming`, through which every repository
command leerie runs is spawned (`_run_contained` included), takes
`grants` as a required keyword and has no unconfined path; the AST scripts
and `mise ls` are started through `_confined_argv` with the same grants.
Every input leerie hands such a command — a path in its argv — lies
inside its grant: a file leerie writes for the command to read (the
re-drive AST gate's base copy) is written in the tree's private temp
directory, never in leerie's own temp directory `<run-dir>/tmp/`, which no
grant reads — and written there without following a link (*Leerie never
writes through a path confined code shaped*).
`_run_streaming` and `_ts_script_run` check every absolute argv path that
exists against the grant before they spawn (`_argv_outside_grant`) and
stop the run (`die`) on one outside it: a command that cannot read its
own input fails as "could not measure", which the re-drive's gate (d+)
read as a void round — every escalated round on a JS/TS repository was
rolled back that way once leerie's temp files moved to `<run-dir>/tmp/`
(review round 20, execution H1).
Fail closed as for a worker: the invocation's entry has already required
Landlock (`_require_confinement`), and the shim refuses where it cannot
enforce, which stops the run, never a pass and never a measurement (*A
confinement failure stops the run; it is never a result*).

**The grant, by kind.** Every kind gets the first block.

| Grant | Path | Access |
|---|---|---|
| devices | as a worker's | write |
| the measured tree | the checkout the command runs in (a committed view, an evaluation tree, a helper checkout, a worker tree an install runs in) | write |
| its measurement directory | `<run-dir>/measure/<tree>-<id>/`: `mise-state/` (`MISE_STATE_DIR`), `state/` (`XDG_STATE_HOME`), `reports/` (the runner report of every run that is not held-out; a held-out run's report path is there inside its sandbox only), `coverage/` (the coverage detector's output) | write |
| its private temp directory | `/tmp/l/<id>/`, what `TMPDIR`, `TMP`, `TEMP` and `XDG_CACHE_HOME` name, its `run/` (`XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`, which holds sockets) and a new `gnupg-<random>/` per grant (`GNUPGHOME`) (*A confined command's scratch is short and private*), carried into its own `/tmp` | write |
| `/tmp`, `/dev/shm` | the command's own, made by the shim, every kind, every tree (*Every confined process has its own `/tmp`, `/dev/shm` and IPC*) | read and write |
| leerie's install, the home | `ROOT` (the AST scripts), `HOME` (unless it holds `/tmp`), named as a worker's are | read |
| the tree's git metadata | for a worktree of the run repository (a view, a helper checkout): `<run-dir>/repo/`; for a worktree of a tree repository: that repository and `<run-dir>/repo/objects/`; for a clone: `<run-dir>/repo/objects/` (its alternates) | read |
| the run's stores | `<run-dir>/worktrees/.stores/stores/` (`_leerie_stores`): every store variable's run-wide directory (*The stores a view installs from are leerie's*) | write |
| the tree's own stores | `<run-dir>/worktrees/.stores/tree-stores/<tree>/` (`_tree_store_env`: uv, cargo, bundler, NuGet, Go's build cache, pipenv, pnpm's metadata cache, pip's user base, the .NET CLI home, bundler's home), for a tree under `<run-dir>/worktrees/` | write |
| the run's mise overrides | `<run-dir>/mise-overrides.toml` | read |
| outside the state root | everything but `/tmp` and `/dev`, as a worker's | read |
| *setup-hook kind* | also `MISE_DATA_DIR` and `~/.local/bin` | write |
| *toolchain kind* (`mise install`, `mise ls`) | also `MISE_DATA_DIR`; `mise-state/` emptied first | write |
| *install kind* (every install leerie runs: a recipe's `install` entries, CI parity's prerequisites, `_install_settles`) | nothing more on disk; the outside network through the egress proxy (*A confined process has its own network*, *An install reaches its inputs*) | — |

Nothing else is granted: not `state.json`, `acceptance/`, `logs/`,
`workers/`, `repo-settings/`, another tree's repository in `tree-repos/`,
the run repository's refs for writing, a sibling tree, or another tree's
measurement directory. The git metadata is read-only because no
measurement needs more: in a confined view `git status`, `log`, `diff`,
`rev-parse`, `ls-files`, `stash list` and `describe` all succeed with the
run repository read-only, and `git status` skips its opportunistic index
refresh (measured 2026-10-31).

*An install that writes the repository's git config is refused, and says
so.* A repository whose root `prepare` is husky runs `git config
core.hooksPath .husky/_` on every install. git writes a worktree's local
config only to its common directory's `config`, here
`<run-dir>/repo/config`, which this grant reads and does not write. So
git reports `could not lock config file <run-dir>/repo/config: Read-only
file system`, husky returns without installing hooks, and the install
succeeds. Measured on barnacle 87580f62: the refusal appeared in all 31
installs in worktrees of the run repository (views, CI parity, the
baselines, the planning tree, the evaluation trees), and in none of the 25
in ref-less clones, whose `config` is the clone's own.

The refusal is this grant working, and the line is git's true report of
it. The run repository's settings are leerie's (§8 *The settings are
leerie's*): in a tree a command can write, leerie puts the same write
back after the command. No measured checkout commits, and leerie's own
git runs with hooks off (§6½ *Hooks off*). So the hooks husky would have
installed have no use there.

The install still runs every lifecycle script, `prepare` included, as
CI's install does. A `prepare` can build what the commit's commands need,
such as a `dist/` the tests import. Telling such a script from one that
only installs hooks would mean interpreting the repository's scripts.

Weighed and rejected:
- *A writable config scope of the checkout's own.* git has none for a
  worktree: a plain `git config` writes the common directory's `config`,
  whatever `extensions.worktreeConfig` says.
  - `GIT_CONFIG` redirects the write, but also every `git config` read.
    Measured on git 2.53.0: `git config --get user.name` returned nothing
    with a repository-local name set, and `git config --global` failed
    with "only one config file at a time". That changes what the measured
    commands see.
  - A repository per checkout (a ref-less clone, as the acceptance
    writer's) keeps the clone's own `.git` in the tree. A view moves to the
    next tip under leerie's git directory, so the measured commands' own
    `git` would read the old HEAD.
  - An overlay over the run repository is undefined while other trees
    commit to it.
- *Skipping `prepare`.* No package manager skips one lifecycle script
  alone. `--ignore-scripts` also skips the `postinstall` generators this
  install exists to run (§8 *Every measurement reads the committed view*).
  A `prepare` that builds would leave the measurement without its build.
- *`HUSKY=0`.* That is one tool's switch, an exemption keyed to the
  symptom. The next hook installer would print the same refusal.

A tree whose path holds or lies beneath one
of the run directory's private entries is no measured tree: the run stops
naming it (`die`), since granting it would grant them.

**The measurement directory belongs to one tree, for that tree's
lifetime.** It is named for the tree and for an id leerie writes into the
tree's git directory on first use (`leerie-measure-id`): a tree removed and
made again at the same path gets a new git directory, so a new id and a
fresh directory, and nothing a measurement left behind reaches the next
tree. The git directory is the one leerie's layout names
(`_run_tree_location`), and for a committing tree it is in the tree
repository its worker writes, so the id is an untrusted key: read and
written from the run directory down without following a link (*Leerie
never writes through a path confined code shaped*), and any value the
worker could leave names only one of that tree's own measurement
directories, or a fresh one. Nothing else that tree's id could hold is
leerie's: no other place keeps the tree's lifetime, since an inode number
is reused (on ext4 the freed one is the next given in its group). A directory whose tree is gone, or whose tree's id has changed, is
removed by the next measurement's sweep (moved aside at once, deleted in
the background). It is never shared between trees: one held-out
evaluation's tree is not another's, and no worker is granted any of them.
It lives under `<run-dir>/measure/`, outside `<run-dir>/repo/`, which
every non-committing worker reads. Leerie reads a report there after the
command exits, without following a link the command left; a held-out
run's report never lands there at all.

**The variables follow the grant.** The grant names its own environment:
`TMPDIR`, `TMP`, `TEMP` and `XDG_CACHE_HOME` point at the tree's private
temp directory and `MISE_STATE_DIR` at the measurement directory, laid
over the caller's environment last. The store
variables stay as `_leerie_stores` and `_tree_store_env` set them, each
where the grant writes.
A recipe entry's or a CI check's own variables still apply; a temp or cache
path they name outside the grant is refused, which is a finding, not a
grant to widen. A fixed `/tmp/<name>` path is not: every command writes
its own `/tmp` as it would outside leerie.

**The run's stores and the tree's.** The run's stores (`<run-dir>/worktrees/.stores/stores/`)
are written by every command leerie runs in the run and read by no other
run (*The stores a view installs from are leerie's*). The tree's own stores
are written by that tree's commands and read by no other tree; they follow
the measurement directory's lifetime: a tree made again at the same path
starts with them empty (`_measure_dir`). No worker is granted any of them.
A held-out evaluation's grant names the run's stores too, but inside its
sandbox every write grant is an overlay whose writes vanish with it (*A
held-out evaluation runs alone*), so nothing it writes there reaches a
later command.

**The setup hook is the user's code, run once before any worker.**
`.leerie-setup.sh` runs in phase 1½, in a throwaway checkout of the
planning commit (§6½ step 1), before any worker that commits exists: it is
the repository's own code as the user committed it, not a worker's. It is
confined with the setup-hook kind, whose extra writes are exactly what §6½
says a hook may do — install a language runtime with `mise`
(`MISE_DATA_DIR`) and a user-space tool into `~/.local/bin` — and nothing
of the state root but its checkout and its measurement directory. The
premise is checked, not assumed: `claude_p` records the first committing
worker's start (`committing_worker_started`), and a hook that has not run
yet when that is set stops the run instead of running.

**`mise install` runs the repository's code only from a configuration it
trusts.** Measured on the image (mise v2026.5.4): a trusted `mise.toml`
runs its `exec()` templates, its `_.source` scripts and a tool's
`postinstall`; an untrusted one makes mise refuse to run; `.tool-versions`
and the idiomatic version files run nothing. So it is confined with the
toolchain kind — it must write `MISE_DATA_DIR`, outside the state root —
and its `MISE_STATE_DIR`, where mise keeps its trust records, is emptied
first: whatever the hook trusted is gone, and mise trusts nothing by code,
not by what a shared `/tmp/.mise-state` happens to hold. `mise ls
--current --json` runs under the same grant.

**The re-drive's self-check** (`scripts/selfcheck.py`) is started by a
confined worker's shell and spawns the runner itself, so it runs inside
that worker's grants (*A worker writes only where it is granted*): no
second grant applies.

### Leerie's git never takes a tree's repository from the tree

**Root cause (review round 19 isolation H1).** Confined code writes its
whole tree: a measurement's install in a committed view, a worker in its
own tree, which for a committing worker includes its tree repository. The
tree's `.git` file is in the tree. Leerie's own git commands on the tree
run unconfined, and every one of them found its repository from the tree
(`git -C <tree>`, or a working directory), so they followed whatever that
`.git` file named and read that repository's configuration. The
configuration names programs git runs on its own, `core.fsmonitor` on every
index refresh among them, so leerie's own git would run what confined code
wrote, outside every grant. The command was confined; leerie's housekeeping
around it was its proxy.

**Invariant: leerie's own git commands never take a repository's location
or configuration from a path confined code can write.** Every leerie git
command on a tree goes through one helper (`_tree_git_args`, and
`leerie_tgit` in the scripts), which names the repository from leerie's
layout:

- A tree is in a run's `worktrees/`. It is a worktree of its tree
  repository, `<run-dir>/tree-repos/<name>` when that exists, and else of
  the run repository. Its git directory is the administrative directory
  of that repository whose `gitdir` record names the tree, found from the
  repository's side. The administrative directory's `commondir` must name
  that same repository, since a committing worker can write its own tree
  repository. A tree that the record names stays a worktree whatever its
  `.git` now is, a directory included. One no record names is a ref-less
  clone of the run repository, read through the git directory leerie made
  for it (below), never its own `.git`.
- The command is `git -C <tree> --git-dir <git dir> --work-tree <tree>`,
  so the tree's `.git` is never followed. It always carries leerie's
  pins: `core.fsmonitor` and `core.untrackedCache` off. The readers that
  need leerie's settings (`_git_view`, `leerie_vgit`) add them as before
  (§8 *The settings are leerie's*). The repository's own `config` and
  `info/` are put back before a read, which covers what a committing
  worker can write.
- A run tree that matches none of this is refused. git then fails, and
  the caller reads that as git unable to answer, never as clean.
- A tree outside every run (the user's checkout, a test's repository) is
  addressed `-C <tree>` with the pins: no confined code writes it.

Guards derived from the source hold every site to it: no leerie git argv
carries `-C` except in the helper, every git command run with a working
directory names its repository, and the scripts that source
`worktree-lib.sh` run git on a tree only through `leerie_tgit`.

*A ref-less clone is read through leerie's own git directory.* The
acceptance writer's, the surrogate fixer's and the falsifier's checkouts
are ref-less clones of the run repository, and a clone keeps its
repository in its own `.git`, inside the tree its confined worker writes —
config, hooks and attributes included. So when `_ref_less_clone` makes a
clone in a run's `worktrees/`, it also makes `<run>/clone-gits/<name>`
(`_make_clone_git_dir`): a git directory whose objects are the run
repository's (an `alternates` entry), whose HEAD is the clone's commit
detached, and whose index is that commit's tree. It is written by leerie
alone, before any worker runs there, in a directory no worker's grant
names. `_run_tree_location` and `leerie_tree_location` locate a ref-less
clone at it and never at the clone's `.git`; a clone without it is
refused. The worker's result — files it edited or added — is read as
before, as working-tree data against the clone's commit, and a commit the
worker makes in its own `.git` is not followed: what it changed is still
in the tree. Measured with a planted config in the clone's `.git` (an
fsmonitor, a clean and smudge filter, a filter process, a textconv, a hooks
path) and `* filter=x diff=x` attributes: reading the clone's own `.git`,
leerie's `git status` ran the planted filter program; through leerie's git
directory it saw the worker's edit and ran nothing. Of the two candidates —
fetching the clone's result into the run repository, or running leerie's
reads confined — this one needs neither a commit from the worker nor trust
in what a confined program reports, and it is the same rule every other
tree follows: the repository is located from leerie's layout. The setup
commands of `_ref_less_clone` itself name the clone's `.git` explicitly,
which is still leerie's until a worker runs.

### Leerie never writes through a path confined code shaped

*Designed 2026-11-01 (review round 21, isolation R1 and R5).*

**Root cause.** Confined code writes more than its own files: every
directory on the way to them inside its grant. A committing worker writes
its tree and its tree repository whole; a measurement writes the tree and
its measurement directory. Leerie's housekeeping around them — restoring a
tree, putting a repository's settings back, keeping a tree's measurement
id, placing a set or a task's report in a checkout, writing a held-out
run's report back to disk — runs unconfined, and it addressed those
directories by path, so the kernel resolved every link confined code had
left there on leerie's behalf. Round 19 found this for git (*Leerie's git
never takes a tree's repository from the tree*); round 21 found it for
leerie's own writes:

- *R1.* A held-out run's report came back through the sandbox's
  descriptor, and `_run_streaming` then wrote it to the path the runner
  had used, in the tree's `reports/`. An ordinary measurement of the same
  view, which runs the worker's code with that directory in its grant, had
  replaced `reports/` with a link to an implementer's tree; the evaluated
  code had copied the placed set into its report. Leerie's write put the
  set's text in the implementer's tree. The descriptor protected the bytes
  in transit, not the place they landed.
- *R5.* `_measure_dir_at` rewrote the tree's `leerie-measure-id` with a
  plain write, and `_restore_settings` copied the settings to a fixed temp
  name in the tree repository before renaming it. A committing worker
  planted a link at either name; leerie's next write went through it, over
  `state.json` and a held-out set, which the worker's own grant refuses.

The class is "leerie, unconfined, resolves a path through a directory
confined code can write", and a check of each site's target would only
find the next one.

**Invariant: an unconfined write leerie makes lands at the path it names,
or nowhere.** It is constructed in three parts.

1. *Leerie's own records live outside every grant.* A held-out run's
   report is parsed from the descriptor's bytes and never put on disk
   (`_run_streaming(report_into=)`; the parse probe's marker and the AST
   facts likewise); the minitest reporter is part of leerie's install
   (`MINITEST_REPORT_LIB`), read by every confined command and written by
   none; the integrator rescue's throwaway index is in leerie's temp
   directory, not the tree's git directory. The one record that must stay
   with a tree — its measurement id, which has to share the tree's
   lifetime — is an untrusted key (*Leerie's runs of the repository's
   commands are confined too*).
2. *Every write into a directory confined code can write is made from an
   anchor down, never through a link.* The anchor is a directory no
   confined process can replace: the run directory, or a grant's own root
   (its entry lies in a directory no grant names, and Landlock grants what
   is beneath a path, not the path's entry in its parent). From there each
   component is opened `O_DIRECTORY|O_NOFOLLOW` (`_open_dir_beneath`); a
   file is made `O_CREAT|O_EXCL|O_NOFOLLOW` at a fresh name in that
   directory's descriptor and renamed over the destination
   (`_write_beneath`), so a link at the destination is replaced, never
   written through, and a link on the way refuses the write. Reads of what
   confined code wrote take the same walk and refuse a link or a FIFO
   (`_read_beneath`); removals and chmods likewise (`_unlink_beneath`,
   `_remove_beneath`, `_add_dir_bits_beneath`, which reaches each directory
   through an `O_PATH` descriptor). A directory of leerie's own layout
   found as a link or a file — a measurement's `reports/`, a tree's stores —
   is removed and made a directory (`_mkdir_private`).
3. *A checkout of committed code is confined code's too.* A set's files, a
   task's report, a falsifier's leads and the planning worktree's extras
   are copied into checkouts whose content a worker committed, links
   included: a committed `tests -> ../wt-a/tests` would carry a set into a
   fixer's tree. Every such copy goes through the same walk, and a path a
   link stands on is a taken path.

A rule over the module holds the line: every function that still calls a
raw write primitive is classified, by why its target is out of every
confined process's reach (leerie's own state, logs and run repository; a
grant's root itself; the host side; code that runs inside a worker's own
confinement), and the functions that write where confined code writes use
none (`tests/test_leerie_writes_never_follow_links.py`). Git's own writes
into a tree are git's, which refuses a path beyond a link; leerie names
the repository for it (*Leerie's git never takes a tree's repository from
the tree*).

### Leerie never reads through a link a repository holds

*Designed 2026-11-02 (review round 26, isolation I1).*

**Root cause.** The section above closed leerie's *writes* through paths
confined code shaped, and its reads of what confined code *wrote*. It left
the reads of what a repository *holds*. The orchestrator is unconfined: its
environment carries `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`, and it can read the CLI's
credentials and the state root with every held-out set. It read many of a
repository's files by path, so the kernel followed every link the
repository held. The most direct case was the PR template.
`_compose_pr_via_llm` read `.github/pull_request_template.md` from `/work`
(`is_file()`, `read_text()`), and `pr_writer` is told to fill the template
into the PR body, which `gh pr create` publishes. A repository whose
template is a committed link to `/proc/self/environ` or to
`~/.claude/.credentials.json` therefore published the token. The
repository did not need to know anything about the run. Its content is a
worker's to shape:

- a cloned third-party repository;
- a merged run branch;
- a worker's own tree or tree repository;
- the output of a measurement.

The same class reached:

- the configuration (`leerie.toml`, `.leerie/config.toml`);
- the manifests, README, workflows and contributing guide handed to the
  provision and dependency-capture workers;
- the CI files a `ci_checks` provenance check quotes;
- the version files mise is pinned from;
- the files the task names, and a task file itself;
- the repository's `.claude` settings applied to every worker;
- a worker-named checkpoint path;
- a coverage summary a measurement wrote;
- a tree repository's worktree records. Unlike the rest, these could hold
  a FIFO, which made the orchestrator's read block for good.

**Invariant: what leerie reads as a repository's content is that
repository's content, never what a link in it points at.** It is
constructed in three parts.

1. *What leerie publishes from the commit the run planned against is a git
   blob.* The PR template is read from the run's own repository at
   `base_sha` (`git ls-tree`, then `git cat-file blob`; `_find_pr_template`),
   never from the checkout. The read matches the committed view the run
   planned against, so an uncommitted edit in the checkout is not
   published either. A template committed as a link (mode 120000) is a blob
   holding a path. It is not a template, and it is skipped.
2. *Every other read of a repository's files by path walks from the
   repository's root without following a link.* The roots are `/work`, a
   worker's tree, a tree repository, a measurement's tree, and a subtask's
   notes directory. Each read uses the same walk as part 2 above
   (`_read_beneath`, `_read_text_beneath`, `_regular_file_beneath`), and a
   link at the file or on the way to it reads as absent. A FIFO is refused,
   never waited on. A listing keeps only entries it reached without a link
   (`_glob_beneath`, `_listdir_beneath`, `_dir_beneath_exists`;
   `os.walk` without `followlinks`). A checkpoint is read only beneath the
   subtask's own notes directory, whatever path the worker names. A task
   file in the checkout is read beneath it. One the operator names outside
   it is theirs. A probe that only tests whether a file exists, to choose
   between leerie's own commands, reads no content and is not covered.
3. *The host reads the checkout the same way.* The launcher refuses to
   start when `leerie.toml`, `.leerie`, `.leerie/config.toml`,
   `.leerie/Dockerfile`, `.claude`, `.claude/settings.json` or
   `.claude/settings.local.json` is a link (`_checkout_config_links`). It
   reads and writes the checkout's files only at those paths (the two
   settings files, when git does not track them, decide Bedrock mode and its
   AWS profile, §6 *A repository chooses no operator authority*; a linked one
   outside the checkout switched a run into Bedrock mode, review round 27,
   execution L2), and the checkout is not written while leerie runs, so one
   check holds for every read after it. Its other looks at the checkout only
   test whether a file exists, to choose between leerie's own commands.
   The operator's `config --apply-capture` rewrites `.leerie/config.toml`
   through `_write_beneath`, so a link there is replaced, never read or
   written through. The Dockerfile generator reads the committed tree from
   git (`git ls-tree`, `git cat-file`, bounded), never the checkout's paths:
   a linked `.npmrc` is a link, which is no input (review round 28,
   isolation A2: it was hashed and named in a `COPY`, and one linked to
   `/proc/self/pagemap` stopped every launch). It reads the operator's
   `.leerie/config.toml` beneath the checkout without following a link,
   bounded. `.leerie/Dockerfile` is read once per image, beneath the
   checkout, bounded (`_repo_image_dockerfile`), and an image is keyed on
   the digest of the bytes that read returned, never on a second read by
   path (review round 29, isolation F4).

A rule over the module holds the line. Every function that still calls a
raw read primitive is classified by why what it reads is not a repository's
content reached through a path the repository shapes:

- leerie's install;
- the run directory and the state root;
- leerie's own copies of the held-out sets, made through `_read_beneath`;
- the kernel's files;
- a file the operator named;
- a listing that follows no link.

The functions that read a repository's content use no raw primitive, and
decide what to read with no probe that follows a link
(`tests/test_leerie_reads_never_follow_links.py`).

**No read is unbounded.** The orchestrator is unconfined. A worker can make a
sparse file of a terabyte at no disk cost (`truncate -s 1T`) in its tree, its
notes or a measurement's output. A read of the whole file then cost the
orchestrator that much memory: `MemoryError` past RAM and swap, which no caller
caught, and below that the container's OOM killer (review round 27, isolation
I3). Every read of a repository's file states its limit. The descriptor's size
is checked after the open, and a file over the limit is refused like a link
(`OSError` `EFBIG`). The read takes at most one byte more than the limit, so a
file that grows after the check is refused too. A caller that uses only the
start of a file reads only that much (`_read_head_beneath`). The limits are
named, by what the file is: configuration, text read whole, and a measurement's
report or a copy of the operator's files.

### No host path comes from a repository

*Designed 2026-11-02 (review round 27, isolation I6).*

**Root cause.** `leerie.toml` is repository content (the section above): a
cloned repository's, or a run branch's that the operator merged, since a
worker may commit a root `leerie.toml`. Five of its keys named a location on
the host or in the run directory, below only the operator's flag and
environment. `log_file = "~/.bashrc"` made the launcher create that file and
append the whole run's output to it, and that output carries worker text
verbatim (a judge's `concrete_case`, a blocker's reason), with its newlines.
The operator's next shell would run it. `state_dir = ".lstate"` put the state
root inside the checkout. In the container that one directory is then both
`/leerie-state` and `/work/.lstate`. Every grant is carved by path, and `/work`
does not contain `/leerie-state`, so every worker's read of `/work` reached
the held-out sets, every other worker's notes and the copies of the
credentials. `inspect_dirs` chose a host directory to mount into the container,
or on Fly and EC2 to copy to the machine. `judge_dir` and `heal_dir`, joined to
the run directory, could name any path the orchestrator can write. "Always
outside the target repo" was written down and never checked.

**Invariant: no host path comes from a repository's content, and the state
root is never at, inside or above the checkout.** It is constructed in three
parts.

1. *A location comes only from the operator.* `state_dir`, `log_file`,
   `inspect_dirs`, `judge_dir` and `heal_dir` have no `leerie.toml` key. They
   come from a flag or the environment (`--state-dir` / `LEERIE_STATE_DIR`,
   `--log-file` / `LEERIE_LOG_FILE`, `--inspect-dir` / `LEERIE_INSPECT_DIRS`,
   `--judge-dir` / `LEERIE_JUDGE_DIR`, `--heal-dir` / `LEERIE_HEAL_DIR`). A
   `leerie.toml` that still sets one stops the launcher before anything else
   reads it, and the message names the key's operator-side replacement: a
   key silently ignored would move a run's state away from where its
   operator looks for it. The orchestrator reads none of them from the file,
   and its one reader of `leerie.toml` refuses those names
   (`REPO_CONFIG_LOCATION_KEYS`). The section below extends this to every
   setting that carries the operator's authority.
2. *The launcher refuses a state root that overlaps the checkout.* It compares
   the two by real path, after every tier is resolved. A state root equal to
   the checkout, beneath it or above it stops the run. Beneath, the checkout's
   mount shows the state root to every worker. Above, the state root's mount
   holds the checkout writable.
3. *The orchestrator refuses a state root reachable by a second name.* Inside
   the container the two are separate mounts, and the launcher's check is the
   only one that sees the host's paths. So the entry every invocation runs
   (`_require_confinement`) resolves each of the two paths to its place on
   disk: the device and the path within the filesystem that
   `/proc/self/mountinfo` gives for the mount holding it. When one lies
   at or beneath the other on disk, but not by path, the state root has a
   second name that no grant carves out, and the run stops. A state root
   nested in the checkout by path as well (the direct-call default,
   `<repo>/.leerie`, which only tests use) is carved out of every grant by
   path, as before.

### A repository chooses no operator authority

*Designed 2026-11-02 (generalizes *No host path comes from a repository*).*

**Root cause.** The section above closed one class of a wider one. Everything
in the checkout that git tracks is repository content: a cloned repository's,
or a run branch's that the operator merged. A worker may commit a root
`leerie.toml`, and leerie's own run branch is the operator's next base. A
host path was one kind of choice that content made below only the operator's
flag and environment. The others were the operator's authority too:

- *credentials and identity.* `aws_profile` and `aws_region` chose the AWS
  account and region leerie provisions in. `ec2_instance_profile` chose the
  IAM identity the machine runs as. `ec2_key_name`, `ec2_security_group` and
  `ec2_subnet_id` chose who can reach the machine that holds the run's
  copied credentials, and from where. `ec2_ami` chose the system those
  credentials are copied onto. `runtime` chose whether the code and the
  credentials leave the host at all. The checkout's `.claude/settings.json`
  and `.claude/settings.local.json` chose Bedrock mode, which stages
  `~/.aws` into the container, and its AWS profile and region; and each
  reached every confined worker's CLI as a settings layer, where an `env`
  `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` sends the operator's token to another endpoint and an
  `apiKeyHelper` or a hook runs in the CLI's own domain.
- *spending.* `ec2_instance_type` and `fly_disk_gb` size a resource billed to
  the operator's cloud account, outside the run. A model, an effort, a
  worker budget or a round count is different: it is how much of the run's
  own work the repository asks for, the operator overrides each per run, and
  the budget preflight bounds it.
- *waivers.* `dangerously_skip_permissions`, `dangerously_allow_uncapped` and
  `dangerously_force_strict_output` each waive a guarantee by name. Each gate
  key (`skip_overlap_judge`, `skip_budget_check`, `skip_satisfied_check`,
  `skip_base_baseline`, `skip_acceptance_check`, `skip_adherence_check`,
  `skip_coverage_check`, `skip_completeness_check`, `skip_integration_check`,
  `skip_classification_check`) switches off a check of the result: a run
  branch that wrote `skip_acceptance_check = true` turned off the held-out
  gate for every later run once merged. `worker_pids_max` and
  `worker_memory_max` are each worker's containment ceilings: no ceiling above
  bounds a worker's PIDs, so raising `worker_pids_max` took the fork-bomb
  bound away.

**Invariant: a repository's content chooses no operator authority.** A host
path, a credential or profile, where worker code runs and as whom, a resource
billed to the operator, a waiver of a guarantee and a worker's containment
ceiling come only from the operator: a flag, the environment, or the
operator's own Claude settings (`~/.claude/settings.json`, and an untracked
settings file in the checkout). Leerie has no user-level configuration file
of its own. It is constructed in two parts.

1. *`leerie.toml` has no key for any of them.* One list,
   `REPO_CONFIG_OPERATOR_KEYS`, holds the five locations above
   (`REPO_CONFIG_LOCATION_KEYS`) and the authority keys
   (`REPO_CONFIG_AUTHORITY_KEYS`), each with its flag and environment
   variable. The launcher holds the same list in the same order
   (`_checkout_config_operator_keys`). It stops on a `leerie.toml` that sets
   any of them, for every verb but `version`, before anything else reads the
   file, and names each key's replacement: a key silently ignored would run
   the operator's next run with a choice they did not make, or without one
   they believe is set. The orchestrator's one reader of the file
   (`_read_toml_key`) refuses every listed name, and no resolver of one has a
   file tier. `.leerie/config.toml` is read only for repository facts, so a
   listed name there is never read.
2. *A tracked settings file is the repository's.* Round 24 layered the
   checkout's settings files into every confined worker's settings, as the
   operator's input, because no worker writes the checkout while leerie
   runs. That holds for the run, not for what the operator merges after it,
   or clones. So the boundary is git's: a checkout settings file that git
   tracks (in the checkout's index) is repository content, and leerie reads
   nothing from it. It is not a worker's settings layer
   (`_checkout_settings_are_operators`) and does not choose Bedrock mode or
   its profile and region (the launcher's `_OPERATOR_CLAUDE_SETTINGS`). No
   merge or clone brings an untracked file, so an untracked one
   (`.claude/settings.local.json`, usually ignored) is the operator's own and
   is read as before. When git cannot answer, the file counts as tracked.
   This is not a refusal, unlike `leerie.toml`: the same file configures the
   repository's own interactive Claude Code users, so refusing would make the
   operator edit shared content to run at all, while leaving it out can only
   fall back to the operator's own credentials. Leerie says what it left
   out: the launcher warns when a tracked file sets
   `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK`, `AWS_PROFILE` or `AWS_REGION`, and the
   orchestrator logs each tracked file it does not apply.
   *Tracked* is a fact about the file leerie reads, not about the name it
   asked for (§6 *A path is the file it names, not its spelling*).
   *Untracked* means no repository holds the file, not only the
   checkout's own index: a submodule's files are in no superproject index
   entry of their own (`.claude` as a submodule is one gitlink entry,
   `.claude`), so a check of the file's own entry read a cloned
   submodule's `.claude/settings.json` as the operator's, and its
   `apiKeyHelper` and `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` reached every worker (review
   round 31, S1; `git clone --recurse-submodules` is all it takes). So a
   checkout file is the operator's only when no index entry is the file or
   any directory above it in the checkout, and no directory above it in the
   checkout holds a `.git` (a submodule, or any repository nested there).
   Every decision that a checkout file is the operator's because git does
   not track it applies this one rule (`_checkout_file_tracked`; the
   launcher's `_checkout_file_tracked`): the settings files above, a report
   the task points at (§8 *A task that points at a report is bounded by the
   report's own scenarios*), and the launcher's test of a
   `.leerie/Dockerfile` that carries leerie's generated mark, which refuses
   a committed one (§6½ *A generated Dockerfile is leerie's output, never
   the repository's*).

**The names an untracked settings file may still set.** Round 28 suggested a
further list of names no checkout settings layer may set, tracked or not:
`ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`, `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`,
`apiKeyHelper`, `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK` and `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX`, and
`AWS_*`. Leerie does not refuse them in an untracked file. The boundary is
who wrote the file. The only writers of an untracked checkout file are the
operator and programs the operator ran on the host with their own
authority, and such a program could write `~/.claude/settings.json` just as
easily. Repository content reached that layer only by being misjudged as
untracked, and the identity rule closes that. A refusal would therefore stop
no writer that the operator's own domain does not already hold. It would
also take away a documented operator channel: Bedrock mode from an
untracked `.claude/settings.local.json`. The same holds for every name the
keep-list carries (*The CLI reads no settings file*: endpoint, credentials
and model mapping), and for each the tracked file sets nothing.

**What a repository still chooses.** Facts about itself and how much work it
asks for, all of which run confined or only tighten a check:
`.leerie/config.toml`'s `build`, `lint`, `test`, the scoped runners,
`test_file_globs`, `capture_deps`; the tool versions mise honours
(`.mise.toml`, `.tool-versions`), installed by a confined command; and in
`leerie.toml` the source-of-truth, clarify, model and effort keys, the round
and budget caps, `max_parallel` (bounded by the per-worker ceilings and the
admission gate), the worker and rate-limit timeouts, verbosity, `no_push`
(it can only withhold a push), `pr_template`, `pr_base_branch`,
`strict_conformer`, `stop_on_blocked`, `stop_on_repo_change` (each only
tightens), `subtask_tests` (the final tree is measured whatever it says),
`skip_repo_map` (context, not a check), the heal and judge tuning, the seed
knobs and `bake_language_deps`. The operator's flag or environment overrides
each.

**Residual.** `.leerie/Dockerfile`, `setup_packages`, `language_installs` and
a dependency lockfile build the image the run's container starts from, and
that build is not confined: its steps run as root in the image, and the
image holds the orchestrator itself. A repository's content therefore still
shapes the orchestrator's own environment. This design does not close that.

### A path is the file it names, not its spelling

*Designed 2026-11-02 (review round 28, isolation A1).*

**Root cause.** Leerie decided things about a path by comparing its
spelling, but the filesystem resolves a path by its own rules. A
case-insensitive filesystem (APFS by default, so every checkout and state
root on macOS and Colima) treats `.Claude/Settings.json` and
`.claude/settings.json` as one file. A normalization-insensitive one treats
the NFC and NFD spellings of a name as one file, and HFS+ and APFS also
ignore some invisible code points. Two decisions broke on this:

- *Tracked or not.* `git ls-files -- .claude/settings.json` matches
  spellings, case-sensitively. A repository that tracked
  `.claude/Settings.json` was reported as tracking nothing, so the read of
  `.claude/settings.json` (which opens the tracked file) counted as the
  operator's own. Its `env` then went into every confined worker's
  settings, and an `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` there sent the operator's token to
  the repository's endpoint. The launcher's Bedrock reads had the same
  flaw.
- *Protected or not.* `_is_protected_path` compared prefixes
  case-sensitively, so a worker could commit `.Claude/settings.json` or
  `.Leerie/Dockerfile`. On a case-insensitive checkout, both are the
  protected files once merged.

**Invariant: a decision about a path a repository or a worker can spell is
made about the file the filesystem resolves it to.** It is built in three
parts.

1. *Tracked is decided by identity.* Leerie opens the checkout's settings
   file without following a link (§6 *Leerie never reads through a link a
   repository holds*) and `fstat`s the descriptor. It then lists the index
   (`git ls-files -z`, no pathspec), and `lstat`s each entry whose top
   directory is the top directory it opened on the way (same device and
   inode). If any of those entries is the same file, or the same directory
   as one above it (a submodule's gitlink, §6 *A repository chooses no
   operator authority*), the file is tracked. This covers case, Unicode normalisation and ignorable code
   points without leerie knowing any filesystem's folding rules. When git
   cannot answer, or the file is reached through a link or is not a regular
   file, it is not read as the operator's. The orchestrator
   (`_checkout_file_tracked`) and the launcher
   (`_checkout_file_tracked`) apply the same test.
2. *A protected path is compared folded.* Before the prefix test, a path is
   normalised lexically and then folded: the code points HFS+ ignores are
   removed (the same list git uses for `.git`), then the path is
   NFKC-normalised, casefolded and NFKC-normalised again. A folded key
   equates at least the spellings any of those filesystems equates, so over
   them the test can only protect more. Every path list the test reads from
   git is read NUL-separated (`-z`), because git quotes a name holding a
   byte outside ASCII and the quoted form never matched a prefix.
3. *No worker's diff adds a second spelling of a path.* A subtask whose
   diff touches a path that, folded, equals a different path or directory
   already in its tree is refused like a protected path
   (`check_diff_scope`). On a case-insensitive filesystem the two names are
   one file. Whichever is checked out last wins, so a worker could replace
   a file it may not touch, such as a test the orchestrator owns, through
   a name it may touch. A collision the tree already had before the subtask
   is not the subtask's, and is not reported.

**Decisions that need no change.** Each was checked against the same
question.

- The Landlock grants are resolved by the kernel to inodes.
- The checkout deny rules (`Edit(//work/**)`) match a container mount point
  on Linux, and `/work` is mounted read-only anyway.
- The held-out sets live outside every tree.
- The launcher's test for `.leerie/Dockerfile` reads repository content as
  repository content: a worker can no longer commit a folded spelling of it
  (part 2), and what a repository's Dockerfile can do is the residual of
  *A repository chooses no operator authority* above.
- `check_integrator_commit` uses the folded test of part 2 and reads its
  list with `-z`.

### A confined command's scratch is short and private

*Designed 2026-11-01 (review round 19, execution H1).*

**Root cause.** The measurement grant put a confined command's scratch
space where leerie keeps its state — `TMPDIR` and `XDG_CACHE_HOME` deep in
the run directory (`/leerie-state/runs/<64 hex>/measure/<tree>-<id>/tmp`,
138 to 166 characters in the container) — instead of where scratch space
must be: at a short path, private to its user all the way up. Nothing ran a
real repository's test suite under the grant before it shipped. Measured
on barnacle: tsx binds its IPC socket in `os.tmpdir()`, and a Unix socket
path holds at most 107 bytes, so 495 tests in 356 files failed confined
against 1 unconfined. Measured on funeralworks: Next's SWC refuses a cache
root with an ancestor writable by another user and not sticky, and the
state root is 775 under the host's umask (`~/.leerie`), so `next build`
died in 6 s.

**Invariant: a confined command's temp directory is short, and readable
and writable by its user alone on its whole path.** Each measured tree has
one, `/tmp/l/<id>/` (`PRIVATE_TMP_ROOT`, `_private_tmp`; `<id>` is 16 hex
digits of the hash of its measurement directory's path, so its length
never depends on the run's id or the tree's name): 23 characters, so tsx's
`<dir>/tsx-<uid>/<pid>.pipe` fits with room to spare. `/tmp/l` and each
directory in it are made 0700 and must be this user's directories, not
links — anything else stops the run, since a command whose scratch it is
could be read or planted (`_own_private_dir`). The shim carries it into
the command's own `/tmp`, sticky, under a root the caller owns (§6 *Every
confined process has its own `/tmp`*), which SWC's check accepts. `TMPDIR`, `TMP`, `TEMP`
and `XDG_CACHE_HOME` all name it; `MISE_STATE_DIR` stays in the
measurement directory, which no tool inspects for ownership. It lives as
long as its tree: the sidecar of the tree's measurement directory names it,
and the sweep that removes the measurement directory removes it too, as
does the release of the run's scratch when its process exits or execs
(`_release_run_dir`, §6 *No copy of the credentials outlives its run's
process*); a directory with no run removes itself at its process's exit.
Every removal is the owner-aware one (`_rmtree_owned`). Every directory leerie makes for a
measurement or a worker — the measurement directory and its subdirectories,
a tree's own stores, a worker's configuration and temp directory, the
workers' caches, a worker's notes — is made 0700 (`_mkdir_private`).

Measured 2026-11-01 on the user's two repositories, each command through
leerie's measured path (`_measured_tree` and `_measure_axes` on staging's
committed view), then the same command unconfined in the same view:
barnacle's `pnpm test` failed 1 test file of 1,298 confined (1 test of
7,172: the repository's own site-vocabulary guard) against 2 unconfined
(that guard, and a 6 s wall-clock bound a loaded host missed); its build
and lint passed both ways. funeralworks' configured `test`
(`./scripts/leerie-test-db.sh pnpm run test`: a postgres started with
`-k /tmp`, its lock at a fixed `/tmp` path, tsx in `pretest`) passed all
1,287 files and 13,036 tests both ways, and `next build` compiled both
ways with no SWC cache refusal.

**A confined command has a gpg home of its own.** *Designed 2026-11-04
(barnacle's Node floor raised to 22.19.0).* mise verifies a Node download
with gpg, importing Node's release keys into gpg's home first. Confined as
the toolchain kind, `mise install` could write `MISE_DATA_DIR` and its temp
directory, but gpg's home defaulted to `~/.gnupg`, which no grant writes,
so every Node version not yet installed died in provisioning: "gpg: no
writable keyring found", "Failed to install core:node@22.19.0". The defect
was there since confinement came in and showed only when a run needed a
