overloaded (the die-path stamp is still needed for discovery) and every
consumer that treats a run as *terminal* instead cross-checks wave
completion against `state.json`. Three gates enforce this:

1. `_derive_run_status` returns `incomplete` (not `done`) when
   `finished_at` is set but `completed_waves < len(waves)` and the run is
   neither killed nor paused.
2. `phase_finalize`'s entry `die()`s rather than writing the real
   `finished_at` when `completed_waves < len(waves)` (a defensive guard —
   the normal wave loop only reaches finalize after all waves integrate).
3. **`host_finalize` (the load-bearing gate) refuses the push+PR** when
   `state.json` shows `completed_waves < len(waves)` and not
   `no_work_required`. All three host-side push paths — the launcher's
   auto-finalize block, `leerie finalize <id>`, and Fly's
   `decide_teardown` — funnel through `host_finalize`, so this one gate
   covers them all. It fails open when `state.json` is absent.

A genuine completion is unaffected: by the time `phase_finalize` and
`host_finalize` run, `completed_waves == len(waves)`.

**A run that died says so.** `leerie list` showed a run that `die()`d
before its waves existed or after they all integrated as `done`: the
die-path stamp of `finished_at` was the only record, and it reads the
same as a completion (review round 22, a preflight death and a held-out
set's death both listed `done`). A run that died of a worker error or an
unhandled exception stamped nothing and listed `in-progress`. The root
cause is that nothing recorded the death itself; the invariant is that
**a run whose last invocation died is listed as died** — an
invocation that continued the run, not one that found nothing to do. The record,
`run.json`'s `failed_at`, has one owner, and it sees every exit of the
invocation: it wraps the whole of `main()` and is armed where the run's
`State` is acquired and its layout accepted, so a death from any
statement after that — the confinement entry, a resolver or
`_orchestrate` itself — is recorded. A
first version gave the record to the exit arms around `_orchestrate`;
a `die()` before their `try:`, the confinement entry's included, then
recorded nothing and the run listed `in-progress`, which a bare `resume`
auto-picks (review round 23). A death is a `die()` at any exit code but
0 and the deferred clarification's, or any other exception but the
operator's interrupt; `main()` returns a pause's, an interrupt's or a
completion's exit code rather than raising it, so a pause, an interrupt
and a clarification wait record nothing — they are not deaths. A
`--phase` verb analyses a run and never continues it, so it is not
armed. Nor is a `resume` of a run that has nothing left to do (it
completed: finalized, or no work was required — the test the resume
itself uses to answer "nothing to resume"). An invocation's death is a
fact about the invocation; the run's status is a fact about the run, and
an invocation that has nothing to continue owns no part of it. Armed
anyway, a no-op resume that died in a resolver (`--worker-memory-max
bogus`) relabelled a finished run `failed`, and the next no-op resume
relabelled it `done` (review round 24, L1). So **a run that completed
stays listed as it completed**, whatever later invocations of it do.
Each armed invocation clears the previous one's `failed_at` as it is
armed, so a run resumed to completion is not listed `failed`. `leerie list` shows such a
run `failed`, or `incomplete` when it died mid-wave (the more specific
status, which a bare `resume` still picks); a `failed` run is resumed by
id, not auto-picked, because a death's message names a fix the operator
owes first.

**Recovery when the orchestrator dies before `finished_at`.** An
uncontrolled exit (SIGKILL, OOM, power loss, or any crash bypassing the
`except SystemExit` handler) before `phase_finalize` leaves a run
`fetch-branch.sh` cannot discover (its predicate requires `finished_at`
set + `pushed_at` unset). `leerie finalize <run-id>` SSHes into the
machine, verifies the orchestrator process is dead (via `orchestrator.pid`
and `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`), patches `finished_at` into `run.json` with
audit fields `recovered_at` and `recovered_via="force-finalize"`, and
falls through to the normal finalize flow. If the orchestrator is still
alive, the non-force path refuses with a message naming the live pid and
suggesting `--force`.

**Subtree collection.** When the orchestrator dies mid-wave, subtask
branches (`leerie/subtasks/<run-id>/<sid>`) may hold committed work never
integrated into the run branch. `finalize` detects un-integrated subtask
branches, runs `setup-run.sh` to ensure the staging worktree exists, and
merges each via `integrate.sh` — conflicts resolved by spawning a
`claude -p` integrator worker (same prompt, schema, and verification as
`integrate_wave()`). Branches the integrator cannot resolve are skipped
and reported. Each branch starts on a clean staging and leaves one: a
skipped branch — no integrator, a crash, a verdict other than `resolved`,
or a `resolved` whose merge is not committed or whose tree is not clean
(I1, §8 *A worker leaves its tree clean*, with no re-ask: the script has
no session to resume) — is restored to the commit before its merge on
the run branch by the one restore (§8 *One restore*: write bits, `reset
--hard`, `clean -ffd`, ignored files kept, the postcondition checked). A reset that fails stops the collection: the
remaining branches are reported skipped, never merged onto a tree the
reset could not restore. A `git merge
--abort` did not do that: it keeps an edit the integrator made to a file
outside the merge, which the next branch's merge then refused or the
next integrator swept in. This runs after the `finished_at` patch and before
`fetch_branch` streams the result to the host. `fetch-branch.sh`'s bundle
already carries the raw subtask branches regardless of whether collection
ran, so a crash between subtask completion and integration is still
recoverable on the host.

**`--force`: stop the orchestrator, then collect.** `leerie finalize
<run-id> --force` extends recovery to runs where the orchestrator is
still alive. It SIGTERMs the orchestrator process inside the machine (not
the machine, which must stay running for collection and fetch), waits for
it to die (polling `/proc`, escalating to SIGKILL after 30s), then runs
the same subtree-collection and `finished_at`-patch flow. The SIGTERM
handler runs `_cleanup_on_abnormal_exit(full_purge=False)`, which removes
worktrees but preserves all branches, so `setup-run.sh` (idempotent)
recreates the staging worktree and collection integrates from what
survived.

The local-runtime path runs the same `host_finalize` block inline in the
launcher (no trap needed — launcher and pusher are the same process).
Both paths share `scripts/host-finalize.sh`; the recovery command
`leerie finalize <run-id>` also sources it — three call sites, one
finalize implementation.

That inline block is the *normal* local path, but it only runs when the
launcher reaches the end of a run. A local run interrupted before then —
Ctrl-C after the waves integrated but before `phase_finalize` — leaves a
complete run branch on the host and no `finished_at` in `run.json`. So
`leerie finalize <run-id>` is the recovery verb for local runs too, not
only remote ones: it resolves the runtime to local (no Fly or EC2 sidecar
present), skips the fetch — there is nothing to fetch, the state root is
bind-mounted and the branch is already in the user's repo — and calls
`host_finalize` directly. The completion gate there keys on
`completed_waves`, deliberately not on `finished_at`, precisely so an
interrupted-but-complete run is finalizable while a crashed-mid-wave one
is not.

**One push choice per run, on every runtime.** A run has one record of
whether its result is pushed: `state.json.no_push`, a sticky run choice
(*A resumed run continues under the choices it was started with*). The
launcher resolves the choice on the host — `--no-push`, then `--push`, then
`LEERIE_NO_PUSH`, then `no_push` in `leerie.toml` — and on a fresh run hands
it to the orchestrator as `--no-push`, the same way on the local, Fly and
EC2 runtimes, because neither the container nor a remote machine sees the
host's `LEERIE_NO_PUSH` (the launcher does not forward it), and a remote
machine may not see an untracked `leerie.toml`. The orchestrator records it
at the run's start, a resume continues it by the one rule every sticky
choice follows, and `run.json.no_push` — the intent the host reads — has
one writer, `_record_run_push_choice`, which computes it each time from the
run's own record: the choice, or `true` while the run has nothing to push
(it last ended without a run branch, as a no-work run does). `main()` calls
it on every invocation but `--phase`, and the run's two terminal states
call it as they finish. A plain resume of a no-work run used to write the
choice over the no-work run's `true` (review round 25, F3); computed from
the record, it cannot. A run that is pushed has its PR written by
`pr_writer` (the deterministic fallback only when the worker fails),
whenever its push choice was made: at finalize when the run is then to be
pushed, and — because a resume may change the choice after finalize
(`leerie resume <id> --push` of a finished `--no-push` run is the one way
to push it) — on a resume of a finished run that continues with a push,
that the host has not pushed yet (no `pushed_at`) and whose `run.json`
holds no `pr_title`, before that resume returns. A run already pushed had
its PR composed under the choice that pushed it, so a later resume does not
compose it again. Binding the worker to finalize alone left such a push with the
fallback body, its PR composed by a choice that was no longer the run's.
`host_finalize` reads
`run.json.no_push` unchanged on every runtime: on a remote runtime the
fetch brings that file home before the host finalizes, and nothing on the
way rewrites it.

This replaced a split that lost the choice on Fly and EC2. The in-machine
orchestrator was always started with `--no-push` as a "mechanism flag"
because the machine has no GitHub credentials, and the user's intent
travelled beside it as a per-invocation `--host-no-push`, re-derived by
each launcher invocation and seeded into `fly-machine.json` (EC2 recorded
none). The orchestrator never pushes on any runtime, so the mechanism flag
guarded nothing; it only made `run.json.no_push` ambiguous. Every host-side
reader then guessed which meaning it held and stripped a `true`: the fetch
on both runtimes whenever a run branch came home, `leerie finalize`, and
`finalize --force`. Measured on the real code with stubbed `flyctl`: a
fresh `leerie --runtime fly --no-push` run was pushed by the auto-finalize,
and a plain `leerie resume <id>` of a paused Fly `--no-push` run passed
`--host-no-push false` and was pushed. The root cause was two owners of one
choice, one of them per-invocation. The invariant now: **the push choice is
recorded once, at the run's start, by the orchestrator; every host-side
finalize reads that record, and its one writer only ever derives it from the
run's record.**

The run branch is pushed to `origin` and a pull request opened via `gh pr
create` against the working branch (HEAD-at-run-start) by default. **This
PR base is overridable** — `--pr-base-branch` / `LEERIE_PR_BASE_BRANCH` /
`pr_base_branch` in `leerie.toml` — without changing where the diff is
computed from: the diff always starts at the commit the run branch was cut
from, `base_sha` (`rev_range = base_sha..run_branch`, *The run's own
repository*), regardless of the override, so the diff base never corrupts
if the override branch isn't the actual fork point.

The PR title and body are written by an LLM worker (`pr_writer`, defaults
to Sonnet) that runs inside the container right before it exits, where
`claude -p` and the run's own repository are both available. The worker
is handed the target repo's PR template if one exists (canonical GitHub
locations, then any `PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE/` directory), read as the blob
committed at `base_sha` in the run's own repository and never from the
checkout (*Leerie never reads through a link a repository holds*), and
fills it out
faithfully — preserving HTML comments, leaving checklists unticked unless
the diff demonstrably satisfies them, honoring "delete if N/A" markers;
absent a template it produces a default structure (Summary / What changed
/ Why / Run metadata). Its primary signal is the **commit log** (`git log
--no-merges working_branch..run_branch`), since every implementer/
conformer worker already wrote those messages in domain language landing
a subtask; a capped diff-stat, dirstat, and sampled hunks from the
heaviest-changed files supplement it. Subtask titles pass through
verbatim; the launcher prepends `leerie: ` to the title.

The worker writes `pr_title`/`pr_body`/`pr_template_used` to `run.json` —
the same container→host handoff channel used for
`finished_at`/`pushed_at`/`pr_url` — and the host launcher passes them to
`gh pr create` via `jq`. This is **fail-open**: any failure (worker
error, schema mismatch, timeout, budget exhaustion, oversized payload) is
logged and swallowed, falling back to a deterministic body composed from
`state.json` (the launcher's inline bash composition, mirroring
`compose_pr_body`, the canonical reference for that shape). Generating a
richer body must never block finalize success.

**The PR's end-state section is rendered by code, from typed state, on
every composition path.** `_format_pr_end_state_section` turns what the run
recorded into at most nine short lists, each under its own heading, each
present only when it has an entry:

- `## Unconverged` — why the PR is a draft: the outcome decider's reasons
  (§6 *The run outcome is decided once*) and every `unconverged` subtask
  with its own reason.
- `## Still failing when the run ended` — every required item unmet on a
  confirmed falsifier probe and every held-out case still failing on the
  tree that ships, each as a test the reader can run (below, *What is
  still unmet when the run ends is shown as tests the reader can run*).
- `## Needs human verification` — one checkbox list, grouped by the
  resource a human must supply, and only entries that carry a typed
  external resource: the task's required items the classifier typed
  `verifiability: external`, subtasks accepted on an
  `external_precondition` blocker that names its `resource` (§13), and
  risks a worker typed `gap: unverified_external` with the `resource`
  it names (§9 *Only an entry naming an external resource is
  external*).
- `## Not verified by this run` — everything else the run could not
  settle, grouped by why: required items whose only evidence is a
  worker's command or whose judge crashed, regression checks the confirm
  budget or a sized-out pass left open, intermittent failures the run may
  have introduced, held-out acceptance sets the final tree left
  unmeasured (§8 *A held-out set the final tree leaves unmeasured is
  never silent*), concurrency risks whose tests only simulate the
  interleaving (`simulated_interleaving`), a blocker that names no
  resource, and audited fix sites resting on an untyped (`other`) change
  that the delivery gate did not settle (§8 *A site resting on an
  untyped resolution is settled by the run*), and every worker round the
  run rolled back, with why (§8 *A rollback says why*). Each is a limit on what the
  run measured, stated with its reason; the reviewer may check it, but
  nothing outside the repository is needed to.
- `## Untested after re-drive` — changed lines that no test executes after
  the coverage re-drive spent its rounds (§9 *Changed lines no test
  executes are re-driven*). Listed, never a reason to draft.
- `## Integration content loss` — work a merge dropped (§6 *When
  integration cannot succeed*).
- `## Repository merge checks still red` — the CI-parity checks confirmed
  red on the final tree (§9 *The repository's own merge checks run too*).
- `## Existing tests changed by this run` — assertions, cases, skip markers
  and deleted files of tests the repository already had, base against the
  final tree, report-only (§8 *Existing tests the run changed are listed in
  the PR*).
- `## Advisory (not verified by this run)` — the whole-PR review's verified
  findings, the contract-literal flags and the site-token hits (§8, §9),
  labelled advisory because nothing waited on them.

*What is still unmet when the run ends is shown as tests the reader can
run.* The invariant: a run that ends with something unmet shows the person
exactly what is unmet, in a form they can run. Barnacle 79c8fbe7 (PR #708)
ended `unconverged` with item 8 "unmet on a confirmed falsifier probe …
which fails under B\*", and the PR showed nothing more: the probe, which
asserted that the step `completed` and that the right anchor showed the
option, stayed in the run directory, while the PR's own new test ran the
same step with `.catch(() => "failed")` and read as a fix. 879de601
(item 8) and b24806a1 (item 13) did the same. The probe was the clearest
statement of what was still wrong, and the held-out cases still failing at
the end were never shown either, only counted.

During the run both are held out (I3): no fixer may see them, and nothing a
held-out evaluation produces reaches one (§8 *Nothing a held-out
evaluation produces reaches a fixer*). That reason ends with the run. After
the outcome is decided nothing of the run is steered by a verdict any more:
the `pr_writer` composes from a payload that does not carry this (the
section is appended to its body), and the rebaser resolves conflicts, not
verdicts. And no later run is weakened, checked consumer by consumer: sets
are written fresh at each run's own start and never carried forward (§8
*Held-out acceptance tests*); the settled bar is recorded only by a `done`
run, which has nothing unmet to show; the prior residual and the dispute
bound read named fields of the earlier run's state (the shown sets' case
names, counts, the dispute record), never the PR, `pr_end_state`, this
record or its files.

So `phase_finalize`, after `_decide_outcome` and never earlier, records
`unmet_evidence` in code, with no worker summarising:

- for each item in `delivery_gate.unmet_final` that the falsifier made
  unmet, from its confirmed sample: the item's text, the probe's path and
  case, its failing assertion (the line the runner's failure names in the
  probe, else the sample's `assertion_quote`, which code already found in
  the case), the B\* verdict, and the runner's failure message from the
  confirm runs;
- for each held-out set in `acceptance.gate.final` that `_decide_outcome`
  counts as work, each failing file with work: its failing case IDs (the
  counted ones when the scope judge bounded the set), each with the
  runner's message and the line its stack names in the file, both recorded
  by the evaluation itself, and the B\* basis of the file's verdict (a held
  case failing again, every B\* rerun failing, failing on every rerun the
  budget allowed, or failing only with resource signatures).

Every file — the probe, and each such set's defect, control and support
files — is copied whole, under its repository path, to
`<run-dir>/unmet-evidence/` (`item-<i>/`, `set-<k>/`), so a file can be
dropped into a checkout of the branch and run with the repository's own
scoped command, which the section names when it can render one. The
section shows each file's source bounded mechanically: a window of lines
around the failing line, a number of cases per file, and a character
budget for the whole section, past which files and cases are counted, not
shown, with the directory's operator path (`_operator_path`). The same
text goes to the run's final log and to `run.json` (`unmet_evidence`,
the text and the directory). It renders on every composition path,
since the record is state and `pr_end_state` carries it to the launcher's
fallback, and its heading is code-owned, so a `pr_writer` copy is
stripped and cannot stand in for it.

A run with no PR can end with something unmet too: at the dispute bound
(§8 *No work is declared on executed evidence, and a dispute is
bounded*) a run ends `no_work` while held-out sets still fail on HEAD
(barnacle 4777d790: five of five). The person still has to see what was
left failing to decide whether the tests or the code are wrong, so that
exit records the same evidence from the same mechanical record, with the
same bounds, from the verdict it ended on, once it has decided to end and
before `_finish_no_work_run` writes `finished_at`: in the final log and
`run.json`, with the directory. When that verdict was known without a run
(HEAD is the commit the sets were validated on, the run's own start), its
messages and lines are the validation's own (`base_failure_messages`),
taken on that same commit.

*Only a typed external resource reaches "Needs human verification".* The
section answers one question — what must a human bring that the run could
not — and an entry the run could have settled with more budget, a rerun or
a reading of its own code answers a different one. 0.44.0 stated the rule
for risks only, and the renderer still filed every other source there: the
user's run 48c48629 (barnacle#665) listed an untyped fix site to read, and
run ebe36d49 (barnacle#670) "Check by hand that no existing test newly
fails … the confirm budget ran out after 2 of 3 base/final rerun pair(s)"
and intermittent test IDs, none of which needs anything outside the
repository; the user found the section confusing for it. So the rule is
structural: the "Needs human verification" renderer reads only the three
typed external shapes above, and every other source renders under "Not
verified by this run" through its own function. A guard test builds one
entry of every source — the ones derived from the code's writers and the
ones read from other state — and fails on any line in "Needs human
verification" that did not come from a typed external resource.

*Every entry the run records for a human renders.* The invariant: an
entry in `needs_human_verification` is a check the run could not make
itself, so the PR shows every one of them — under "Needs human
verification" when it carries a typed external resource, else under "Not
verified by this run", in a group per source where the source has one, and
an "Other checks the run could not make" group for any source that does
not. (The state key keeps its name.) Review round 14 H1 drove the root cause: the
renderer was a hand-kept chain of one branch per source, unconnected to
the writers, so the two sources that round added — a final delivery
judge that crashed on every attempt (`delivery_judge_unknown`) and a
ratchet that could not re-verify a met item (`ratchet_unverified`) —
were written to state and rendered nowhere: a non-draft PR with nothing
for the reviewer to check. Both now render under "Task requirements";
and a guard derives every source the code writes (each `*_GAP_SOURCE`
constant and each literal `source` in a writer of that list) and fails
on one the group table does not name, so the next source is placed
deliberately rather than falling to the catch-all.

It replaces a generic dump of every worker's self-reported risk, verbatim,
under one "Residual risks" heading — which mixed in-container gaps,
process notes and external checks, and filed integration content loss
under "Self-reported by workers". Benched as Q5/G (sonnet judge, two
samples with the order swapped): on a fresh 10-PR corpus the typed lists
were preferred for "what do I do" and as less confusing on 10 of 10 PRs
in both samples; summed over the two samples, 92 of 92 entries were
actionable against 1 of 485 in the dump, which carried 268 noise entries. The section is written to
`run.json` as `pr_end_state` beside `finished_at`, so the launcher's
LLM-less fallback appends the same text rather than re-deriving it in
`jq`; on the `pr_writer` path it is appended to the accepted body. The
`pr_writer` prompt tells the worker not to write these headings; the
guarantee is the append (§12) — a worker-emitted copy of any of them is
stripped, span-limited to that section, whether or not the run has
anything to append. The risk-derived and untested lists render only
subtasks whose work the PR contains (not `blocked`, `unconverged`,
`accepted_external`, or `accept-blocked`ed); integration content loss is
listed precisely because the work is not there.

When the target repo has multiple templates inside
`PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE/`, the alphabetically first `.md` wins by
default; `--pr-template <name>` (also `LEERIE_PR_TEMPLATE`,
`pr_template` in `leerie.toml`) overrides. A non-matching selector is
not fatal — leerie warns and falls back to the alphabetical default.

**Rebase-onto-base before push (`rebaser` worker) — a scoped, fully-agentic
exception to §12.** A run that takes a while can finish against a
`pr_base_branch` that has since moved, so the PR it opens conflicts at
merge time or is stale by review. `host_finalize` addresses this with a
best-effort rebase step, inserted after the empty-branch guard and before
the push, that is deliberately **not** driven by mechanical bash
rebase/conflict/abort logic. Instead a single autonomous worker
(`rebaser`, Sonnet, `EFFORT_DEFAULT_PER_WORKER["rebaser"] = "medium"`,
matching `integrator`) is handed a disposable worktree of the run branch,
in a host-side repository of its own (*The run's own repository*), and told to fetch the latest `pr_base_branch`, rebase the
run's own commits (`working_branch..run_branch`) onto it, resolve any
conflicts itself — preserving both sides' intent — and abort the rebase
itself, leaving the branch untouched, if a conflict is genuinely
semantically irreconcilable rather than merely textually messy. It
reports a schema-validated verdict (`status ∈ {rebased, irreconcilable,
failed}` + `diagnosis`, the same trichotomy shape as
`SCHEMAS["integrator"]`).

This is a **named, deliberately scoped exception** to §12 ("prompts are
advisory, code enforces"), the same shape as the existing
`--dangerously-skip-permissions` carve-out but narrower: scoped to one
worker acting inside one disposable worktree, not a run-level flag. It is
warranted because the procedure itself — switch branches, detect a
conflict, judge whether it is resolvable, resolve or abort — is not
usefully decomposable into mechanically checkable sub-steps the way "did
the merge commit complete" is for `integrator`; the abort-or-resolve
judgment call *is* the task. Validated empirically before adoption: two
live trials (a resolvable adjacent-line conflict, and a genuinely
irreconcilable same-function mutually-exclusive conflict) both produced
the intended outcome, confirmed by inspecting the resulting git state
rather than trusting the worker's self-report.

What stays mechanical, because it is cheap, objective, and losing it would
be a real regression:

- **Isolation.** The worker never operates on the user's real checkout, the
  user's repository, or the run's primary worktree — only a disposable
  worktree of a repository of its own (a `--shared` single-branch clone,
  its `origin` the user's remote),
  matching the containment already used for every other `ACT_TOOLS` +
  `autonomous=True` worker (`implementer`, `conformer`, `integrator` — §6;
  none of their call sites pass a real-repo `cwd`).
- **Post-hoc mechanical verification of the claimed outcome**, not the
  reasoning behind it: on `status: "rebased"`, `host_finalize` confirms
  the worktree is not mid-rebase and carries no conflict marker the
  rebase produced — one present on neither side it combined, the
  pre-rebase tip or the base it replayed onto, so a marker-shaped line
  either side already carries is content, not a leftover; on
  `status ∈ {irreconcilable, failed}`, it confirms the worktree's tip is
  unchanged from the pre-rebase run branch — the same "don't trust an
  integrator's self-report" discipline §12 already establishes. A check
  git cannot answer is a mismatch, never a pass.
- **`working_branch` bookkeeping.** A rebase changes the run branch's
  parent chain, so a naive `working_branch..run_branch` diff after
  rebasing would silently pick up unrelated upstream commits. Only on a
  verified successful rebase does `host_finalize` advance `working_branch`
  to `origin/<pr_base_branch>` (git ref and `run.json`) so
  `rev_range`/`DIFF_BASE` keep computing the PR diff correctly; on an
  aborted or failed rebase, `working_branch` is left untouched.
- **Routing the outcome.** `host_finalize` reads the worker's
  schema-validated verdict and branches on it — push the rebased branch,
  or push the original with the worker's `diagnosis` folded into the PR
  body — without re-deriving *how* the worker reached that verdict.
- **Never blocking the run.** Every branch (worktree-creation failure,
  success, a resolved conflict, an aborted rebase, a worker seam failure,
  or a malformed response) falls through to a push — the rebase step is
  strictly best-effort and never returns non-zero, pauses, or blocks
  finalize.

Two flags control push and PR independently of body composition:

- `--no-push` skips both the push and the PR; the run completes with the
  run branch local-only, for the user to inspect, push, or PR by hand.
- `--no-verify` passes `--no-verify` to `git push`, skipping pre-push hooks.
  Worker commits inside worktrees still run all hooks normally — only the
  push gate is affected. This is the explicit per-invocation override to the
  project's "never skip hooks unless asked" principle; defaults to off.

**A `pre-push` hook is a gate on the host, not on the run — so it is
probed at run start.** git runs `pre-push` in the repository root against
whatever is *checked out*. leerie never checks out the run branch — the push
happens from the user's own checkout, and the finalize rebase uses a
disposable worktree of its own repository — so a hook that lints, typechecks, or tests the working
tree measures the host's state and can reject a push for reasons no run
could have caused or prevented (a stale `node_modules`, a tool missing from
the hook's PATH, a half-finished dependency bump). Measured: every recorded
push rejection in one operator's state directory was of exactly this shape,
the most expensive arriving after 2h19m and $57 of work.

leerie does not treat that gate as a verdict on the run — it already ran the
equivalent checks in-container — but can't ignore it either, since the push
genuinely won't happen. Because the hook reads the host checkout, which
leerie never modifies during a run, a probe at run start predicts the
finalize outcome by construction. `git push --dry-run` runs the hook and
creates no ref, so the launcher runs it during host preflight and warns
(never refuses — a hook can legitimately fail on a tree the run is about to
fix, and preflight must never become a new way to decline to start). A
chain probes once per *wave* (its jobs share one checkout, so N probes would
compute one answer N times concurrently); a group probes per member, since
its members are separate repositories. Same "fail fast at the cheapest
moment" reasoning as §13's budget feasibility.

**A fresh run refuses a stale base.** The complementary t=0 hazard is the
checkout being *behind* its upstream. The operator loop that leerie's
convergence story assumes — run, merge the PR on the forge, re-run — has
a race in it: the merge lands on the remote, and nothing guarantees the
local checkout saw it before the re-run starts. Measured on one repo's
corpus: a re-run started one minute after its predecessor's PR merged,
planned against the pre-merge tree (`repo_state_before_planning.head`
identical across the two runs), re-solved the same findings from
scratch, and its finalize rebase-onto-base landed the older, weaker
solution OVER the just-merged fix — a regression the following run had
to re-fix. Three runs' spend for negative progress, invisible to every
in-run gate because each run was self-consistent against the tree it
saw.

So host preflight ends with a freshness check
(`host_base_freshness_check`, host-side because the fetch needs the
host's credentials — the container has none): a best-effort
`git fetch` of the current branch's upstream, then a mechanical
ancestry comparison. It refuses to start — with the pull command and
the env escape hatch (`LEERIE_SKIP_FRESHNESS_CHECK=1`) in the message —
on exactly the measured signature: HEAD a strict ancestor of its
upstream. Equal, ahead, and diverged pass silently (equal has
nothing to be behind; ahead/diverged mean local commits exist and
the operator is doing something deliberate — "behind" is the
signature).
Beyond the trivially clean cases above (equal, ahead, diverged), the
degrade-to-permissive set is exactly: a local (same-repo) upstream, no
origin remote, detached HEAD, no upstream (or an unresolvable,
configured-but-gone one) when origin has no same-named branch, and a
failed fetch when the last-fetched state
shows nothing behind — because a guard that blocks offline work gets
switched off. Two cases that look permissive are deliberately NOT:
a branch with no usable upstream (none configured, or a
configured-but-gone one) still refuses when a
**same-named origin branch** exists and is ahead (the merge→re-run
race does not care whether tracking was configured), and a failed
fetch still refuses when the **last-fetched** tracking ref already
shows the checkout behind (the staleness is proven by information
already on disk; going offline must not erase it). Fresh runs only —
a resume deliberately continues its recorded baseline.

**Push and PR are honest about failure.** A push or PR step that fails does
not pretend the run failed: the local work is intact on the run branch. The
orchestrator records what was attempted and what failed in a per-run
sidecar (`run.json` — `pushed_at`, `push_error`, `pr_url`, `pr_error`). Push
failure exits non-zero with a message naming the run branch (where the work
lives), the working branch (the diff fork-point, unchanged from run start),
and the PR base branch (`pr_base_branch`, defaulting to `working_branch`),
shows the captured push output — stderr plus any pre-push hook stdout,
since git forwards a hook's stdout to its own and that's where
`tsc`/`biome` report — and gives the exact retry command. PR-creation
failure is non-fatal: the push already succeeded, so the user gets a
warning with the pushed branch's URL and the exact `gh pr create` retry
command.

**`pushed_at` gates re-finalize by branch position, not mere presence.** A
re-invoked finalize (`leerie finalize`, a second launcher pass, Fly's
`decide_teardown`) must be idempotent, so a run whose `pushed_at` is already
set is normally a no-op — but `pushed_at` records *that* a push happened,
not *what* it pushed, and a finalize that fired while the run was still
integrating can leave it set on a **partial** branch. The short-circuit
instead compares the local run-branch tip against the pushed origin tip:
**equal tips → no-op** (the common case); **origin a strict ancestor of the
local tip (or origin absent) → fast-forward re-push + re-open the PR**,
gated behind the same completion check (`completed_waves == len(waves)`,
itself fail-open on a missing `state.json`). A **diverged** origin is not
treated as a partial push — it keeps the idempotent short-circuit rather
than attempting a push that cannot fast-forward. This prevents a partial
push from permanently wedging a run while preserving idempotency, the
chain wave-skip signal (which reads `pushed_at`, still set, not the tip),
and the invariant `pr_url ⇒ pushed_at`.

**Why push by default.** A successful unattended run that leaves work only
on a local branch is a silent failure mode — the work exists but nothing
signals it needs review. Defaulting to push + PR turns every run into a
reviewable artifact. `--no-push` exists for offline use or repos without a
GitHub remote.

**Branch cleanup at finalize.** Finalize deletes no branch. The
per-subtask branches `leerie/subtasks/<run-id>/*` are refs of the run's
own repository (*The run's own repository*): only the run branch is
brought back into the user's repository, so the subtask branches never
reach it, and they go with the run directory when `leerie prune` reclaims
it. Finalize's `cleanup.sh` removes the run's worktrees only. The **run
branch** itself
(`leerie/runs/<run-id>`) is *kept* — it is the PR head, and deleting it
locally before the PR is merged would dangle the PR base reference. The
per-run state directory (`state.json`, `run.json`, logs, criteria,
checkpoints) is also kept as an audit trail. A user who wants to
completely scrub a finished run can do so with
`scripts/cleanup.sh --run-id <id> --branches`.

**The run outcome is decided once.** `_decide_outcome` is the single
writer of state's `outcome` — `done`, `no_work` or `unconverged` — and every
terminal path reaches it: the planning-time no-work exits and finalize's
empty-branch exit (both through `_finish_no_work_run`) and the normal
finalize path. The rule, benched as the P7 outcome simulation (90 historical
runs, 2000 trials each): the run is `unconverged` when any subtask settled
`unconverged`, when the failing-test-ID diff confirmed a new failure (§9
*Which failures are new*), when a measured held-out acceptance set still
fails (a set typed `broken` by the set audit does not count — §8 *A set
that keeps failing is audited, and rewritten once*), when a required item is still unmet after the delivery recheck (or, once final delivery detection has run, unmet by the judge or a confirmed falsifier on the shipping tree — §8 *Delivery detection*), or when one of the repository's own merge checks is confirmed red on the final tree (§9 *The repository's own merge checks run too*), or when the delivery re-drive declared a `conflict` (the same fix-for-regression trade recurred — §8 *Delivery re-drive*; the reason names both sides), or when the final-tree conformance left an actionable solution defect unfixed after its last round (§9, final-tree pass; the reason names each defect's kind, location and case), or when an existing test's base form fails on the tree that ships (`existing_behaviour_changed`, §8 *What an existing test pins on the base holds on the tree that ships*) —
consulted *before* the no-work check, so an empty branch that left work
unfinished is never reported as "no work required". Otherwise an empty run
branch is `no_work` and anything else is `done`. The outcome is mirrored
into `run.json`, and the host launcher opens the PR as a **draft** when it
is `unconverged` — the PR still carries everything that did converge, but it
cannot be mistaken for finished work — and the body says why: the end-state
section (§6 *Finalization*) opens with `## Unconverged`, the decider's
reasons followed by each unconverged subtask's own. Before this, no-work was decided in
five scattered places and a run with unfinished work shipped an ordinary PR.

*A delivery verdict counts only on the tree it was measured on.* Each
delivery pass records the committed tree it read beside its verdict
(final detection's `final_tree`, the recheck's and the pre-pass's
`judged_*.tree`), and the decider takes the latest one only when that tree
is the tree that ships — the run branch's tree,
`refs/heads/leerie/runs/<id>^{tree}`, read from the repository, which is
the ref finalize pushes (review round 15 H1: read from staging's HEAD, it
was "" once finalize's `cleanup.sh` had removed staging, so every run with
a delivery verdict ended `unconverged`; and staging's HEAD is not what
ships unless I1 holds staging on the branch). Every pass stamps its verdict
with that same ref's tree. Any other verdict, or none of the shipping tree at all, makes the
run `unconverged` with the reason "the required items were not read on
the tree that ships". The root cause this removes (review round 14 M2):
the decider read whichever unmet list existed — final detection's, else
the recheck's, else the pre-pass's — with no check of which tree it
described, so a final judge that failed in a way its retry did not catch
(a checkout `RuntimeError`) left detection with no verdict, the recheck's
"nothing unmet" of an earlier commit decided the outcome, and the run
ended `done` on a tree nothing had read. A delivery re-drive that moves
HEAD re-keys detection's verdict to its final commit and tree only when
every routed and every unverified item was read there; otherwise the
verdict stays of its own tree and the run says so. And a final judge that
fails in any way, not only a worker crash or timeout, is a judge that read
nothing: its items are `unknown`, never `met`.

*`done` rests on measurements that ran (review round 19).* Root cause:
every regression check stepped aside when it could not measure. The
failing-test-ID diff returned "nothing to diff" when the test axis gave no
verdict or its install failed, and the decider read an absent diff as no
new failure. An unmeasured held-out set was "no evidence". So in two
measured runs every install failed, nothing was measured, and the run
ended `done`; one shipped a broken test. Invariant: `done` is a claim
about the tree that ships, and it holds only when the measurements it
rests on ran on that tree. Each one the run could not take makes the run
`unconverged`, with the reason naming what was not measured and why, and
the PR's "Needs human verification" listing it as before:

- *The tests,* when the repository has a test command: a failing-test-ID
  diff of exactly the tree that ships. No diff, or a diff of another tree,
  is not measured. `_refresh_test_id_diff` records why it could not take
  one (`shipping_tests_gap`), and the decider names it. Failing tests that
  the base could not be rerun against (`no_verdict`) leave the diff's
  answer unknown for them, so they count too. A test command the task
  forbids is the task's own constraint, listed by its own gap, and does
  not count.
- *The held-out sets:* every set the final tree left unmeasured, the same
  sets `_acceptance_unmeasured_lines` lists for the PR.
- *The existing tests' base forms:* a base-form check of another tree, one
  that raised, or a file it gave no verdict for.

The rule is in the decider, read from what the measurements recorded, so
any future cause of an unmeasured tree ends the same way, whatever it is.

### Credential strategy

**A containerized headless run must prefer the long-lived token.** The
host's interactive Claude Code session authenticates with a short-lived
subscription OAuth token — corroborated at roughly 8h, though the exact TTL
is undocumented (community reports range 2–15h), so leerie never
hard-codes a duration and instead reads the credential's own authoritative
`expiresAt` field. That token is refreshable only by the interactive host
session that owns it — Claude Code renews it silently in the background
while the user is logged in.

A leerie container cannot participate in that renewal. Keychain and
`~/.claude/.credentials.json` never traverse the Lima VM boundary directly
— the launcher copies whatever credential it resolves into a fresh
`mktemp -d` staging directory and bind-mounts it read-through into the
container, so the container holds a **snapshot**, not a live view. It
cannot refresh a token whose refresh state lives in the host's Keychain,
and Anthropic's refresh flow **rotates the refresh token on every use** —
a container-side refresh, even if it succeeded, would silently invalidate
the host's own copy out from under the still-running interactive session.
Copied subscription credentials are documented upstream as not refreshing
at all once removed from their original context
(anthropics/claude-code#21765). Container-side token refresh is therefore
**architecturally impossible**, not merely unimplemented.

The credential Anthropic's own docs prescribe here is the **long-lived
OAuth token** minted by `claude setup-token` — lasting roughly a year,
meant for CI/automation, and — critically — still authenticating against
the user's Claude subscription rather than the API, preserving leerie's
no-API-key constraint. Sessions authenticated via `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`
never see the "OAuth session expired" failure at all, per Anthropic's own
error reference, because they never depend on the saved, host-refreshed
login — a container invoked with it set is immune to the mid-run expiry
class of failure by construction, not by any retry or backoff leerie adds
on top.

Consequently, credential resolution takes `$CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`
**first**, ahead of Keychain and the credentials file — an inversion of the
historical precedence, which silently preferred the 8h token even when a
user had minted a durable one. A user who has set nothing is unaffected:
resolution falls back to Keychain, then the file, as before. The emitted
JSON shape is unchanged regardless of which branch resolved the credential
(`{"claudeAiOauth":{"accessToken":…,"scopes":["user:inference"]}}` — the
`scopes` field is required by the CLI's file-auth path, which rejects a
scope-less blob as "Not logged in"), matching what `seed-auth.sh` already
stages into the container.

**Keychain/file resolution requires a real token, not just non-empty
JSON.** The macOS Keychain entry and `~/.claude/.credentials.json` are
shared with Claude Code's own MCP-server OAuth state — a documented
upstream bug (steipete/CodexBar#1844) lets a background MCP-plugin auth
flow overwrite the shared `Claude Code-credentials` Keychain item with only
`{"mcpOAuth": {...}}`, dropping `claudeAiOauth` (the actual session token)
entirely. That blob is syntactically valid, non-empty JSON, so a
presence-only check accepts it, stages it into the container, and the CLI
fails with "Not logged in" despite the launcher reporting success. Both
the Keychain and on-disk-file branches now additionally require a
non-empty `claudeAiOauth.accessToken` before accepting the blob; a blob
failing that check is treated as if that source were empty and resolution
falls through the same chain (Keychain → file → the existing "could not
extract credentials" hint) rather than short-circuiting on a false
positive.

**The expiry preflight is best-effort, not a hard gate.** Before staging a
resolved *subscription* credential (the long-lived token has no
`expiresAt` and is exempt entirely), leerie parses `claudeAiOauth.expiresAt`
and compares it to the current time, mirroring the pattern already proven
for AWS SSO token freshness in `scripts/remote/aws-credentials.sh`:

- **Already expired** → refuse to launch and print `claude /login`, rather
  than starting a run doomed to fail at worker #1.
- **Inside a near-expiry threshold** (proposed 90 minutes — long enough to
  cover realistic run durations without false-alarming on every launch) →
  warn with the credential's exact expiry time and point at
  `claude setup-token` as the durable fix, but still launch.
- **`expiresAt` absent or malformed** → proceed silently. The 1-year token
  has no `expiresAt` field at all, and a best-effort freshness check must
  never harden into a hard requirement for a field that legitimately may
  not be present — that would break the exact non-expiring credential this
  strategy exists to prefer.

**Auth failures split into two classes with different remedies.**
`_is_auth_or_quota_failure` (see *Cleanup on abnormal exit* below for the
full taxonomy) treats numeric 401/429/529 statuses as **transient**: the
gateway rejected one request, but a retry after backoff has a real chance
once the rolling usage window clears or gateway overload subsides. An
expired or revoked *session* is categorically different — Claude Code's own
error handling clears the saved credential locally and, per Anthropic's
docs, sends no further request at all once it detects that state. Backing
off against a session that will never renew itself just burns the full
`auth_retry_max_sec` budget — this was the `b57027d3…` incident's D2
defect: two retries fired 1.2s apart against the same dead session before
the run gave up with a schema-error message that misattributed the
failure.

The fix is a **terminal** auth-failure class, checked before the transient
classifier ever runs: envelope text carrying "failed to authenticate,"
"oauth session expired," "session expired and could not be refreshed," or
"not logged in" (measured against 611 historical `is_error` envelopes: 215
true positives, 0 false positives) never enters the backoff loop, raising
immediately into the same **resumable pause** leerie already uses for
out-of-credits (`EXIT_LOCKED`, exit 75) — worktree-only cleanup, state and
branches preserved, a `leerie resume <id>` hint logged. Like a billing
shortfall, an expired session doesn't resolve on a clock, so auto-resume
would spin uselessly; the run's completed work is preserved and picked
back up on `resume` once the operator re-authenticates or sets
`CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`.

**The same refresh-vs-static distinction applies to Bedrock auth.** The
launcher's Bedrock support defaults to AWS SSO/profile auth:
`detect_bedrock_mode()` reads `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK` out of the operator's
merged Claude `settings.json` files (never a tracked one in the checkout, §6
*A repository chooses no operator authority*), then `bedrock_preflight()` requires the host
`aws` CLI and a live `aws sts get-caller-identity` before staging `~/.aws/`
read-only into the container. SSO access tokens are short-lived (~12h) and
refreshed only by the host's interactive `aws sso login` browser flow — the
identical container-cannot-refresh problem this section already solved for
subscription auth.

`AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK` is the Bedrock analogue: a static bearer
credential the Claude CLI sends directly to the Bedrock runtime endpoint,
with no refresh-token/expiry machinery near it (verified against the CLI's
own bundled source and live end-to-end testing — the token alone is a
no-op unless `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK` is also set). Because it needs no
`aws` CLI, no SSO session, and no `~/.aws/` staging, leerie triggers this
path from a plain host env var, independent of the settings.json-driven
gate, and skips `bedrock_preflight()`/the `~/.aws` mount entirely when set.
When both are present, the bearer token wins, matching the Claude CLI's own
resolution order.

**Multi-token rotation reduces quota exhaustion the same way the
long-lived token above reduces expiry risk — by picking the credential
least likely to fail, rather than reacting after it does.** A single
`CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` still has one shared 5-hour/7-day usage window; a
long run (many workers, high `max_parallel`) can exhaust that window
mid-run even though the token itself never expires. `leerie` supports
`CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKENS` — a comma-separated list of tokens — which
**supersedes** the singular var when set:

- **Start-of-run smart selection.** Each token's remaining runway (5h/7d
  utilization, reset time, per-model weekly sublimits) is probed via the
  same undocumented usage-telemetry surface Anthropic's own `/usage` view
  and Claude Code's statusline read internally: `GET /api/oauth/usage`
  (`user:profile`-scoped tokens) with a fallback, for
  `user:inference`-scoped tokens such as a `claude setup-token` mint, to
  reading the `anthropic-ratelimit-unified-*` headers off a minimal
  `/v1/messages` call. The token with the most runway is selected before
  any worker spawns — not round-robin, which would burn a nearly-exhausted
  token at the same rate as a fresh one.
- **Mid-run failover.** If the active token gets rate-limited mid-run,
  leerie rotates to another token with runway and **continues in the same
  container** — no re-exec, no restart — by threading the active token
  through each worker spawn's environment. If every token is limited,
  leerie picks the one whose window resets soonest and falls through to the
  existing reset-wait auto-resume path. This covers both surfaces a rate
  limit can reach `claude_p` through: a completed envelope carrying a
  401/429/529/auth-message, and the protocol-level `rate_limit_event`
  stream event that raises `RateLimitedExit` directly out of the streaming
  loop before any envelope is produced.

**This is deliberately structured data in, deterministic Python out — no
LLM worker** (§12). Ranking is `min(1 − 5h_utilization, 1 −
7d_utilization)` with a furthest-reset tie-break, computed identically
given the same inputs.

**Both probe endpoints are undocumented and explicitly best-effort.**
Anthropic can change or remove either without notice; every probe path
degrades to "use the current/first token and react to the next 429" rather
than fail the run. A probe response missing an expected field (contract
drift, distinct from an ordinary transient failure) is logged at WARNING
with a stable marker so a silent endpoint-shape change doesn't quietly
degrade this feature for weeks with no signal. Each token's probe result
is cached for a floor of ~180 seconds and identified in logs only by a
short fingerprint — the raw token value is never written to a log line,
`calls.ndjson`, or `run.json`. `state.json`'s `active_oauth_token` field is
the one place the raw active token persists at rest (local-orchestrator-
owned, not published), and it travels with `state.json` on the existing
Fly/EC2 `fetch-branch.sh` state sync.

**Decomposition needs the same discipline against the loss of in-progress
spend.** §5½ (P1)'s `fit_judge` and coupled-minority `splitter` calls have
no crash barrier: a single `WorkerError` mid-decomposition discards every
fit/split judgment already paid for on that planning pass, not just the
node being judged — the same class of loss D3 measured in the motivating
incident, where decomposition was 27.8% of the run's total spend. The
remedy mirrors disciplines `_recursive_decompose` already applies
elsewhere: a `WorkerError` from either call degrades that node to a
**leaf**, the same way the existing depth-cap and no-progress-guard cases
resolve uncertainty by accepting the node as-is; and `phase_plan` snapshots
decomposition progress into state as each top-level subtask finishes
expanding, the same way `plan_snapshot` persists the post-`_schedule()`
plan. Like `plan_snapshot`, this snapshot is **diagnostic only** — nothing
reads it back. The resumable-planning cursor (§6) checkpoints
`phase_plan`'s output as a whole, so a pause mid-decomposition still
re-runs the entire `phase_plan` invocation on resume rather than
rehydrating from partial leaves; finer-grained resume is a separate,
not-yet-shipped capability.

### Cleanup on abnormal exit

A run can end abnormally four ways: the user hits Ctrl-C, an external
process sends a signal (SIGTERM/SIGHUP from CI, systemd, a terminal close),
an unhandled exception fires, or the Claude Code subscription rate-limit /
session-limit is hit mid-worker. In each case the orchestrator runs a
cleanup pass before exiting, and the cleanup *scope* is uniformly
conservative — **state and branches are always preserved**; only worktrees
are torn down. The run is always resumable via `resume <id>` after any
abnormal exit.

**Auth failures split into transient and terminal, and only one benefits
from backoff.** 401/429/529 — a rejected request against a still-valid
session, whether from the rolling subscription cap or transient gateway
overload — is **transient**: the session is fine, so retrying after
backoff has a real chance once the window clears, handled by the existing
auth/quota retry loop (`_is_auth_or_quota_failure`, taxonomy below). An
expired or revoked session — "OAuth session expired," "failed to
authenticate," "not logged in" — is **terminal**: per Anthropic's docs,
Claude Code clears the saved credential and sends no further request at
all once it detects this state, so every retry fails identically to the
first and backoff only burns the `auth_retry_max_sec` budget for no
benefit (see *Credential strategy* above). Terminal auth failures are
checked *before* the transient classifier and routed straight to the same
resumable pause (`EXIT_LOCKED`, exit 75) used for out-of-credits below —
worktree-only cleanup, state and branches preserved, `resume` picks back
up once the operator re-authenticates.

**A mid-stream transport disconnect is a third transient class, and it
gets the same backoff.** When the network connection carrying a worker's
streaming response drops mid-answer, `claude -p` surfaces a result
envelope with `is_error` set, `terminal_reason` = `"api_error"`, a *null*
`api_error_status` (the connection died before any HTTP status returned),
and result text `"API Error: Connection closed mid-response. The response
above may be incomplete."` This is the same *family* as the 529 overload
case — the session is fine, the request just never completed — so a fresh
session after backoff has a real chance of succeeding. It is distinct
from a schema mistake, which is what the immediate corrective-note retry
exists for; routing a transport drop through that path retries once
against the same bad network window with a nonsensical "conform to the
schema" nudge, then fails the subtask. `_is_transient_transport_failure`
classifies it (keyed on `terminal_reason == "api_error"` with no numeric
`api_error_status`, or — as a secondary catch — a narrow connection-drop
text-marker set) and routes it through the *same*
`_is_auth_or_quota_failure` tenacity backoff loop, checked after the
terminal-auth classifier so an expired session is never mistaken for a
transport blip. Measured over 9,020 worker logs: 58 sids hit this drop; of
the 56 that did **not** also hit `max_turns` (the pure-transport
population), 83% recovered on a later attempt and 73% on the very next
one — a network transient, not context exhaustion (a third of drops fire
at ≤3 turns). The two `max_turns`-coupled sids recovered 0% — an oversized
subtask that also drops is a *decomposition* problem (see §5½ P1
*Sub-file*), not one backoff can fix. This path mirrors Claude Code's own
remedy for a mid-stream drop (an automatic retry, CLI v2.1.219); leerie's
backoff is the fresh-session complement for when the CLI's in-session
retries are exhausted.

**A client-side context refusal is a fourth class, and it is terminal.**
Claude Code enforces a context ceiling *itself*: when the assembled prompt
exceeds the window it believes the model has, it emits a synthetic
assistant message (`model=<synthetic>`, usage all zeros) and ends the
session with `terminal_reason` = `"blocking_limit"` and result text
`"Prompt is too long"` — without issuing an API call at all. Retrying
identical input therefore cannot succeed, putting this in the same bucket
as terminal auth rather than the transient classes above.
`_is_context_overflow` requires *both* `terminal_reason` and the result
text (the reason alone is shared with other blocking limits; the text
alone could appear in a worker's own correct output), is checked
immediately after the terminal-auth classifier and before the generic
corrective-note retry, and routes to the same resumable `EXIT_LOCKED`
pause — the remedy is an operator change, not a wait.

Before refusing, the CLI attempts reactive compaction, which summarises
**message groups**; a conversation with fewer than two of them fails
`too_few_groups` and the refusal follows immediately. Every worker holds a
multi-turn conversation and compacts normally — the **preflight smoke
test does not**, since it is a single exchange whose tokens are almost
entirely system prompt, tool schemas and `CLAUDE.md`, none of which
compaction can touch. So for that one invocation the effective limit is
the *compaction trigger*, not the context ceiling itself.

That is why the smoke test runs in an **empty working directory**: it
validates the CLI (auth, streaming, `--json-schema`), not the repository.
Loading the repo's own `CLAUDE.md`/skills/commands is by far the largest
term (measured: 126,022 prompt tokens in this repo vs. 17,222 empty,
against a failing run that reached 183,485). Since `CLAUDE.md` only grows,
the margin has to be structural rather than a number someone re-tunes — an
empty cwd is the only one whose prompt size is bounded by construction.
The cost is real: preflight no longer proves the CLI can start *in this
repo* (e.g. a malformed `.claude/settings.json`), which now surfaces at
the classifier instead — acceptable because the refusal there is
classified rather than printed as a bare string. Left unclassified, this
failure was actively misleading: the envelope fell through to the
two-attempt schema loop and surfaced as *"worker failed schema-valid
output twice: Prompt is too long"* — blaming schema validation for a
context refusal, costing three misdiagnoses before the real cause was
measured (2026-08-06). The pause message therefore names the actual
contributors (task text, the repo's `CLAUDE.md`), and, when the
strict-output proxy is active, names it first (see §7 *Forcing
constrained decoding*).

**Worktrees are also pruned mid-run, not only at cleanup.** Once
`integrate_wave` reports a subtask's branch merged into staging, that
subtask's worktree is dead weight — the commits live in the branch, which
survives worktree removal — so `phase_execute` removes it at the end of
that wave rather than waiting for run end. The prune runs **once per
wave**, after every subtask in it has been integrated, so peak worktree
coexistence is the size of a wave. Without this, every worktree a run ever
created persisted until the run finished: at 30–87 subtasks against a repo
whose `node_modules` is ~1.4 GB, that is the measured 51 GB that killed
two runs with an unhandled `ENOSPC`.

The prune is scoped to *integrated* subtasks specifically. A `blocked` or
`failed` subtask keeps its worktree, because that tree is exactly what an
operator inspects by hand before settling it with `accept-blocked` or
`accept-integration` — pruning the whole wave instead would destroy that
evidence.

**A settled subtask's trees go when it settles** (*designed 2026-11-08,
the navegando run a70fb4a6*). The invariant: *a tree lives only while
something can still read it; what a later step needs is made again from
committed refs.* The per-wave prune bounded coexistence to one wave, and a
wave is as wide as the plan makes it: a70fb4a6's first wave held 14
subtasks, and every one that had settled `complete` kept its worktree and
its committed view until the last of the 14 had settled and the wave was
integrated — 14 views of 1,549 MB, seven worker trees of 1.2 GB, staging's
view and the planning tree: 33.8 GB of the run's 36 GB, and the host at
1.5% free. What reads a subtask's trees once it has settled:

- its *view* (`_committed_view`): the coverage re-drive's evaluation
  (`_measure_subtask_coverage`, `_settle_typed_gaps`) and nothing else
  before its tip moves — the integration gate's conflicted-area tests run
  in their own trees at each parent (`_integration_tree`); B\*, the
  intermittent-discovery repeats, the falsifier, the base-form check, the
  ratchet, the acceptance gate and final conformance all measure staging;
- its *worktree*: a re-drive's worker (blocked or coverage), which
  `new-worktree.sh` already makes from the subtask's branch in the run
  repository when the tree is absent, and the rollback of a re-drive that
  did not end `complete`, which runs while that re-drive's tree stands;
- its *branch*: integration (`integrate.sh` merges it from the run
  repository, where leerie took it as each worker exited), the settled
  head, the undo of an interrupted re-drive (which resets the branch in
  the run repository when the tree is gone).

So when a subtask settles: the coverage re-drive's first evaluation runs
then, in the view the settle measured (`_evaluate_subtask_coverage`, inside
the wave's `max_parallel` slot), instead of after the whole wave in a view
made again; the view is dropped when any evaluation ends; and a `complete`
subtask's worktree and tree repository go too, its branch taken first
(`_release_settled_trees` → `_prune_subtask_worktree`). A `blocked` or
`failed` subtask keeps its worktree, as above; its view goes. A later
reader makes what it needs from refs: the view from the branch tip in the
run repository (`_view_repo`), the tree by `new-worktree.sh`, each
installing afresh (`_forget_installs`) from the run's own store, which —
now that a tree links from its store (§6 *The write grants on one mount
are one mount*) — costs a link pass, not a copy. A resumed run finds the
same: its trees gone, its branches in the run repository.

Peak on a70fb4a6's shape (14 subtasks in one wave, `max_parallel` 5), from
per-tree sizes measured on that run and on its lockfile in scratch: a
view's private bytes 1,549 MB before, about 392 MB after (74 MB of pnpm's
`node_modules`, 298 MB of `infra/node_modules` that npm copies by design,
the checkout); a worker tree 1,229–1,251 MB before, about 89 MB after.
The run's worktrees measured 33.8 GB. With links alone they come to about
7.2 GB; with links and the release, at most five settling subtasks hold a
tree and a view at once beside staging's view and the planning tree:
about 3.4 GB, the run directory about 6 GB with its stores.

**Why a worktree costs what it does.** Package managers like pnpm are
content-addressed and normally *hardlink* from a shared store into each
`node_modules`, so a second checkout of the same dependency set costs
almost nothing when store and tree share a mount (measured once, on one
host: 92.6% of `node_modules` bytes shared, private remainder 102 MiB
against a 1.35 GiB tree — illustrative, not a verified general quantity).
But leerie used to bind-mount the package-manager store and the state
directory as *separate* mounts, and Linux refuses `link()` across different
mounts even when both resolve to the same filesystem (`do_linkat`'s
`EXDEV`) — so the store could not hardlink into a worktree, pnpm fell back
to copying, and each worktree paid full freight. That is the multiplier
behind the 51 GB, and the mid-run prune bounds coexistence to one wave's
worth of trees.

**The pnpm store shares the worktrees' mount.** Every package store lives
in the state mount, beside the worktrees, so an install can hard-link from
its run's store (a hard link cannot cross mounts). Inside a confined
process they must stay one mount too: from the isolation of 2026-11-01
through 0.48.0 the shim bound each grant onto itself, which split them
again and made every confined install a copy (§6 *The write grants on one
mount are one mount*). There are three sets, all
set by the orchestrator through environment variables, with no mount or
`-e` of their own (*The stores a view installs from are leerie's*, *Which
stores an install may share*, below), and every one is inside its run's
directory: the run's own, `<run-dir>/worktrees/.stores/stores/<name>`, for every command
leerie runs; each run's workers', `<run-dir>/worktrees/.stores/cache/<name>` (the
held-out side's at `<run-dir>/worktrees/.stores/cache-held-out/<name>`); and each run
tree's own, `<run-dir>/worktrees/.stores/tree-stores/<tree>/<name>`. The state root is
`/leerie-state` locally and `/work/.leerie` on Fly. The host cache mounts
that used to hold them (pnpm, pip, Go, Cargo, corepack) are gone. Copying
was not only a disk cost: concurrent installs copying whole trees ran past
their timeouts, and three chains lost work to it (an install that "did not
finish within 600 s", held-out sets discarded on install timeouts). pnpm's
store is content-addressed with atomic writes, so concurrent installs into
one store are safe. Ownership follows the worktrees on every runtime,
because it is the same mount: measured rootful (real uid switch), five
worktrees installed into one store with 0 EACCES, the worker owning every
new store file, one package file carrying 6 links (the store's and one per
worktree), and no chown. EC2 keeps its image-default store.

**The stores a view installs from are leerie's.** The invariant: *no
store is shared across runs or repositories.* Every package store and cache
an installer the provision recipe can name reads — pnpm, npm, yarn (classic
and berry), bun, corepack, pip, uv, poetry, pipenv, go (modules and build),
cargo, bundler, composer, NuGet (`_STORE_VARS`) — is the run's own, and
writable by every command leerie runs in that run; one mechanism covers
every manager, and no manager is configured differently because of it:

- *The run's*, `<run-dir>/worktrees/.stores/stores/<name>`, set on the orchestrator's own
  environment once the run directory exists, before anything installs
  (`_leerie_stores`). Every install, build, test and measurement leerie
  runs in the run reads and writes it (the measurement grant names it,
  *Leerie's runs of the repository's commands are confined too*); no
  worker's grant does, and a worker's environment replaces every variable
  (below). It is the run's process's scratch: removed at the process's
  exit with the trees' stores (*No copy of the credentials outlives its
  run's process*), so a resumed process installs cold again, and a
  finished run keeps no store until it is pruned.
- *The run's workers'*, `<run-dir>/worktrees/.stores/cache/<name>` with
  `XDG_CACHE_HOME` at `<run-dir>/worktrees/.stores/cache/xdg`
  (`_worker_cache_env`, in the worker's spawn), one set per side of the
  run, shared by that side's workers: the held-out side's workers
  (`HELD_OUT_LOG_WORKERS`) have their own, `<run-dir>/worktrees/.stores/cache-held-out/`,
  which no fixer's grant names (§8 *Nothing a held-out evaluation produces
  reaches a fixer*). Per side rather than per worker, because what a worker
  leaves in a cache can mislead only another worker of its side, while
  every cold copy is paid again: a cold pnpm store costs 9–23 s and
  0.5–1.3 GB; on funeralworks, Playwright's chromium costs 20.1 s and
  656 MB cold against 2.1 s warm, and a warm-store install with a cold
  `XDG_CACHE_HOME` 14.8 s against 11.8 s (corepack's pnpm 23 MB, Prisma's
  engines 22 MB). A worker's configuration and temporary directory stay its
  own: they carry hooks and sessions, a cache carries neither. The set goes
  with the run directory.
- *Each run tree's own*, `<run-dir>/worktrees/.stores/tree-stores/<tree>/<name>`
  (`_tree_store_env`): the stores that hold one tree's environment or build
  (*Which stores an install may share*, below).

A variable pointing beneath the image's bake root (`/opt/`, the
*persistent out-of-repo dependency bake*) is left alone on every side:
those are dependencies leerie built into the image, which the recipe no
longer installs.

*Why the shared read-only store was replaced* (2026-11-04). Until 0.44.3
leerie's commands shared one store per repository across runs,
`<state-root>/.stores/leerie/`, filled by a scripts-free fetch
(`pnpm fetch --ignore-scripts`, `npm ci --ignore-scripts`, …, in a
staging directory holding only the lockfile) and read-only to every
install, which copied from it (`package-import-method=copy`,
`UV_LINK_MODE=copy`, bun's `--backend=copyfile`). It answered one measured
attack: pnpm hard-links a package's files from its store, so an in-place,
same-size, mtime-restored edit of `node_modules/<lib>/<file>` — by a worker
in its tree, or by a committed `postinstall` — edited the store's own copy,
and the next install anywhere linked the edit (pnpm 10.4.1 on barnacle;
review round 18 H1). That attack came from a review round's demonstration,
not from a run: across all 619 runs under `~/.leerie/*/runs` on the
measuring host (2026-11-04), no worker's edit or write tool call touched a
file inside `node_modules`. The protection, meanwhile, broke pnpm three
times, each time with a package-manager-specific workaround: pnpm 11 opens
its store's SQLite index read-write for every install (worked around with
`frozen-store`, pnpm 11's alone); pnpm 11 opens it again before every
`pnpm <script>` (worked around with `verify-deps-before-run=false`); and
pnpm 10.27 onward symlinks every project it installs into
`<store>/v10/projects/` (its project registry, read by `pnpm store prune`
to sweep the global virtual store; registration is unconditional in
`getContext`, with no setting that turns it off, and pnpm 11 skips it only
under `frozen-store`), which failed every install of a repository pinning
pnpm 10.28.2 (`EROFS … symlink … pnpm-store/v10/projects/<hash>`, the
user's `web` run 6f147a0c on 0.44.3: the planning install, then the
base-health baseline's install, so its build read `prisma: not found`).
Leerie is multi-language: a store contract each manager must be fitted to,
version by version, is the wrong shape. So the store is per run and
writable, and every manager runs as the repository runs it, at whatever
version it pins.

What still holds: nothing one run's code writes reaches another run or
another repository — a run's stores are its directory's, and a new run
starts with none. What is given up, deliberately: *a measurement never
sees a file its own run's code changed.* Within one run, a committed
`postinstall` or a worker's in-place edit of an installed dependency can
reach a later install of that run through a hard link into the run's
store. Two things bound it. The workers that write code are told never to
edit an installed third-party dependency (`node_modules`, a virtual
environment's `site-packages`, `vendor` and the like) but to change the
repository's own code or use the project's own patch mechanism
(implementer, conformer — which also runs the acceptance gate's repairs —,
integrator and surrogate fixer prompts). That rule is advisory (§12): what
bounds the damage is the per-run store, which a run's process removes at
its exit. A mechanical form was weighed and not added: the CLI's
permission rules match paths, so a deny on "an installed dependency" is a
per-ecosystem list of directory names (`node_modules`, `site-packages`,
`vendor`, `.venv`, …) that grows with every manager and still misses a
shell's `sed -i`; the one generic predicate, "ignored and untracked by the
repository", also refuses a worker's legitimate writes to its own ignored
files (a local `.env`, build outputs).

**Which stores an install may share.** Within a run, every manager's
download store and cache is the run's (above). One class is narrower:
*per tree* — uv, cargo, bundler, NuGet, Go's build cache, pipenv's
environments, pnpm's metadata cache, pip's user base, the .NET CLI home and
bundler's home (`_TREE_STORE_VARS`) — one set per tree, at
`<run-dir>/worktrees/.stores/tree-stores/<tree>/<name>`, set for every command leerie runs in
a tree under `<run-dir>/worktrees/` (`_tree_store_env`, applied by
`_run_streaming`), and emptied whenever a view's tip moves: a replaced
view's go with it, and a moved view is a new tree to every measurement
(§8 *A view moves to the next tip when the install's inputs are
unchanged*). These hold one tree's environment or what its build writes as
it builds — pip's user base and bundler's path are where an install puts
the tree's dependencies, pipenv's environments are the tree's, and uv's
install of the project, cargo's package lock and Go's build cache write
the store as they build — so two trees at two commits never share an
environment. The class also holds where a user-level install lands when
the system location is not writable — pip's user base (`PYTHONUSERBASE`),
the .NET CLI's home (`DOTNET_CLI_HOME`) and bundler's home
(`BUNDLE_USER_HOME`) — because each otherwise falls back to `$HOME`, which
no measurement grant writes. Review round 19 exec H2 found every pip
recipe failing in every view that way. Measured as the leerie user with
`$HOME` read-only: `pip install` answered "Defaulting to user
installation" and failed, and succeeded with `PYTHONUSERBASE` set, the
package importable from it; `dotnet restore` failed needing `~/.dotnet`;
bundler warned and fell back to a temporary home. npm, yarn, bun, uv, cargo,
go and composer needed no `$HOME` write once their store variables were
set.

A user base carries one more property than its files: pip puts a
package's console scripts in `<user base>/bin`, which only `PATH` finds,
and the image has the default base's `~/.local/bin` last on `PATH` for
that. Relocated, the scripts were on no `PATH`: measured on a real run of
a pytest repository once its install reached PyPI (*An install reaches
its inputs*), pip installed pytest into the view's user base, warned
"installed in '…/pyuser/bin' which is not on PATH", and every test run
read `pytest: command not found`, so the base and every test axis went
unmeasured. *Wherever leerie points a confined process's
`PYTHONUSERBASE`, that process's `PATH` carries its `bin`, last*
(`_with_user_scripts`, in `_worker_cache_env`, `_tree_store_env` and
every command `_run_streaming` starts), in place of the value it replaces,
and after the image's tools, so a user-installed script never shadows a
baked one. A value beneath the bake root is the image's and is left
alone. Never on the orchestrator's own `PATH` (`_leerie_stores` sets the
store variables there, not `PATH`): leerie's unconfined process never
resolves a program from a store directory, which a confined command writes
(review round 23 isolation, an observation f0ce3e56 opened).

**A worker started in a tree leerie installed for runs on that tree's
stores.** Leerie prepares some trees for a worker: the acceptance writer's
and the surrogate fixer's checkouts, each falsifier lane, the set audit's
tree and, with `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, the planning worktree
(`_ensure_worktree_deps` in each, before the worker starts). Where a
manager installs inside the tree (`node_modules`, a `.venv`) the worker
saw the install; where it installs into a per-tree store it did not.
Review round 23 exec M1 measured it on a pip repository: leerie's install
of each falsifier lane put pytest in that lane's user base
(`<run-dir>/worktrees/.stores/tree-stores/<lane>/pyuser`), the falsifier ran with
`PYTHONUSERBASE` at its side's cache, and all 6 first samples answered
"pytest isn't installed" (`could_not_demonstrate`); each re-ask
improvised a `pip install --target /tmp/…` through egress. The root
cause: the stores leerie's install of a tree writes and the stores a
worker started in that tree reads were chosen by two functions
(`_tree_store_env`, `_worker_cache_env`) that never agreed on a tree, so
"a checkout with dependencies installed" held only for managers that
install inside the tree. The invariant: *a worker started in a tree leerie
installed for sees that install* — its interpreter, its manager and its
`PATH` resolve what the install put in the tree's own stores. So one
function chooses a tree's stores for every process started in it:
`_tree_store_env` sets every per-tree variable (uv, cargo, bundler, NuGet,
Go's build cache, pipenv, pnpm's metadata cache, pip's user base and its
`bin` on `PATH`, the .NET CLI and bundler homes) for leerie's commands
there and, laid over the worker's side cache, for a worker started there
once leerie has installed for it (`_installed_tree_stores`: the tree is in
this process's install record, the one that keeps leerie from installing a
tree twice). The worker is granted the tree's stores as it is granted the
tree: written by a worker that writes its tree (the writer, the surrogate,
the falsifier — committing workers, whose code already runs in that tree
and whose tree's stores no other tree reads), read by one that reads it
(the set auditor; the judgment workers in the planning worktree). Nothing
is copied into the worker's cache, and nothing crosses trees: a tree's
stores are that tree's alone. A read-only worker cannot write what its
manager writes there as it builds (Go's build cache), as it cannot write
