classifier used to extract `required_items` only when the task was
"genuinely enumerable", with a when-in-doubt-omit posture. A requirement
it never extracted was enforced by nothing downstream: the planners, the
no-work judge and the delivery gate all verify the items they are
handed. So the classifier now accounts for the WHOLE task, and code
checks that it did, by set arithmetic over identifiers it assigned
itself:

- **Python cuts; it never reads.** The task text is cut into spans
  `S1, S2, …` at markdown delimiters only: a heading, a blank line, a
  list item at any indent; a fenced block stays whole
  (`_d1_split_spans`). Each nested list item carries a `parent` link —
  the nearest preceding list item of smaller indent in the same block —
  computed from indentation alone. Each referenced report (a markdown
  file the task names that is not tracked at HEAD, so a report filed
  for this task rather than a standing repo document such as a
  CLAUDE.md) is cut at its headings into sections `R1, R2, …`
  (`_d1_split_sections`). Python assigns the IDs and nothing else (§12
  *Delimiter-only cutting is not the deleted heading harvest*).
- **All meaning comes from the classifier's JSON.** One
  `span_dispositions` entry per span: `items` when the span states
  something the delivered work must do, contain, preserve or never
  contain — a negative constraint ("never X", "out of scope: X") is an
  item — or `no_requirement` with a typed `kind` (`heading`,
  `background`, `restatement` with the S/R id it `restates`, or
  `process_note`). One `section_roles` entry per report section:
  `requirement`, `evidence`, `suggestion` or `context`, the last three
  carrying the requirement section they `supports`. Exactly one
  `required_items` entry per `items` span and per `requirement`
  section, anchored on it by `span`. A findings table whose rows the
  task asks to address yields one item per row, typed by `table_row`
  (the row's first cell, copied). Each item is typed
  `verifiability: tree | external | execution` and, when its whole
  content is that some paths must not change, `untouched_paths`. An item
  or part decided by whether the repository's existing tests newly fail
  ("no regressions", "existing tests still pass", "don't break the X
  tests") is typed `execution` with `check: test_id_diff` — the whole
  item, or, inside a mixed item, the part (`part_checks`, each naming one
  of the item's `parts` verbatim).
- **The coverage gate is set arithmetic.** `_d1_coverage_holes` sends
  back, by ID, every span without a disposition, section without a
  role, `items` span or `requirement` section carried by no item (or by
  more than one, unless each carries a distinct `table_row`), item
  anchored elsewhere, `no_requirement` span without a valid `kind`,
  `restates`/`supports` link that resolves to no requirement, nested
  span typed a restatement of its own ancestor, and `table_row` that is
  not found verbatim in its anchor span (a quote check after whitespace
  normalisation, never a parse of the table). These ride the
  classifier's existing `judgment_check_rounds` loop. A report with no
  `requirement` section is asked about **once**; a second answer of no
  requirement stands, since a referenced file can be pure background.
  The closure — `items` spans, `requirement` sections, restatements
  that resolve to one of them (directly or through a heading whose
  block holds an `items` span), and sections supporting a requirement —
  is persisted in `state.data["requirement_coverage"]` with any
  residual holes. Residual holes after the rounds are logged and the
  run proceeds: the gate improves the item list, it never stops a run.

Measured (bench D1, sonnet, frozen designs). v6 (top-level list items
only) on 22 fresh tasks, 2 samples each: deliverable-closure Jaccard
≥ 0.8 between samples 22/22; hand-checked real requirement losses 0/22
tasks; but of the 8 recorded instances where a lost requirement caused
or contributed to a repeat run, v6 surfaced 6 as their own item and
missed a causal one — a nested sub-bullet folded into its parent's
coarse item. v6.1 (list items at any indent are delimiters, with the
parent link) surfaced the replayed targets as their own item in 12/12
sample-instances (4 targets × 3), bringing the 8 to 8/8 (causal 3/3),
and held Jaccard ≥ 0.8 on 12/12 tasks with changed spans, at 2.9× the items
(446 → 1,293 over those 12 tasks). v6.2 (one item may carry several
sibling spans) was rejected: still 2× the items and its coverage loop
did not converge. The item count is paid on the verification side
instead (*Grouped judging*, below).

**The delivery gate: required items are verified on the tree that
ships.** The no-work judge above enforces `required_items` against the
tree — but only at the START of the run AFTER the one that shipped.
Measured cost of that asymmetry: a run shipped deliverables violating a
standing constraint carried in its own required items (an explicit
"never reference X in the code" instruction), every in-run gate passed
them, and the next run's no-work judge — correctly — refused to declare
the task done over exactly that violation. Fail-open sent it to
planning, and the cycle was structurally able to repeat: whatever the
terminal gate checks that the shipping gates don't is a guaranteed
extra run per violation.

So the same standard runs at finalize, in the run that ships. After the
last wave integrates and before the final-conformer pass, a
**`delivery_judge`** (read-only, TREE_READER_TOOLS, cwd = the
integrated staging worktree — the exact tree the PR will carry)
verifies each required item and returns one typed verdict per item,
aligned by integer `item_index` — mechanical alignment, never prose
matching (Language-to-JSON). Two reliability rules shape the consumer:

- **Majority vote on disputes only.** Single-trial LLM judging is
  measurably noisy (the demoted `task_coverage_judge` returned a
  different finding set 85% of the time on identical input), and the
  published reliability curves show most recoverable agreement arriving
  by 3–5 votes. A clean first pass confirms at one spawn; only when the
  first sample flags something do two more run, and an item is
  confirmed unmet only at 2-of-3. Voting cannot fix an error the judge
  makes consistently — that residual is accepted and covered by the
  fail-open below.
- **Route into the existing fix loop; re-check mechanically.**
  Confirmed-unmet items ride the final-conformer pass as a prompt
  section (`_format_unmet_required_items_section`) rather than getting
  a fix loop of their own — the conformer already edits, commits, and
  is bounded, clobber-checked, and rollback-protected on staging. After
  that pass, the judge runs again (same vote rules): the fixer's
  self-report is never trusted, same discipline as
  `check_rebaser_worktree_state`.

A residual after the recheck ships anyway — fail-open toward shipping,
recorded loudly in `state.data["delivery_gate"].unmet_after` — because
a blocking gate with a noisy judge gets switched off, and the cross-run
backstop now exists (*A dispute's evidence is planning input*: the next
run's no-work judge vetoes and its evidence steers the next plan at the
residual). One flag governs required-items checking on both sides:
`--skip-coverage-check` suppresses the plan-side advisory coverage
judge and this gate alike. A run whose classifier extracted no
`required_items` pays nothing.

**The judge's turn budget scales with the item count.** A verifier's
workload is proportional to what it verifies, and a fixed cap converts
a thorough judge into a crashed one: measured on the gate's first two
outings (one task, 2026-09-29, 9- and 6-item lists), all four judge
attempts across both runs died at `error_max_turns` one turn over the
fixed cap, mid-list, while verifying conscientiously — so the gate
whose whole purpose is catching an unmet item was skipped (advisory)
in a run where a bench replay of the same payload flags an item
unmet. The budget is therefore derived per call — a setup base plus
a per-item allowance approximating the measured thorough pace (the
live traces show ~5–6 turns per item, measured as total turns over
items covered at death; an efficient batched style finishes far
under the base) — with a ceiling, which binds from ten items, so a
runaway list cannot buy unbounded turns. The ceiling is an honest
trade: the further past ten items a list runs, the further the
budget falls behind the measured pace, so a long list (roughly a
dozen items and beyond) can again exhaust the cap and skip the gate
— an accepted, bounded residual, preferred over an uncapped budget.
The same failure hit the satisfied-probe
(§ *satisfied-probe* below). Both of its call sites judge the same
single criterion (the HEAD-probe helper — serving the provider-subset
pre-spawn check, and until settle-by-execution replaced it the no-commit
rescue — sends the same one
`success_criteria_seed` payload the pre-schedule probe sends); what
balloons the cost, at either site, is a criterion that is met or
audit-shaped on the judged tree, because a probe cannot say
"satisfied" without verifying every part. Measured in one run: the
pre-schedule sweep's confirming probes ran 14–21 turns, two of
twelve first attempts died at `error_max_turns` one turn over the
cap and were recovered by `claude_p`'s retry — while every
HEAD-probe attempt for one genuine no-op subtask (two pre-spawn and
four rescue attempts, six in all) died the same way, and no rescue
means retryable-failure, so the retry cap turned a correct no-op
into `wave has unresolved subtasks`. The asymmetric caps are therefore
justified by CONSEQUENCE, not workload shape: a HEAD-probe cap-out
had no recovery below the run level, so that helper carries the
larger cap; a pre-schedule cap-out is retried, and a double cap-out
merely fail-safe-keeps the subtask — one wasted implementer round
whose resulting no-op then lands on the larger-capped rescue — so
the small cap stays acceptable there.

**Grouped judging at coverage item counts.** Requirement coverage
(above) hands the gate about three times the items, and one prompt
does not survive that: measured on 12 recorded delivery-judge calls
(bench Q7/D1, 9–58 items per prompt even at the old item counts), the
single-prompt judge left 59% of all items not met — 317 of them unmet
with no citation, "not inspected" — so its adjudicated false-unmet
rate on labelled controls was 46% and it flagged a labelled defect for
the right reason in 2 of 34 samples. So the gate judges in packs
(`_d1_judge_packs`):

- **Group by root ancestor.** An item's group is the root of its
  anchor span's parent chain; items on one report section share a
  group; an item whose anchor is unknown is its own group. Groups,
  ordered by their smallest item index, are packed consecutively while
  a pack stays within `d1_pack_items` (20); a single group larger than
  30 is cut into consecutive chunks of 30, so a nested requirement and
  its siblings are judged side by side.
- **Each prompt knows its slice** ("these are k of the task's N
  required items… return a verdict for exactly these item_index
  values"), carries the global `item_index` of each item, and gets the
  turn budget of its own pack size. Verdicts merge by `item_index`; a
  verdict for an index outside the pack is ignored. Packs run
  concurrently up to `max_parallel`. The dispute vote above applies per
  pack (a pack whose first sample flags nothing costs one spawn). The
  one per-item re-ask is the next rule's, for items a sample did not
  inspect; an item a sample did judge is never re-judged item by item.
- **Every item is judged before its vote counts.** A sample can hand an
  item back unread: a verdict whose parts are typed `not_inspected` and
  none `unmet` ("Not inspected."), or no verdict for it at all. Measured
  on two barnacle runs of 34 required items each (2026-11-05/06, packs
  of 14, 20 and 30): one sample in three left 5–21 of its pack's items
  `not_inspected`, two returned 1 and 2 verdicts for a 14-item pack —
  each finishing at 8–55 turns of a 90-turn budget, no call at the
  budget. The judge stopped; nothing cut it off. Counted as votes, a
  `not_inspected` verdict was an unmet vote and an omission a met one,
  so an item no sample read was routed to the conformer as a defect —
  9 of one run's 14 recheck residuals, all 7 of the other's — or shipped
  `met` because a sample left it out (13 of 14 items in one final
  detection pack). So code asks once more: the items a sample left
  uninspected go back to the judge in the same prompt shape for exactly
  those `item_index` values — a smaller pack, halved when the sample
  inspected none of its pack — and the follow-up's verdicts replace the
  sample's for them. An item still uninspected after that casts no vote
  from that sample; one a majority of a pack's samples could not inspect
  is `unknown` — never confirmed unmet, never met, named under "Needs
  human verification", and read as `unknown` by every reader of the
  pass, as a worker-only met is (*Execution-shaped items are judged from
  the run's own records*). A first sample that leaves an item unknown
  draws the two dispute samples, as a flag does. The pack size stays:
  no sample reached its turn budget, so the budget a pack size sets is
  not what left the items unread.
- **Code settles what code can.** An item typed
  `verifiability: external` (a PR description, a deploy, a human
  action) is never judged: it goes to `state.data
  ["needs_human_verification"]`, the list the PR shows. An item whose
  whole content is that some paths stay unchanged is settled by
  `git diff --name-only <own start>..HEAD -- <paths>` on the integrated
  tree (`_d1_untouched_verdict`): empty output is met, a listed file is
  unmet with that file as evidence; an unsafe path, an unknown own
  start or a git error sends the item to the judge.
- **A test outcome is the failing-test-ID diff's to settle, never prose.**
  An item typed `execution` / `check: test_id_diff` is never judged, never
  falsified and never sent to an implementer: code reads the final tree's
  failing-test-ID diff (§9 *Which failures are new*) — **met** when B\*
  confirmed no new failing ID on the tree being judged: the diff had no
  candidates, or every candidate failed on every base rerun
  (`pre_existing`); **unmet** when it confirmed new ones; **unknown** in
  every other case — no diff for this tree (no IDs on either side, no
  measurement, or a tree that moved since), or a candidate B\* never
  settled: no rerun produced a verdict for it (`no_verdict`, which is what
  every candidate gets when the base checkout could not be created), its
  reruns disagreed (`resource_affected`), or the confirm budget left it
  unsettled (`budget_short_unsettled`: no base/final pair finished, a
  discovery find the budget cut, or a file sized out — the reason says
  "could not confirm within the budget: <files>", and for a file never
  rerun "not rerun (sized out of the budget): <files>"). A candidate the budget
  alone kept short, at least one pair finished and every finished rerun
  agreeing, is new (§9 *Which failures are new*, step 4), so the item is
  unmet. A candidate that failed on the final tree and was
  never measured on the base is not confirmed absent; reading it as met
  shipped a "no regressions" item as met with the candidate never checked
  (review round 4 M2). Unmet needs nothing more: the confirmed new IDs
  already make the run `unconverged` (§6) and already drive the final
  conformance's next round. Unknown goes to the PR's "Needs human
  verification" list with its reason (which candidates, and why B\* could
  not settle them); like any human-verification gap it is not unfinished
  work, so it does not by itself change the run outcome, but the item's
  row reads `unknown`, never `met`. Inside a
  mixed item the judge types such a part `kind: test_outcome` (the
  payload names the classifier's `part_checks` for it), and code drops
  that part from the verdict before it is checked or voted: the item is
  met or unmet on its other parts. Its row still carries the diff's verdict
  for that part. When the other parts are met and the diff did not say
  met, the row reads the diff's verdict — `unknown`, its reason
  `met except: <part>, unknown — <why>`, or `unmet` when B\* confirmed
  new failures — never `met` over a part B\* did not settle (review round
  5 L3: a compound item read `met` while its "no regressions" part was
  unknown, though the gap was written). The row also says its other parts
  were met, so the delivery ratchet keeps protecting them, and like a pure
  test-outcome item it never reaches `unmet_final`. In a replayed run (barnacle 45fa4253,
  pass 1) the judges held an item unmet on its "no regressions: the
  final-tree full test run must not show new failures" part, read from a
  record that said only "red", and the delivery re-drive spent its whole
  budget — four implementer sessions, about 25 minutes — on an unmet item
  no implementer could change: each ran its own base-vs-tree comparison,
  reported "33 failed on both", committed nothing, and the item stayed
  unmet.
- **The finding-level contract** (below) is asked of the first pack
  only, so it is judged once, not once per pack.

Measured (bench Q7/D1, arm (c): routing, packs of 20, table rows typed;
dev and fresh cases, hand-adjudicated): real false unmet 3/116 = 2.6%
(CI 0.9–7.3; all three the "note it in the PR" half of a mixed item),
right-reason catch 13/39 = 33% (on the dev cases 7/17 targets, equal to
grouped judging without routing, against 1/17 for the single prompt),
at $2.54 per pass — 7.3× the single prompt. Arm (d) — per-part typing,
packs of 30, and the per-item re-judge — was **not** adopted: its catch
was unchanged (2/14 against (c)'s 2/14 on the same cases), its false
unmet rose to 7.4% (conservative), and the re-judge made a pass 8.6×
on average and 15–32× on large tasks.

**Typed evidence for the delivery judge.** Two mechanical checks hand
the judge evidence it would otherwise have to find by reading, each as
a section of its prompt that is present only when there is something to
show (a run without either sends a byte-identical prompt). Neither ever
re-drives on its own: what happens to an item is the judge's verdict,
under the same dispute vote.

- **Site tokens.** When the report's inline examples carry
  site-identifying tokens (§5 *The report's own example inputs are
  captured too*), every line the run's diff adds is matched against
  them, case-insensitively, on identifier-segment boundaries (`_`, `-`,
  `.`, `/` separate segments, so a token is found inside
  `Token_Forms_Field`). A guard test's bare term list — a test file
  whose added line is nothing but quoted or regex literals of single
  terms — is a denylist, not a leak, and is not a hit. There is no
  base-tree skip. Hits, with the report example each token came from,
  go to the judge for any item that forbids naming the sites (at most 3
  per file and 30 in all, the total stated). Measured (bench Q5/N7a,
  whole-word rules): with the base-tree skip the check was inert (0 of
  74); without it and with the provenance, the gated judge called 17 of
  17 fresh leaking PRs unmet against 6 of 17 for one sample of today's
  judge, and 30 of 30 clean PRs met. The segment-boundary rule comes
  from the later lever round: on its no-harm stress the judge kept all 29
  clean PRs it judged met (31 calls; one of the 30 clean cases was never
  judged), while of the 4 PRs that touched a guard list, 3 were judged
  unmet (6 of 7 calls) — the residual harm the guard-line exclusion only partly
  removes, and the reason the hits stay evidence, never a gate.
- **Contract literals.** An implementer's `external_contract_assumption`
  risk says its change is right only if something outside its subtask
  holds. A `contract_extractor` worker types each one once: the
  counterpart subtask of this run (or none), the exact literal, its kind
  (`string_value`, `identifier`, `route_path`, `other`), and a carrying
  symbol; code drops a counterpart that is not another subtask of the
  run and marks a literal not found verbatim in the risk unverified.
  The check (v7e) then reads the counterpart's integration diff and the
  integrated tree: only a plain token literal is checked; a route must
  be served by an app-router page or appear on a counterpart added line;
  a string or identifier is honoured by a counterpart added line, else
  only by a non-test code file outside the owner's own files — a doc,
  an i18n file or a migration does not honour a code contract — and is
  flagged even then when the counterpart's added lines carry a
  near-variant of it (`autopay` for `auto`). Flags go to the judge with
  the risk text. Measured (bench Q10, held-out half): v7e flagged 157 of
  162 synthetic mismatches (one side of a verified real producer/consumer
  pair renamed) and 0 of 105 unmutated controls, where the rule set
  without the code-only and near-variant rules flagged 106 — every miss
  of that one was a literal still present in a doc or another consumer.
  On the recorded real risks (Q5 worlds), which v7e was designed on, so
  these are design-set numbers and not held-out evidence: 6 of 8
  violations flagged, 0 of 288 false flags. The checks read JavaScript/TypeScript repos;
  the code-file and test-file patterns also take other languages'
  usual suffixes.

**A site resting on an untyped resolution is settled by the run.** An
audited `fix` site whose resolution kind — the audit's or a claim's — is
`other` passes the claims check without a typed match (§5 *Every `fix`
site is claimed*), so nothing has compared it with what changed. 0.44.0
handed every such site to a human: the user's run 48c48629
(barnacle#665) listed "Check `src/scraper/session-shared.ts` … (D8) is
resolved" under "Needs human verification" — a reading of the
repository's own code, which the run can make as well as any reviewer,
under the heading kept for a resource only a human can bring (§9 *Only
an entry naming an external resource is external*), and the user found
the section confusing for it. So the call that asks the contract verdict
(below) also asks, per such site, one typed answer: `site_verdicts`
entries of `site_id`, `resolved` and the citations of the code that
resolves it. Code settles a site only on a majority of that pass's
samples voting `resolved` with at least one citation, every one of which
verifies against HEAD (`_verify_delivery_cite`, the items' rule); a
fabricated quote settles nothing. The settlement is recorded on the
site's `site_claims` row and re-taken by every pass that asks the
contract, so the last tree judged decides. A settled site is not shown.
One the gate did not settle — never asked (no gate ran, it crashed), voted
unresolved, or cited nothing that verifies — is listed under "Not
verified by this run" with the judge's evidence when it gave one,
never under "Needs human verification". It does not gate: the contract
verdict already judges every audited site, and an unmet contract is what
re-drives.

**The gate judges the finding, not only the items.** Measured across
three reports' repeat-run loops (14 of the 17 v0.32.x runs,
2026-09-28..30): every run that shipped a fix shipped an
internally-consistent narrowed one — each satisfying the
items-level gate, shipping fail-open past it with its residual
recorded, or (three runs) shipping after a judge crash skipped the
gate entirely; where the gate judged, every residual it shipped
past the recheck was a standing no-regressions constraint,
recorded fail-open (in one run that residual was a concrete
reopened regression, not a mere cannot-verify) — while the
*reported finding* stayed open, costing one full run per
sub-shape (the create-account tag/role campaign, then a
classification predicate re-fixed across
four PRs, the last two at sites an earlier run's audit had already
enumerated). Items are necessary but not sufficient: they verify
what the classifier extracted, not what the report demanded. So
when the run carries an applicable defect audit (§5:
`defect_scope.applicable` with non-empty `sites`), the same
delivery-judge call also returns a typed **contract verdict** —
`met`, `unmet`, `conflict`, or `unverifiable` — judging whether
the audited
`defect_shape` (the violated behavioral contract) holds on the
integrated tree and whether every audited site is either fixed or
ruled out with recorded evidence. A flagged contract buys the same
3-sample dispute vote as a flagged item (an absent contract object on
an asked call escalates as a flag but tallies as a no-vote; no
verdict reaching 2 of 3 resolves to met, the items' own fail-open
direction), and the asked call carries a +12-turn allowance under
the unchanged 90 ceiling — which the combined budget then reaches
from eight items instead of ten. `unmet` rides the final-conformer
pass and its recheck exactly like unmet items; `conflict` — two
pinned contracts contradicting at one decision site, the measured
shape where one subtask's fix was reverted by another protecting a
prior bug's guards — is persisted and logged with both contracts
named, because it needs an operator or a discriminating-predicate
design, not another fix loop. The fourth verdict, `unverifiable`,
exists because `met` must not be reachable on hypothesis-shaped
evidence: measured on one task's ten runs across three leerie
versions (2026-09-28..10-01), the report pinned its defect to named
external data no worker could ever read (§5 *Report-named ground
truth*), every proof then rested on synthetic fixtures authored by
the run itself — each encoding the run's own hypothesis about what
the real data contains — and both completed v0.33.0 gates verdicted
`met` that way, silently; the cross-run residual channel (below)
then correctly stayed empty, so each next run re-derived the same
contract cold. So the gate's payload states which of the audit's
extracted ground-truth inputs are absent in this environment, and
the judge is directed to return `unverifiable` — naming exactly
which missing input blocks which part of the contract — when the
contract is data-triggered by absent inputs and in-tree evidence
cannot decide it (bench-measured on the live run's verbatim payload
and tree: the control replay reproduces `met`; with the availability
fact and the fourth verdict available, 2/2 replicates flip to
`unverifiable` and discount the synthetic fixtures unprompted).
Because this guarantee matters and is mechanically checkable (§12),
the code enforces what the prompt advises: a `met` majority reached
while the audit says data-dependent and every named input is absent
is recorded as `unverifiable`, the judge's raw claim preserved
beside it. `unverifiable` does not ride the conformer pass — there
is nothing on the tree for a conformer to fix; it persists like any
contract residual, steers the next run through
`prior_delivery_residual`, and is stated loudly in the run's
output at whichever gate half records it — the delivery pre-pass
(where the final-tree conformance pass still follows), or the
recheck directly before finalize, when the pre-pass confirmed
unmet items or an unmet contract and the recheck's own contract
verdict then lands unverifiable — with the exact `--inspect-dir`
remediation when the audit's own record
established the data-absence case (data-dependent, with named
inputs absent); any other voted unverifiable states the judge's
evidence instead, because asserting a data-absence narrative the
run's own audit does not support would put an unverified claim on
exactly the channel this verdict exists to keep truthful. The
operator learns the gap on run one, not from a post-hoc telemetry
investigation ten runs in. The present case is the converse duty,
and it closes a measured gap: on the first run with the data
mounted, workers read the archive extensively — host
distributions, capture ordering, the real declarations — and still
verified every fix against run-authored synthetic fixtures; zero
end-to-end executions of the report's repro appear in its records,
because the acceptance test was nobody's assigned work (the only
worker that evaluates the finding is read-only, and nothing tasked
an acting worker with running it). So, in the §12 shape — prompts
assign, records verify, the gate enforces: planners, whose
`defect_scope` ctx already carries the audit's `ground_truth`, are
directed that resolved-present inputs plus a repro command mean
the plan CARRIES a subtask that executes the repro against them
and records its outcome — the campaign's acceptance check, owned
like any other subtask; that execution lands in the per-worker
logs and therefore in the executed-commands digest; and the judge
is directed that with inputs PRESENT the record's repro evidence
decides the contract — a met resting only on synthetic fixtures
while the repro was never run must state why in-tree evidence
suffices, else return an ACTIONABLE unmet naming exactly that
(bench-measured on the live run's verbatim recheck payload: 2/2
replicates return unmet leading with the unexecuted repro), which
rides the ordinary final-conformer route — an acting worker with
execution rights, whose repro run then shows in the recheck's
fresh digest. Fail-open stands unchanged: a residual
ships, recorded in `delivery_gate.contract_after`; what closes the
cross-run loop is that a fresh run's planners receive the most
recent COMPLETED same-task run's residual as ctx
(`prior_delivery_residual` — completion means the orchestrator's
own exit code 0; `finished_at` is a discovery sentinel the die()
path also writes and does not qualify — the *dispute's evidence is
planning input* discipline extended across runs), so run N+1 plans
at the recorded gap instead of rediscovering it.

**Execution-shaped items are judged from the run's own records.**
Measured on three of the gate's completed outings: the dominant
unmet item was "no regressions", with evidence citing the sandbox's
command-approval gate — the judge is deliberately read-only
(TREE_READER_TOOLS), so an item demanding an executed suite is
unverifiable *by construction* from inside the gate, and every such
run paid the 3-sample dispute vote plus conformer routing for a
verdict that could never change. The evidence already exists: every
worker's per-run JSONL log carries structured `tool_use` records of
each command it actually ran, with results. The gate's payload now
includes an executed-commands digest (the run's build/lint/test
invocations with verbatim result tails, extracted mechanically by
BLT-verb token match — command strings are mechanical, and the
JUDGE interprets the result prose, never Python — with the verb set
widened by the lead verbs of the audit's own `repro_command` when
one exists: measured on the motivating repository, the report's
repro was node-led while the repo's BLT verbs were all pnpm-led, so
a record the judge is told is exhaustive would never have contained
the acceptance run it is directed to look for, and the
repro-decides rule would have produced a false, unclearable unmet
that the conformer's own re-run could not clear), and the judge is
directed to verify execution-shaped items against that record,
citing it. The record contains only what the run actually ran —
conformers execute targeted falsifiers, not necessarily a full
suite — so an item whose commands appear nowhere remains honestly
unmet, and its remediation is the routed conformer RUNNING them,
which the recheck's fresh record then shows. The record also carries
the orchestrator's OWN results, which no worker log holds: the
final-tree build/lint/test axes it measured, the test IDs B* confirmed
newly failing, and each held-out acceptance set's final verdict
(`_orchestrator_results_digest`), so an execution-shaped item is not
called unmet merely because the run that settled it was leerie's own.
Only those lines can verify a `met`: a worker's runs happened in a
worker's working tree — the final conformer's and a re-drive
implementer's in staging, beside files that may not ship — so a cite of
one is shown to the judge and kept as a falsifier lead, but verifies
nothing on its own (§8 *Every post-execution verdict is of the committed
tree*).

**What a worker ran is read from its own transcript, never from a
command's output.** Leerie's record of what a worker executed — the
worker half of this record, the dependency capture's install-command
hint (§6½), the settle-time declared-command check (§9), the conformer's
axis-run warnings, the falsifier's probe activity, the malformed-envelope
retry, the session a re-ask resumes, the run-health telemetry — is the
structured events of that worker's own `claude -p` session, keyed by the
worker it was spawned as, and one reader yields them to every consumer. A build, a test run, CI parity or any other
measurement prints whatever the code under measurement prints, and a line
it prints in the shape of a tool call is not one. Measured: the record
took every `logs/*.log`, which also holds leerie's runs of the
repository's commands (the base baseline, CI parity, coverage, the
settle-time execution check), and the per-subtask and final conformers'
axes were measured into the conformer's own transcript file — so a test
printing a `tool_use` line for `pnpm test` and a `tool_result` line
saying it passed entered the record as a passing run, in the conformer's
name. So: a worker's transcript is written in its log directory's own
`transcripts/` directory (`logs/transcripts/`, `logs/held-out/transcripts/`),
which only leerie's spawn of a worker writes, and every log of a command
leerie runs is written beside it, never in it. The two are separate
namespaces, so no command's output path can name a transcript, whatever
names the two sides pick. Measured (review round 22 H4): while both were
`<logs>/<name>.log`, a command log and a transcript met whenever the
names did — the acceptance writer's transcript and its set's validation
run were both `logs/held-out/acceptance-<k>.log`, the refusal below fired
on leerie's own path, and every run that wrote held-out sets died at the
first set's validation; earlier, per-site suffixes (`-axes.log`) had kept
the conformers' axes out of their transcripts one name at a time. The
root cause was the shared namespace, and the invariant is that no
command's output path can name a transcript. Leerie also registers each
transcript as it spawns the worker (`transcripts.ndjson` beside it), and
a reader that enumerates transcripts takes only registered ones; a
measurement refuses any path in a transcripts directory, or a registered
transcript's; and within a transcript only the stream's own events count — a line of
the CLI's stderr, which leerie writes into the same file under its own
header, is never parsed as an event. The stream is the CLI's alone: no
command the worker runs can write into it, because each runs in a Landlock
domain nested inside the CLI's (§6 *A worker's commands cannot reach its
CLI*; review round 21 R4 wrote a forged `tool_use` into it through
`/proc/<cli>/fd/1`). A second reader was the gap: with
the record closed, the re-ask's session choice and the health scan still
parsed `logs/` text on their own, so a printed `session_id` could steer
which session a re-ask resumed. A run directory made before the registry
is never resumed by this leerie (§6 *A run directory is continued only by
a leerie of its layout*), so a missing registry line always means "not a
transcript", never "written before records existed".

That rule leaves an item whose only evidence is a command the
orchestrator never runs itself — the audit's repro, `npm run e2e`,
`make docs` — with no measurement of the committed tree: the judge cites
the worker's run and the cite cannot verify. Such a `met` is neither
confirmed nor refuted, so it is `unknown`: the vote is typed
`record_worker_only`, and an item whose unmet votes are all of that kind
is not confirmed unmet — it goes to "Needs human verification" with the
commands the worker ran, never to a re-drive (review round 12 L3: an
implementer cannot make a worker's past run count either, so a re-drive
of it could only end `unconverged`).

`unknown` has to hold everywhere the judge's pass is read, not only in
the human list. Review round 14 (claims M1, execution L3) drove the gap:
the judge's pass reported only the items it confirmed unmet, and every
reader took "not unmet" for "met" — so the worker-only item went to a
human while its detection row read `met`, the delivery ratchet counted
it among the items met before a repair (and so re-verified, and could
"regress", an item nothing had read), and a re-drive's re-check of it
rewrote the row `met`. The root cause is a two-valued interface for a
three-valued verdict. So a judge pass records, per item, that its met
rests only on a worker's run, and every reader reads it: the detection
row is `unknown` (with the reason), the item is not prior met for the
ratchet, and a re-check that finds the same writes `unknown`. The
invariant is the one this section opens with: a verdict becomes `met`
only on a read of a commit.

An entry names its item by the item's index in the run's required
items, and every pass keys it that way — the invariant is that an item
index means one item everywhere it is written. Review round 14 M4 drove
the root cause: the judge numbered the items it was handed, and the
re-drive's re-check handed it only the items it re-checks, so a re-check
of item 1 judged it as item 0 and replaced item 0's entry — erasing the
human check of an item it never read — and an entry it wrote carried the
same wrong index. The judge is now always given the whole list and told
which indices to read.

Leerie does not re-run the worker's command to settle it. That was built
(review round 12 L3) and withdrawn (round 14), for two measured reasons.
It never ran: of the 252 distinct worker commands the two bench replays'
logs put on the record, none qualified under the rule a safe re-run
needs — the repository's own build, lint, test or repro command as one
plain argv, with only its runner's options and paths in the commit;
workers write `pnpm test <file>`, not the configured `pnpm run test`,
and chain `cd`, `mkdir`, pipes and heredocs. And it was risk surface:
review found two high-severity defects in it (round 13 H1 —
the worker's own result tail entered the store a cite verifies against,
so whatever a worker's run printed verified; and an interpreter-led
record entry, `python3 -c <worker code>`, ran in the orchestrator). A
mechanism that measured nothing in practice and executed worker-chosen
argv when it did is removed rather than narrowed further; every such
item already ended at a human once the re-run was refused, and now
reaches one directly.

**Delivery detection: a cited judge, or a falsifier that proves it
by execution.** A read-only judge misses the defects that only
execution shows — measured on the labelled delivery corpus (bench
N2e, 14 pre-registered undelivered items, 52 delivered controls), the
cited judge alone caught 3/14 (1/52 false unmet), and the misses were
behaviours (a threshold, a delay, an input shape on a second code
path) the code *reads* as delivered. So the final verdict on each item is a union of
two detectors, each checked by code (bench Q2 *F+*, frozen design):

- **The judge cites, and code checks every citation.** Each verdict
  splits its item into typed `parts` (`static` / `behavioral`, status
  `met` / `unmet` / `not_inspected`), each carrying `cites`
  `{path, line_start, line_end, quote}`. Code verifies every quote as a
  whitespace-normalised substring of that file at `HEAD`
  (`_verify_delivery_cite`); `path: "RECORD"` is checked against the
  executed-commands record; `path: "ABSENT"` / `"ABSENT:<pathspec>"`
  is the absence claim, which code re-runs as `git grep -E` and accepts
  only when nothing matches. A `met` whose parts are not all `met`, or
  whose every part does not carry at least one verified citation, is
  rejected — counted as an unmet vote — so a fabricated quote cannot buy
  a `met`. The pack and the 2-of-3 dispute vote are unchanged; the
  benched pipeline's per-item re-judge is not added (*Grouped judging*
  measured it at 8.6× a pass for no catch). Unlike the benched verifier,
  a real quote cited at the wrong lines still verifies: it is a
  mislocation, not a fabrication.
- **A falsifier tries to prove the item undelivered.** After the
  held-out acceptance gate, on the tree that ships, every item the
  judge is asked about (never an `external` item, never an
  `untouched_paths` item — code and the PR's "needs human
  verification" own those) gets up to `falsifier_samples` (3)
  independent `falsifier` samples. Each runs in a disposable checkout
  of the final commit with dependencies installed (and, on a Prisma
  repository, a fresh throwaway database — §8 *Prisma repositories get
  a real database*), and gets the item,
  the run's own diff (start commit and stat), the run's shown
  held-out acceptance files, never a held-back one (§6 *A falsifier
  reads only what a fixer may read*; read-only, git-ignored in that
  checkout only, leads only), and
  the judge's typed unmet parts for that item (hypotheses, never
  expected values). It writes ONE new probe test through a public entry
  point, asserting the item's own words, and runs it.
- **What ships is what was measured.** The falsifier's system prompt
  is the frozen F+ prompt and its leads addendum, concatenated
  verbatim, and its input is the frozen F+ user prompt. The only
  differences are the ones the code requires:
  1. the leads directory `.q2ctx/` is `.leerie-falsifier/`
     (`FALSIFIER_LEADS_DIR`), twice in the addendum;
  2. when the run's start commit cannot be read, the input says
     `START COMMIT of this run: unknown.` in place of the commit and its
     diff stat (the bench always had one);
  3. the item's `source_ref` is its typed span when it has one (the
     bench corpus carried `source_ref` directly);
  4. the item's classifier `parts` ride inside THE ITEM TO CHECK, and step
     1 of the prompt says each part is required and a part covering many
     places fails when any one of them falls short (bench SW, *The
     falsifier gets the item whole* below).
  5. its leads are the shown sets only, where F+ read every valid set
     (§6 *A falsifier reads only what a fixer may read*). This one is not
     a mechanical difference: on a run with four or more valid sets it
     takes two sets of leads away (132 of the 179 held-out corpus items;
     16 of F+'s 23 held-out catches were on such runs). It is benched as
     arm `shown` against arm `base` (F+ as frozen) on the same corpora —
     on the items whose final commit still exists, 24 of the 31 held-out
     targets and 125 of the 148 controls (measured 2026-11-06; most
     barnacle run branches are gone) — held to a catch at most 2 below
     base's and a false-unmet count not above base's
     (`bench_falsifier_shown.py`). *Status: detection ran, closure did
     not.* On the 102 of those items whose leads differ (12 targets, 90
     controls; the other items' leads are byte-identical), catch is 10 of
     12 in both arms and false unmet is 10 of 90 against base's recorded 9
     of 90: one over the gate, with 5 items new and 4 gone, the arm fresh
     against a record of 2026-10-26. No catch was lost. Whether a fixer
     shown a probe closes the defect is what this input is for, and it has
     its own bench, frozen before any worker ran: recorded genuine
     falsifier-only items and a few that are not report defects, the probe
     shown against the item words alone, on a bar of closure at least twice
     the control and at least half. It ran twice. Lane XC (leerie 0.46.0,
     barnacle items from the RCA) passed closure, 6 of 10 genuine shown
     samples against 2 of 10 blind, and failed its harm rule: a fixer
     obeyed a probe that contradicts the report and broke two existing
     tests (N3), another bent code against pinned tests (G4-shown-2), and
     the worker-reported contest was used once in 14 shown samples. That
     led to the measured conflict and to zero progress counting the probe
     (§8 *Delivery re-drive* rule 4). Lane X2 then ran fresh cases with
     production's post-commit path simulated (frozen before any worker
     ran: six falsifier-only items of the week of 2026-11-08 — barnacle
     4f9a4b4f i13, b24806a1 i13, 79c8fbe7 i8, 879de601 i8, navegando
     e99c1df1 i0, e0d101e3 i0 — five genuine, one not a defect, hand
     labelled before running; 2 samples per arm). Closed means kept by
     that path, the probe passing, and a root fix by reading the diff:
     shown 7 of 10 genuine, blind 0 of 10, today 0 by construction. On the
     not-a-defect item both shown samples tried the change the probe asks
     for, saw an existing test break, reverted and objected
     (`breaks_existing_test`), so nothing reached the check; nothing
     harmful survived
     (a blind sample's change that drops the endorsed fallback for
     optional selects did). The conflict fired on both shown samples of
     e0d101e3, a genuine item: each fix was right and still rolled back,
     because the audit table's existing test pins the hardcoded header,
     and each also left one Spanish value identical to English, which an
     existing parity test caught. One shown sample (e99c1df1) fixed only
     the input the probe names and left three sibling controls with the
     same defect: kept, and not counted closed. The cases are clustered
     (two pairs share a report section) and only one is not a defect. The
     Q2 numbers below describe F+, not this input.
  The first shipped prompt also told the worker what the orchestrator
  checks and offered the executed-commands record as a lead, and its
  input carried that record: none of it was benched, so the Q2 numbers
  did not describe it. All three are gone. The checks were already in the
  benched prompt's own words — one NEW file, run with the repository's
  test runner, outside the leads; the item span copied
  character-for-character; the failure confirmed by a second run; the
  failing assertion copied from the probe; no source reads, code
  evaluation or test-only imports, "discarded automatically".
- **Code decides whether a falsifier demonstrated anything.** A
  sample is confirmed only when all of these hold: the probe is one
  new file, outside the leads and not an acceptance file, that the
  repository's scoped test runner can run; the item quote it claims to
  test is verbatim in the item's sentence or one of its parts (after
  NFC/whitespace normalisation);
  its named case fails under B* on a pristine installed copy of the
  final commit (`_confirm_still_failing`, serial runner, so a load
  flake never confirms), the probe placed in a held-out sandbox over that
  copy, never written into it (§6 *A held-out evaluation runs alone*); the failing assertion it quotes lies inside
  that case's reachable code and is an assertion (*The quoted assertion
  is one the test framework makes*, below); and the AST coupling check is clean —
  the case reads no source or document text, evaluates no code text,
  and imports no symbol only tests use (`_falsifier_coupling`, over
  the TypeScript AST of the probe, policy in Python). A symbol is used by
  production code when any production code, its own module included,
  refers to it outside its own declaration — read from syntax, so a call is
  told from the definition and a self-recursive call is not a use; a helper
  whose only production caller shares its module is not test-only. A
  file read is of the tree's text unless the file cannot be one of the
  tree's: a JSON path, or a path inside a directory the case made fresh
  (`mkdtemp`) joined only with plain segments — traced from syntax
  through the probe's own bindings, each name to its declaration, every
  value a binding is given having to be such a path — when nothing the
  case runs copies, links or moves another file in. Such a file was
  written while the probe ran, by the code it exercises, so asserting on
  it observes behaviour, not the tree's source. Every other read, a path
  the trace cannot follow included, still counts. Measured: barnacle run
  87580f62 item 9 ("… no literal secrets are written back"). Its sample 2
  ran the script on a flow file in a fresh directory, walked the run
  directory the script wrote and found the literal secret in the written
  flow record. The old rule, which counted every read whose path is not a
  JSON literal, rejected it because the path is a variable. The item
  shipped `met`, shown unmet in 5 of 6 samples, and an independent audit
  reproduced the leak 3 of 3 times. Replayed under this rule it confirms.
  A probe that runs a generator writing into the tree and reads what it
  wrote still counts as a read (a2a825c2 item 19): the trace sees a path
  under the tree, and syntax cannot tell a new file there from an old
  one. The coupling
  check is JS/TS-only, as benched. Its facts are syntax-only — a parse
  of one file, no type checking, no program — so the repository's own
  compiler version does not matter to them, and any TypeScript with the
  JS compiler API reads them the same. The facts script therefore uses
  the tree's own `typescript` when that package has the compiler API,
  and otherwise a pinned 5.x the image ships for exactly this: a
  repository on the TypeScript 7 native port, whose package exports a
  version string and no compiler API, would else leave the falsifier
  able to run but structurally unable to confirm anything. Availability
  is tested as the compiler API being loadable, never as a package name
  resolving; inside the image it always is. Where it is not (a host run
  without the bundled copy and no usable tree copy) the falsifier is not
  spawned and detection is the judge alone. A sample whose facts still
  fail to load records that as its own gate (`facts_read: false`), an
  infrastructure miss, never as a failed assertion or coupling check —
  the falsifier did not lose, the check did not run.
- **The quoted assertion is one the test framework makes.** The sample's
  `assertion_quote` is the anchor of *it failed at its assertion* (§8 *A
  repository's browser suite is a channel the run provisions*, point 4):
  a failure counts when it is at the quoted line or in a statement whose
  value that line reads. Were any quoted line accepted as the assertion,
  that gate would check only that the probe failed where the falsifier
  said it failed, and a falsifier that quotes the line that threw — a
  setup call, a navigation, a helper — passes it with a failure the item
  never reached. So a quoted line counts only where it lies in one of the
  case's assertions, read from the probe's syntax by the facts script,
  never from the quote's words: a call of the test framework's assertion
  API in the case's reachable code — `expect(…)` (or `expect.soft(…)`,
  `expect.poll(…)`) and its matcher chain, `assert(…)` and `assert.<x>(…)`
  — whose `expect` or `assert` is the global the runner provides, a
  binding of that name imported from any module (a framework, or a
  fixture file re-exporting it), or any binding imported from Node's
  `assert`. A quote with no line in such an assertion fails the quoted
  assertion's gate, and only its lines that are in one anchor the
  at-assertion check. The prompt always asked for "the failing assertion
  line"; code now checks it, and nothing in the prompt changed. Measured,
  barnacle run e7512406 item 8 sample 0: the probe's helper `runStep`
  threw ("probe found no candidates on page", a probe the independent
  audit found unsound), its assertion `expect(dd?.textContent)…` never
  ran, and the sample quoted the helper's call `const { window,
  trajectory } = await runStep(…)`. It was rejected only because the
  innermost probe frame was inside the helper; the same probe with the
  helper's body written in the case, quoting the call that threw, passed
  every gate. Of the 127 quotes recorded (one per run, probe and quote) in
  the 53 run states under `~/.leerie` on 2026-11-10, that quote is the
  only one holding no `expect(…)` call. An assertion written by hand (`if (…) throw …`) or through
  an API other than these (node:test's `t.assert`, chai's `should`) is
  not read as one, so such a probe is not confirmed.
- **One re-ask.** A sample that answers `could_not_demonstrate`
  without having both left a probe in its checkout and run it is
  resumed once in the same session and tree with a fixed note. Each
  half is read from what happened, never from which tool did it: the
  probe is a test-shaped file the sample's checkout holds untracked
  outside the leads when the worker returns (leerie's own listing of
  the checkout, before the next sample's restore), whatever wrote it —
  the falsifier writes with a shell heredoc as often as with an editor
  tool; it ran when one of the commands the sample executed (the Bash
  calls of its registered transcript) invokes a test runner on that
  file or on a directory holding it. A runner invoked on neither — the
  whole suite, another path — does not count: a missed re-ask could
  lose a demonstration, an extra one costs one worker. (Review round 24
  M1: reading `created` from `Write`/`Edit` calls classed all 15 of 15
  real first samples, each of which had written and run a probe in one
  heredoc command, as having done neither, and re-asked every one.)

An item is unmet when the judge confirmed it unmet OR any of its
samples is confirmed (`delivery_gate.unmet_final`, with the per-item
record in `delivery_gate.items`); the samples of one item run in order
and stop at the first confirm, which cannot change an any-of-k verdict.
Measured (bench Q2 F+, held-out, pooled over three fresh corpora, 31
target / 148 control items, frozen labels): F+ k=3 caught 23/31 =
74.2% with false unmet 12/148 = 8.1%; on the adjudicated labels 27/35 =
77.1% and 8/144 = 5.6%; with the re-ask, 24/31 and 13/148 (adjudicated
28/35 and 9/144). One sample alone caught 19/31.

**The falsifier gets the item whole.** An item is the classifier's
one-sentence wording of a span, with `parts`, and the sentence can leave a
part out: a whole-site sweep's requirement then lives in a part no
detector was shown. Measured on navegando 4134b78c (leerie 0.48.0, "make
the translations fully complete for the entire site"): the item's sentence
named only the two catalog files; its fourth part was "Coverage: the
entire site's user-facing strings are present in the messages files". The
judge was handed the sentence and wrote parts of its own, none of its 11
samples about the site's strings; the falsifier was handed the sentence
and the judge's leads, all about one catalog, and demonstrated one catalog
defect; after the re-drive fixed it, the re-check re-ran only that probe
(*A re-check replaces a verdict only on a tree that changed*, below). The
run shipped `met` while an independent audit of the merged tree found
about 13 components still hard-coding Spanish and about 255 server
messages shown untranslated. On the earlier run of the same task
(e0d101e3), whose sentence did say "all site strings covered", the
falsifier's first sample demonstrated a hard-coded component. So the
falsifier's input carries the item's `parts`, its prompt says each part is
required and that a part covering many places fails when any one place
falls short, and its `item_span_quote` may come from the sentence or a
part (the quote gate and the coupling check read both). Measured (bench
SW, the real falsifier in leerie's container on each run's shipped tree,
dependencies installed, pre-registered): on 4134b78c's shipped tree the
falsifier with the parts confirmed a remaining hard-coded component in 4
of 5 samples, without them 0 of 5; on e0d101e3, 2 of 3 with them and 3 of
3 without; on the non-sweep controls (two web runs, one item each; two
barnacle runs, 3 and 14 items; 3 samples per arm) no sample of either arm
confirmed an item labelled met but one: the barnacle umbrella item "fix
every issue the report lists", confirmed once in each arm on the report's
layered-dropdown finding, which the report itself lists as not fixed — a
real gap, not a false unmet — and the one known-unmet item was confirmed
in 3 of 3 samples with the parts and 2 of 3 without. On the responsive
task (a70fb4a6) neither arm confirmed anything (0 of 3 each): its gaps are
layout, which no probe in its test environment observes. Handing the
read-only judge the same parts was tried first and did not change its
verdict (bench SW part 1: 5 of 5 `met` with the checklist and 5 of 5 with
a sentence against proxy evidence, each citing the tree's own heuristic
guard test as proof that no hard-coded string remained), so the judge's
input is unchanged. Not re-run: the Q2 corpora F+ was frozen on; the
change is held to the controls above instead.

**A met is only what the run could observe.** Both detectors above can
only show an item *unmet*; a `met` is what is left when neither does. That
reads absence of evidence as evidence wherever the run has no way to see
the item's behaviour at all. The run observes in exactly two ways: reading
the tree, and running the repository's own test command in the environment
its configuration gives. Measured on navegando a70fb4a6 (leerie 0.48.0):
the item asked that every part of the site work on phones; the five
held-out sets were source scans and DOM-emulation renders checking for a
16px class (the writers said why: "I did not write Playwright tests,
because the e2e suite needs a running app"), all three falsifier samples
rendered components in the same DOM emulation and found the class there,
the judge cited class names, and the item was `met` — while an independent
audit of the merged tree found the header pushing the availability toggle
off a 375px screen, a composer text box about 60px wide, a reply button
shown only on hover, and long links overflowing their bubble. A DOM
emulation computes no layout: there, a test sees which classes an element
carries, never what they render, so each of those checks would have passed
on the broken tree as well. The repository's mobile browser suite existed
(its Playwright config names iPhone and Pixel projects) but its test
command does not run it, and CI parity leaves a browser check to a human
(`left_to_test_axis`, `browser` in `CI_EXTERNAL_REQUIRES`).

So after the falsifier, an `observability_judge` types every part of every
item the falsifier was asked about (the classifier's `parts`, or the item
as its one part): `reading` (a fact about the files), `test_command` (a
behaviour a test the test command runs, in its environment, could exercise
and would fail on), or `neither`, with what it needs —
`rendering_engine` (layout, what is visible on screen, viewport, hover,
touch), `physical_device`, or `external_service` (what a system outside the
repository does, where its tests hold only a double) — and, for `neither`,
a cite of the test configuration or setup line that shows the environment
the command provides. Code checks every cite against the tree's HEAD
(`_verify_delivery_cite`). A part counts as unobservable only when a
majority of `OBSERVABILITY_SAMPLES` (3) samples typed it `neither` with
every cite verified; a failed sample or an unproven claim is a vote for
observable, so the rule can only withhold a `met`, never invent a finding.
An item no detector found unmet but with such a part is `unknown`, never
`met`: listed under "Not verified by this run" (`unobservable_here`), with
each part, what it needs and the cited environment, and kept out of the
delivery ratchet's prior met. An item the judge or a falsifier found unmet
stays unmet: a check through a proxy can show a gap (navegando e99c1df1's
falsifier did, through the same DOM emulation), it cannot certify that
there is none. The typing is reused only on the commit it was made on, and
a judge that fails leaves every verdict as the detectors left it.

Measured (bench RT, pre-registered, frozen prompt, schema and rule; 6
samples per case, scored as two production draws of 3). On navegando
a70fb4a6's item and its earlier run e99c1df1's, the rule flagged the
layout parts in 4 of 4 draws; on nine items written from the independent
audit of the merged tree, the six layout and device findings were flagged
in 12 of 12 draws and the three observable ones (a history entry, a class
on every input, a search filter) in 0 of 6. The first bench's controls had
been labelled run by run, and failed its own rule: one control, a proof
step of evals "×22" against a live API and model, was flagged in both draws.
A second bench, pre-registered after that result, had an independent
adjudicator label every part blind to the judge: it labelled that item
unobservable, and over 108 fresh items it labelled observable (six runs,
four repositories) the rule flagged 0 of 216 item-draws, and over the first
bench's 54 relabelled observable controls 0 of 108. Misses lean safe: one
fresh item the adjudicator labelled unobservable (a style-rules item with
one "responsive UI" clause) was not flagged, which leaves today's verdict.

What this does not do: it makes no run able to see layout. A repository
whose test command itself drives a real browser types `test_command`, and
the rule never fires there. A repository whose CI runs a browser suite gets
that suite as a third channel when it runs here (next).

**A repository's browser suite is a channel the run provisions.** *Built
2026-11-09 (lane BR).* The rule above made the responsive task honest — its
layout parts are `unknown`, "Not verified by this run" — but no run could
finish it: the run's channels were fixed at reading the tree and the
repository's test command. **Root cause:** the repository declares a third
channel, and leerie read it and dropped it. CI parity's `ci_checks` worker
recorded navegando's browser suite — `pnpm run test:e2e --project=chromium`,
kind `test`, `requires: [database, browser, network]`, with its CI
environment and its prerequisites (`db:generate`, `playwright install
--with-deps chromium`) — and code set it aside as `left_to_test_axis`,
which is false for a suite the test command does not run, while the image
ships Chromium and the suite starts the app itself (its `webServer` runs the
dev server, its global setup seeds the database). Measured before building
anything (lane BR feasibility, the real shim, rootless, navegando's image
with a PostgreSQL server in its worker root): on a70fb4a6's shipped tree a
probe file run through the suite's own command, in a held-out sandbox with a
database of its own, brought the dev server up, seeded it, logged in through
Chromium at 375×812 and read the header: the "Nueva conversación" link at
x = 444.9 and the sound toggle's right edge at 436.9, off a 375-pixel screen
(the audit's first finding); on a commit hiding three header controls below
the `sm` breakpoint the same probe passed. **Invariant:** a way the run
observes is one code has seen work here, and every one the repository
declares and the run can provide is offered; a part such a channel could
show is never `unknown` for want of it, and no worker is promised one that
did not run.

The mechanism:

1. *Which check is the suite* (`_browser_suite_candidate`, code over CI
   parity's typed records): the first merge-gating `test` check that
   `requires` a browser, runs at the repository root, passes the checks'
   provenance rule (its argv and environment appear in the CI file it
   names), resets no database, runs nothing the task forbids, and whose
   command — resolved through `package.json` when it is a script call —
   runs a `BROWSER_SUITE_RUNNERS` runner *bare*: only options after the
   runner, so a file appended runs that file under the suite's whole
   configuration (navegando's second e2e check, which names one spec, is
   not the suite). The runner table is a fixed CLI surface, as
   `_RUNNER_REPORTS` is; `playwright test` is its one entry, and a
   repository whose suite runs another runner has no channel until that
   runner's row (its file filter and its report) is added.
2. *Seen running here, then offered* (`_establish_browser_suite`, in CI
   parity's baseline): in a checkout of the base, the check's
   prerequisites run as installs (`_ci_prepare`; a database push among them
   is not run — the wrapper's is the only one), then the suite's own command
   as a measurement, confined, with a database of its own when the check
   requires one (`_test_db_argv`), its runner's JSON report requested
   (`playwright-json`: one case per file and title across the suite's
   projects, failed when any project failed it; a run error naming no file
   — a web server that never came up, a global setup that threw — is the
   run's load error, never a case). `ci_parity.browser_suite.viable` is
   true only when a case passed: then the app, its database and the browser
   all came up here. Its environment is the CI's: what every CI service
   sets in a job (`BROWSER_SUITE_CI_ENV`, `CI=true`: a suite's
   configuration reads it for its CI form, one worker, retries) and the
   check's declared variables (measured: without `CI`, navegando's suite
   ran a worker per core against one cold dev server and 29 of 71 cases
   failed, most of them waits that timed out).
3. *Its browser is the tree's own store.* A runner's own browser
   download (`PLAYWRIGHT_BROWSERS_PATH`) is one of `_TREE_STORE_VARS`
   (§6 *Which stores an install may share*): the tree's install fetches it
   into the tree's own stores, which a held-out sandbox over the tree
   overlays — where a private temp directory would be an empty copy
   (measured: the tree's `XDG_CACHE_HOME` is empty inside its held-out
   sandbox) — and a worker started in a tree leerie installed for runs
   that browser (§6 *A worker started in a tree leerie installed for runs
   on that tree's stores*). In the run's shared stores it was invisible to
   the falsifier, whose store variables name its side's cache: both
   samples that wrote a browser probe failed at the browser's launch
   ("Playwright's chromium executable is missing").
   The image ships the operating-system libraries; a CI step that installs
   them as root (`playwright install --with-deps`) fails here (no root, by
   design) and installs no browser: the repository's provisioning provides
   one (its recipe's `playwright install chromium`), or the suite does not
   run at the baseline and is not offered — stated in the log, the run
   unchanged.
4. *A probe runs through it.* The falsifier's payload names the suite's
   one-file command and its environment (`_browser_suite_payload`) — less
   the database URL when the suite requires a database: the run's
   (`TEST_DB_ENV_NAMES`, what `scripts/sandbox-db.sh` exports) replaces
   the CI's and is already in the worker's environment, and a worker
   handed the CI's set it over its own (measured: both samples that ran
   the suite in their session failed at the seed, "denied access on the
   database") — and says that a part about layout, what is visible, the
   viewport, hover or touch is one only the suite can show, so it is
   probed there (measured: without that sentence 0 of 6 samples ran the
   suite, each anchored on the held-out DOM-class leads); a
   sample whose own shell commands ran its probe through the suite's runner
   (`_browser_suite_ran_probe`, a mechanical read of the commands it ran)
   is confirmed through the suite's command (`_capture_failing_test_ids
   (suite=)`), in a held-out sandbox over the confirm checkout with a
   database of its own, under every gate a test-command probe meets: a new
   file, not a lead, the named case failing, B*, the quoted assertion in the
   case, no coupling to the implementation — and one more, for every
   probe of either channel: *it failed at its assertion*
   (`_falsifier_failed_at_assertion`). A case counts only when some
   failing run's message names no line of the probe (the runner gave no
   location: as before) or names a line of the quoted assertion — a quoted
   line inside one of the case's assertions (*Delivery detection*, *The
   quoted assertion is one the test framework makes*), its
   statement, or an earlier statement of the same function that binds a
   name the assertion reads, followed through such bindings. A value bound
   to a local first is the same assertion as one computed inside it:
   `const v = f(x); expect(v)…` fails where `expect(f(x))…` does, and a
   throw from the code under test while computing `v` is the assertion's
   failure. A statement that binds nothing the assertion reads is setup,
   wherever its failure comes from (measured, barnacle run e7512406: item
   0's call under test threw on the line binding the value its `expect`
   read and was rejected as setup; item 8's probe threw inside a helper's
   step that binds nothing, and stays rejected). The probe frame read is
   the innermost one, so a failure inside a helper the case calls is that
   helper's statement's. The statements come from the facts script. Measured:
   on the loaded bench host the hand probe's first two attempts failed
   before its assertion — the login's wait and the chat page's navigation,
   each `TimeoutError: … Timeout 90000ms exceeded` — and only the third
   reached it. A case whose every attempt fails like that is named, fails
   again under B* on the same host, and holds its quoted assertion: every
   earlier gate passes it. A failure at another line is the environment's,
   not the item's; the prompt always said so
   ("not ... an environment problem"), and now code checks it. A browser
   case's message leads with its error's location (its last attempt's:
   a retried case's verdict is its last attempt's), so the cap on a long
   call log keeps it. The confirm checkout and every lane run the suite's
   prerequisites first.
5. *The judge is told.* The observability judge's payload names the same
   channel and says a part a test written for it could exercise in this
   browser, and would fail on, is `test_command`; `rendering_engine` is then
   only for what this browser cannot show (another engine, a device).
6. *No channel, no change.* A run whose CI declares no browser suite, or
   whose suite did not run here, has no `browser_suite` (or one with
   `viable` false), and the falsifier's and the judge's payloads are byte
   for byte the ones benched before (pinned). No recorded run of barnacle or
   web declares one (every `ci_parity` record scanned: 0 browser checks).

Measured (bench BR, pre-registered; RT's harness for the judge, SW's
container harness for the falsifier). *The judge*, with the channel, 6
samples per case as two production draws of 3, the same on the shipped
payload and on two earlier forms of its environment line: the audit's four layout and
touch items (header, composer width, URL overflow, hover-only reply)
flagged in 0 of 8 item-draws (8 of 8 without it, bench RT); a70fb4a6's
"layouts responsive across viewport sizes" part 0 of 2 (2 of 2); the two
items a Chromium suite cannot show (an iPhone's notifications, Safari's
voice recording) 4 of 4, typed `physical_device`; the three observable
items 0 of 6. One reading leans the unsafe way and is listed: e99c1df1's
part "iOS-specific issues are handled (viewport/safe-area, 100vh, input
zoom)" was never typed `neither` (18 of 18 samples over the three forms),
where safe-area insets are a device's. *The falsifier* on a70fb4a6's shipped tree (its one item, SW's container
harness, real confinement; navegando's image with a PostgreSQL server in
its worker root and its runner's browser in its recipe — what leerie now
provides itself, below): with today's channels
0 of 4 samples confirmed, each a DOM-class probe (SW: 0 of 6). The channel
took four pre-registered rounds of 6 samples, each fixing what the last
measured: as first built, 0 confirmed and no sample ran the suite, each
anchored on the held-out DOM-class leads; with the layout sentence, 0 —
the 3 that wrote browser probes failed at the seed on the CI's database
URL; with the URL withheld, 0 — the 2 that ran one found no browser in
their session (it was in the run's stores, not the lane's); with the
browser a tree store, as shipped, 2 of 6 confirmed, both through the
suite, both at their assertion line, and 5 of the 6 samples ran their
probe through it. Both are layout defects no earlier channel showed and
the static audit did not list: the auth pages scroll sideways at 320 px
(scrollWidth 351, the language switcher past the edge), and the privacy,
terms and DPA pages at 375 px. Discrimination through the confirm path
(`_capture_failing_test_ids(suite=)`, held-out sandbox, own database): the
320 px probe fails on the shipped commit and passes on one hiding the
wordmark below 360 px, and still fails on the header fix; the hand header
probe fails on the shipped commit and passes on the header fix. No sample
found the audit's header finding itself: each probed page-wide overflow,
which the app shell's own scroll container masks.

What the suite needs that its CI provides is leerie's to provide (lane
BP): the database server, which a CI starts as a service, ships in leerie's
base image (§6½ *A database server in the base image*); and the runner's
browser install runs in the form that needs no root (§9 *A prerequisite
runs in the form that needs no root*). As first built, both were left to
"the repository's own provisioning", which no repository can learn of:
navegando's image had no server (its CI starts one as a service; its
configuration names the client), so the seed failed, and its CI's
`playwright install --with-deps chromium` stopped at "Switching to root
user to install dependencies ... su: Authentication failure" and installed
nothing — on its real image the suite did not run and was not offered.
Measured after the change (lane BP, a real launch on navegando's checkout,
its committed `.leerie/` unchanged, the image built by the launcher): the
`ci_checks` worker typed that prerequisite `root: part` with the rootless
form `pnpm exec playwright install chromium`, which downloaded the
runner's browser into the tree's stores; each command's cluster started
from the image's server; the suite at the baseline ran 74 cases passed, 1
failed, 2 skipped, and was offered to the run. Leerie offers what it saw
run, and says why it did not.

What is not built: the held-out acceptance writers are not offered the
channel — their sets are written before planning, and CI parity discovers
the suite at the execution phase; moving discovery ahead of them is the
next step. No other runner has a row yet, and a suite that needs a service
besides PostgreSQL (navegando's CI also starts Redis, which its app does
without) gets none from leerie.

**A probe is re-run through the channel that confirmed it.** *Built
2026-11-09 (lane SR).* A probe confirmed through the browser suite was
confirmed once, through the suite, and every later run of it went through
the repository's test command, which cannot run a browser spec: the
re-drive's re-check (`_redrive_recheck_items`) re-ran the saved probe that
way, so its verdict came from no measurement. Measured on a70fb4a6 (leerie
0.54.0, lane BR's hand header probe, which fails through the suite on the
shipped commit): the re-check ran `vitest run e2e/br-header.spec.ts
--passWithNoTests`, which the repository's vitest configuration excludes,
ran no test, exited 0, and read the item met on the shipped commit, the
defect still on screen. And a fixer could not be shown such a probe at all, since its
self-check ran the test command only: it was declined (*Delivery
re-drive* rule 4, as first built), stayed unreproducible, was never
driven, and the conflict with an existing test could not be measured for
it either. Navegando's responsive task is the case: its layout defects are
found only through the suite, so none of them could ever reach a fixer.
**Root cause:** which channel a probe ran through was recorded on its
sample (`via_browser_suite`) and read at the confirm alone; nothing that
re-ran the probe carried it. **Invariant:** every run of a probe goes
through the channel that confirmed it — the fixer's self-check, the re-runs
after a group's commit (its progress and the conflict check), the
re-check, and the command the PR names for it — and a run that has no such
channel gives no verdict, never the test command's.

The mechanism: the mark travels with the probe. The shown probe
(`_falsifier_shown_probe`) and the probe set every re-run is built from
(`_redrive_probe_sets`, `_falsifier_probe_set`) carry `via_browser_suite`;
an evaluation runs such a set's file through the suite's own command, in
its CI environment, with a database of its own, in a held-out sandbox over
a checkout its prerequisites set up — the confirm's terms
(`_acceptance_set_suite`, `_run_acceptance_file(suite=)`) — and B\*
confirms a failure as for any set. The self-check runs each file through
its own channel: the shown sets' files and test-command probes through the
test command, a suite probe through the suite's command over the copy of
the fixer's tree, in the suite's CI environment less the database
variables, which are the fixer's own — each command through the one gate
every launch passes (§9 *A command the task forbids*): a channel the task
forbids is never launched, and its files have no verdict, never a pass; the suite's prerequisites set
staging up first, as they set up the checkout the probe was confirmed in,
since the copy shares staging's ignored paths and stores. A probe is shown
only when the run has the channel to run it through; a run with none (its
suite record gone) leaves it unreproducible and any re-run of it
unmeasured (`no_browser_suite`).

Measured (lane SR replay, the a70fb4a6 case on lane BR's harness:
navegando's image with a PostgreSQL server, real confinement, the hand
header probe recorded as a sample confirmed through the suite with
shown-only leads; no worker spawned, `claude_p` refused). On 0.54.0 the
probe was not shown (the item `unreproducible`), and the re-check read the
item met on the shipped commit, through vitest as above. With this change
the re-drive's split handed the probe on (`via_browser_suite` on the note
and its self-check set); on the shipped commit the re-check and the re-run
of a group's probes each ran the suite's command and read `fail`, B\*
confirmed (3 of 3 reruns); after the header fix was committed in staging
and taken into the run's repository, the re-run read `pass` and the
re-check read the item met.

Built since (*The self-check's copy is a tree of its own*): on navegando
the app's server did not start in the self-check's copy, whose ignored
paths were symlinks out of it, so a fixer shown such a probe could not see
it pass before it committed. The copy now holds them as its own, and the
same replay's self-check failed the probe on the shipped commit and passed
it on the uncommitted fix.

**A probe that breaks another part of its own item is a contested reading,
not a finding.** *Status: designed, not built — see the last paragraph.*
An item is the classifier's one-sentence wording of a span of the source,
with `parts`; the falsifier is handed the sentence and its `source_ref`
only, and told not to reinterpret it from other documents. So it cannot
see that the reading it asserts breaks another part of the same item, and
nothing checks. Measured on barnacle a192d275 (leerie 0.44.3): the item
paraphrased a report's "add `redirect` … **and/or** follow redirects inside
`rawFetch` … **at minimum** return headers and the final URL" as "call
