onResponse for every hop", with the part "Default behavior for existing
callers preserved"; the falsifier's confirmed probe required per-hop
callbacks in the *default* mode — reachable only by changing the default —
noted the ambiguity in its own reason, and was confirmed. The readings are
not unachievable: an opt-in follow loop satisfies both, and barnacle
48c48629 had built the default-mode loop once and rolled it back because
it broke a control case for a caller-supplied manual redirect. Chasing
one reading through the fix loop swings between shipping the gap and
breaking the default. The design:

1. *The classifier records what the source leaves open.* An item whose
   span offers alternatives or a floor carries them typed —
   `alternatives[]` (each a verbatim quote of the span) and `minimum`
   (the span's own floor, quoted) — instead of collapsing them into one
   sentence. Code checks each quote is a substring of the span's source,
   as it checks every quote.
2. *The falsifier gets the rest of the item.* Its input already carries
   the item's `parts` (*The falsifier gets the item whole* above); it adds
   `alternatives` and `minimum`, and the span's source text, and it
   returns, besides the part it probes, `other_parts_held[]`: per other
   part, whether its probe's asserted behaviour can coexist with that
   part, with the quote. A sample whose probe is confirmed but which
   reports another part it cannot coexist with is typed
   `contested_reading` (`{item_index, probed_part, contested_part,
   quotes}`), never `confirmed`.
3. *A contested reading goes to the conflict path, not the fix loop.* It
   is recorded with the contract judge's `conflict` verdicts and handed to
   the re-drive as a typed note whose instruction is to find one design
   that satisfies both parts (here: opt-in per-hop following, default
   untouched), measured by the probe AND the part it contested. A group
   that satisfies one by breaking the other is a trade (rule 5,
   `trade_pairs`); the same pair twice is the re-drive's `conflict`, the
   run `unconverged`, and the PR a draft that names both readings.

**A report-pointer task's no-work confirmation includes the report's own
repro, executed.** *Status: designed, not built.* The `no_work_judge`
reads and never runs: in two runs on the same report (331df50b,
81028d11) it confirmed "already fixed" having run nothing, one saying it
had not read the report; in a192d275 the
acceptance writers, shown the fixed tree first, wrote tests of the
reading the tree already met, and every set was discarded as
`fixed_on_head_by_execution`. When the defect-scope audit recorded a
`ground_truth.repro_command`, a no-work confirmation is held until that
command has run on HEAD under the settle-by-execution machinery, and the
audit types the report's stated buggy outcome so code — not prose
reading — decides whether HEAD still shows it; still showing it is a
dispute with the run's own evidence.

These two rules change what the falsifier and the classifier are given,
and *What ships is what was measured* binds the falsifier's input to the
frozen F+ bench: shipping either without re-benching would leave the Q2
numbers describing a different worker. What remains: the classifier and
falsifier schema fields and prompt text; the `contested_reading` gate and
its routing into `contradictions`/`trade_pairs`; the typed repro outcome;
and a bench of the falsifier on the Q2 corpora plus the a192d275 and
48c48629 items, held to F+'s catch and false-unmet rates.

**Delivery re-drive: unmet work goes back to the subtasks that own it.**
Detection alone ships a PR that says what is missing; the next run then
re-plans from scratch. After the repository's merge checks have run on the
final tree, every piece of confirmed-unmet work is handed back to the
subtasks whose work it is, on the integrated staging tree, in the same
pass (benched as P8b–P8d and Q3, frozen rules):

1. *What is unmet.* A held-out set that fails on the final tree, confirmed
   under B\*, forces unmet — whatever the judge said. A set typed `broken`
   (the set audit) is settled and never chased; a variant set of a
   report-pointer task never counts as work (*A task that points at a
   report is bounded by the report's own scenarios*). Neither one makes
   an item unmet by any road: not through the gate, and not through the
   delivery judge's record, which states such a set's failure as settled
   (broken) or as outside the report's own scenarios (variant), never as
   plain failed, and names a failing set's failing cases, never the cases
   its writer declared. In a live run (barnacle ddd383ea, leerie 0.44.7)
   the record told the judge "set 1 … failed" for a set typed broken whose
   counted cases were none, listing declared cases that had passed; the
   judge marked two items unmet on it, and no tree change ever re-judged
   them (*A re-check replaces a verdict only on a tree that changed*), so
   the run ended `unconverged` on failures rule 1 calls settled. The
   re-drive reads every result against the run's record of every set,
   broken ones included, and a result whose set it has no record of is not
   routed: the lookup never defaults an unknown set to an unbounded,
   unbroken one. An item in
   `delivery_gate.unmet_final`, and a red merge check
   (`ci_parity.final.unmet`), are unmet too. So is a solution defect the
   final-tree conformance left unfixed after its last round
   (`conformance._final.residual_defects`, §9 final-tree pass): it goes
   as a typed `solution_defect` note (kind, `where`, concrete case), is
   routed like a failing control — to the subtasks whose integrated diff
   touches the file its `where` names, with none the same fallback a
   control takes — and is driven once. No step re-verifies it
   mechanically, so its re-check before each group (rule 3) reads the
   record: it is closed once a group that was handed it is kept, and no
   later group, in that round or a later one, is handed it. A group that
   is rolled back leaves it open, whether at once or after the last round
   by a flip (*A kept group that turns a met item's confirmed probe from
   passing to failing is rolled back*): its change is gone from the tree,
   so the next group the defect is routed to, in that round or the next,
   is handed it. It stays in the outcome's reasons either way.
   So is an existing test whose base form fails on the tree the re-drive
   starts from (`existing_behaviour`, measured just before it): one typed
   `base_form_case` note per test file, routed like a control, driven once
   and once more on opus for the cases still failing, never again (*A fix
   that keeps both, on opus when sonnet could not*).
2. *Who owns it.* The planner types, per subtask, the required items it
   delivers (`claims.items[] = {item_index, kind: deliverable | process}`).
   An unmet deliverable item re-drives **every** claimer. A process item
   (a constraint over the whole change: root causes only, no regressions)
   is no one subtask's deliverable, so its claimers are not its owners;
   but a confirmed probe that it fails is a concrete defect in specific
   code. It is driven on such a probe alone, when the probe is shown, to
   the subtasks whose diff touches a production module the probe imports
   (the import graph, as for a defect file): a subtask's diff is its
   `leerie: integrate <sid>` merge and every kept re-drive group it was a
   member of, since a group's commit is its members' change too. With no
   shown probe, or no subtask whose diff it reaches, it is recorded as
   reaching none (*An unmet item reaches its owner, or is recorded as
   reaching none*, below), reason `no_code_target`: a judge's verdict on
   "no band-aids" is prose, and code does not read a target out of it.
   Before this, a process item was never routed and never recorded. In
   barnacle 87580f62 (leerie 0.55.2) both subtasks claimed item 0 ("…
   root cause … Introduce no regressions in existing behavior …")
   `process`; the shipping-tree falsification confirmed a regression
   re-drive round 2 wrote (`isLoopbackOrLinkLocalHost("::0:5")` true,
   false at the start), and the item got no group and no record. Its probe
   imports `src/scripts/recon-http.ts`, which no integrate merge touched
   and both members' kept groups did. A failing defect file
   goes to the subtasks whose production diff — the files their
   `leerie: integrate <sid>` merge changed — touches a file that test file
   imports (the import graph, mechanical); with none, to the audited fix
   sites' claimers; with none, to every integrated subtask. A failing
   control file goes the same way, to the subtasks whose diff touches what
   it exercises; a red merge check is routed like a failing control (its
   diagnostics' files, a coverage glob's files).
3. *Groups, in sequence.* Subtasks that share a production file re-drive
   as one implementer session (their scopes merged), and groups run one
   after another on the same tree. Before each group the open work is
   re-checked, and a group with nothing left failing is skipped.
   A red merge check is re-checked like a set: its note goes to a group
   only while the check is still red on that group's start. The
   measurement read is the one already kept for that commit
   (`ci_parity.measured`). Every kept group's commit is measured whole by
   *A kept repair keeps the repository's merge checks green*, so the
   re-check runs nothing. The check is closed when that measurement
   reads it green: a gate that passed; a strict lint with no diagnostic
   new since the base in a file the run changed; a coverage ratchet with
   no threshold firing. A closed check's note goes to no later group. A
   start with no kept measurement leaves the check open as last read. A
   group whose every note is closed is skipped, and its members draw no
   round (rule 8).
   Routing alone cannot fix this. A plain red gate names no file, so no
   diff owns it, and rule 2 sends it to every group. Sequence makes that
   affordable, but only if each group re-reads the check before it is
   handed on. A note handed after the check went green also breaks rule
   4: it is a failure the fixer cannot reproduce. Leaving the round
   uncharged would not cure that, since the fixer is still sent after a
   failure that is gone. Before this rule, a check's note went to every
   group it was routed to, whatever the earlier groups had done. In
   barnacle 39c4c5ad (leerie 0.60.0), lint was red on the final tree and
   named no file. Round 1's group 0 turned it green: `1a6d3d8`, which
   its own ratchet measured green. Groups 1–3 (`bugfix-003`, `004` and
   `006`) were handed only that note, and each spent a round on it,
   about 80 seconds in all. Each reported that it could not reproduce
   the red lint and changed nothing.
   A solution defect is re-checked the same way, by its record (rule 1):
   once a kept group was handed it, its note goes to no later group. A
   defect whose `where` names no subtask's file goes to every group (rule
   2), as a plain red gate does, so the same waste was open to it. Before
   this rule, a round's notes were built once, and every group a defect
   was routed to was handed it, whatever an earlier group of that round
   had done; only the next round's notes left it out. This was found by
   reading the code while fixing the merge-check case; no recorded run
   hit it, since every recorded re-drive started with no unfixed solution
   defect.
4. *A self-check, then a re-check.* The implementer is given a command
   that runs the shown sets against a copy of its current working tree,
   outside that tree (*A held-out set never enters a tree a worker commits
   from*, below), and the sets' source, readable outside the tree: without
   a self-check (bench Q3 arm L3) whole-set closure was 0 of 4, against 18
   of 24 with one (every one of the 24 closed its sets). The self-check
   reproduces every failure a note hands on: every set a group's note
   names is a shown set that is not typed broken, and every set file it
   names is among that self-check's files. The re-drive never hands a
   worker a failure its self-check cannot reproduce, and the code checks
   it before a group is driven: a note outside its self-check is a leerie
   defect, raised, never driven. In ddd383ea it was driven: four
   implementers were told to fix set 1's defect file, ran a self-check
   holding only set 2, read "Tests 9 passed", and changed nothing.
   The rule covers every note, not only a set's. A note hands on only
   evidence its fixer can reproduce or read: a shown set's failing file,
   through its self-check; a delivery judge's confirmed vote, whose
   evidence and verified cites name code on the tree the fixer holds; a
   change under paths the item keeps unchanged, which `git` shows; a red
   merge check, whose command the note carries; a solution defect's
   concrete case; a confirmed falsifier probe whose sample read shown
   sets only (§6 *A falsifier reads only what a fixer may read*),
   through its self-check. Such a probe is a shown file: the re-drive
   copies the saved probe into the self-check of the group it drives, as
   a set of its own (`sets/probe-i<k>/`), so the self-check's test files
   include it, and the item's note names its file, its failing case, its
   quoted assertion and the sample's reason; the fixer runs it as it runs
   a shown set's file. A probe whose sample read a held-back set — a
   sample with no `lead_sets`, recorded before leads were shown sets
   only, or one whose `lead_sets` names a set the run holds back — is
   held-out content: its fixer can neither run nor read it, and all a
   note could say is that some input in the item's words fails. A probe
   its sample confirmed through the repository's browser suite
   (`via_browser_suite`) is shown like any other, and its self-check, the
   re-runs after the group's commit and the re-check all run it through
   the suite (§8 *A probe is re-run through the channel that confirmed
   it*); only in a run with no browser channel to run it through is it
   unreproducible. An item whose only unmet evidence (`by`) is a probe
   its fixer cannot be shown is therefore not driven: it is recorded as an
   `unrouted_item` with reason
   `unreproducible` (*An unmet item reaches its owner, or is recorded as
   reaching none*, below), stays unmet, and spends no round. An item
   unmet on such a probe and on reproducible evidence too is driven on
   the reproducible part alone, and its probe recorded as reaching no
   worker, reason `unreproducible`: its note carries only that evidence,
   never the probe's, and the re-check after the drive still re-runs the
   saved probe, so the item leaves `unmet_final` only when both are met.
   Code decides this from the item's typed `by`, the evidence each
   source recorded (`unmet_final[].evidence_by`) and the confirmed
   sample's `lead_sets` against the run's shown sets, never from the
   evidence's prose; the same pre-drive check raises on an item note
   naming a falsifier source without a shown probe, or whose probe's
   `lead_sets` names a held-back set. In barnacle 4b5c564d (leerie
   0.44.10) item 1 was unmet on a confirmed probe alone; its
   implementers were handed "a falsifier probe of the item's words …
   fails under B\*", ran a self-check of the shown sets that passed 18 of
   18, and changed nothing in two rounds (about 413 s of re-drive budget
   and $0.30); across the 24 runs whose state carried a delivery gate in
   the three days before, four such items in four runs, and a re-drive
   closed none of them. That probe's author had read a held-back set
   (§6), so it is not shown even now; under shown-only leads the fixer
   would have been handed `p.test.ts`, whose `export const
   XPayloadSchema` input the declaration matcher misses.

   *A shown probe is contested only by a measured conflict with an
   existing test; a fixer's objection is a note, never an exemption.* A
   shown probe never forces a change that breaks what an existing test
   pins. After a group that was handed a probe commits, the probe is
   re-run on the commit in a sandbox, as at the re-check
   (`_redrive_probe_verdicts`), and the commit's test results are read as
   for any group. A case an existing test pins is one of the base-form
   check's `changed` cases (a test file the base had and the run changed,
   run in its base form: §8 *What an existing test pins on the base
   holds on the tree that ships*), or a confirmed new failure in a test
   file the run's base had and the commit leaves as the base had it, whose
   base form is itself (`_redrive_pinned_breaks`). When the probe now
   passes and any such case fails, satisfying the probe is measured to
   break what an existing test pins: the group is rolled back, and the
   probe is recorded as contested (`delivery_redrive.contested_probes[]`,
   `{item_index, probe_test_file, tests[], round, group}`). The probe is
   never handed to a later group, so no round is spent against it again;
   the item stays in `unmet_final`, re-checked at the end like any other,
   so the run is `unconverged`; and the outcome's reasons and the PR's
   *Still failing* entry for the item say that the probe conflicts with
   the existing tests named, for a person to decide. A probe that still
   fails is no conflict, whatever else broke: that commit is rolled back
   as worse, or as zero progress (below), and the probe stays shown.

   Nothing else contests a probe. A fixer may still say why it thinks a
   probe is wrong (an input the product never gives the entry point, a
   behaviour the task forbids, a test it could not keep) in
   `probe_objections[]` (`{probe_test_file, kind: input_outside_domain |
   contradicts_task | breaks_existing_test, reason}`). Code keeps only an
   objection naming a probe the group was handed, records it
   (`delivery_redrive.probe_objections[]`) and puts it in the PR as the
   fixer's unverified words; it changes no routing and no verdict. The
   first form of this rule (lane XC's branch, never released) accepted a
   `contradicts_task` contest whose `task_quote` was verbatim in the task
   or a required item, and an accepted one removed the probe from later
   groups. A quote check filters how a claim is worded; it is no evidence
   that the claim is true. Lane TB benched the same check on tracked-test
   declarations, and 4 of 6 real weakenings passed it with quotes that say
   nothing about the behaviour, such as "We need to fix the root cost. No
   band-aids please.", a sentence in every task of that repository. The
   measured conflict is the evidence: the check runs the tests.

   Neither the conflict nor the objection judges whether the probe is
   right. A probe can be right and the existing test wrong, a test that
   pins the very defect the task reports (navegando e0d101e3 item 0: the
   audit table's existing test finds its column by the hardcoded Spanish
   header the item says must be translated); the conflict then stops a
   correct fix and hands it to a person, unless the two tests are shown
   to contradict each other (below). No worker decides, from a probe or
   the task, that an existing test may break.

   *A pinned case a required item's probe contradicts is task-required.*
   Barnacle 5ddc1d67 (leerie 0.62.0): items 0 and 1 asked the HTTP client
   to keep POST and its body across a 303; the repository's
   `http-client.redirect.test.ts` pinned "degrades a 303 to GET and drops
   the body". All three re-drive groups made the probes pass and broke
   that case, each was rolled back, and the run ended `unconverged` on a
   fix the task asked for. No implementation can pass both tests: they
   drive the same client with the same request and assert opposite
   methods. That is a fact about two tests and the code they reach, not a
   reading of the task, and a judge can be asked it. When a group's commit
   makes a shown probe of item *i* pass and breaks cases an existing test
   pins (the conflict above), a `contradiction_judge` (opus, effort high)
   is asked, per pinned case, whether any implementation of the
   production code can make both the pinned case and the probe pass. It
   reads a payload directory and nothing else of the run: the pinned
   test file **as the run's base has it** (never the run's or the group's
   rewrite of it, which would be a test agreeing with the probe), the
   probe, and every production module either test reaches through the
   import graph at the base (`_contradiction_code_files`; B3's one
   sonnet miss, below, lacked a module). It answers four facts — the same
   entry point, the same input by meaning, the same observable, and
   `mutually_exclusive` — with quotes. Code then checks every quote is
   verbatim in the file it names, and that each test supplies at least
   one quoted assertion inside its named case's assertion spans
   (`scripts/test-case-facts.cjs` `asserts`, run on the base form and the
   probe in a held-out sandbox, as the falsifier's facts are). Only when
   all four facts are true and every check holds is the verdict
   `exclusive`, and only when every pinned case the commit broke is
   `exclusive` with some item's probe does the rule change: the cases are
   task-required. They stop counting as the commit's base-form changes and
   as a conflict, the probe is not contested, and the group is judged by
   everything else as before; the round may change those tests. On the
   tree that ships, a task-required case whose base form fails is listed
   in `existing_behaviour.task_required`, not `changed`, so it does not make
   the run `unconverged`, and the PR names it under *Existing tests changed
   by this run*: "existing test changed because required item *i*
   contradicts it", with the probe's quoted assertion. A pinned case the
   commit left as the base had it, now failing, is still a new failure:
   the round must change the test, not leave it red; the note handed to
   the next group then says the item contradicts it. Any other verdict —
   `both_can_hold` (a verified answer that both can pass), or `unsettled`
   (no verified answer: a quote not found, no assertion quote, a fact
   false while `mutually_exclusive` is true, a failed worker) — leaves
   today's rule exactly. Verdicts are kept per case and probe
   (`delivery_redrive.contradiction_verdicts[]`) and reused, since neither
   input changes during the run. The judge runs only in the delivery
   re-drive: an acceptance repair round runs before final delivery
   detection, so no confirmed probe exists while it runs. JS/TS tests only,
   where the facts script reads assertion spans; elsewhere no verdict can
   be verified and today's rule stands.

   Why this question and not the task's meaning: T9 bench 1 asked a judge
   whether the task required an existing test's change, with verified
   quotes and a majority of three, and it accepted a2a825c2's inverted
   #358 case 6 of 6, because the report names the pinned behaviour as the
   defect. A task can be read either way; whether two tests can both pass
   is checked against the code, and a judge that must try to build the
   joint implementation finds it where one exists. Measured (lane B3,
   pre-registered, 6 samples per case per arm, payloads and checks as
   above): opus at effort high judged 5ddc1d67's pinned 303 case and its
   probe `exclusive` in 5 of 6 (6 of 6 against the other item's probe),
   and gave no false `exclusive` in 42 samples over seven pairs that can
   both hold — a2a825c2's #358 case against the run's own requirement
   test, a79384a4's four post-click-settle cases against the late-body
   acceptance row, the same file's 301/302 case against the 303 probe, and
   an unrelated navegando pair. Sonnet at medium said `exclusive` once on
   a2a825c2, with every quote verified, which is why this worker is on
   opus.

   Fitting a fix to the probe's wording (lane XC's G1: a generic passive
   "is …ed" pattern that made the probe sentence a no-op) is not caught
   by any of this, and no mechanical check is added for it. The candidate
   was a second, independently written probe of the same item, held back
   from the fixer, judging its commit. Recorded data cannot measure it —
   the falsifier stops at its first confirmed sample (any-of-k), so every
   confirmed item on record has exactly one confirmed probe — so lane X2
   ran a fresh falsifier with shown-only leads once per bench item. It
   confirmed a second probe on all six, in 1 to 3 samples, and each shown
   sample's recorded diff was run against both probes: on two items both
   passed, and on three the first passed and the second failed in every
   sample. Those three second probes tested another site or another
   aspect of a broad item (a note textarea beside the inbox search, the
   reset-password form beside the audit table, the primitive's own path
   rather than the step's outcome), so they failed the fix read as root
   (e99c1df1's first sample, which fixed every input of the list) exactly
   as they failed the one read as fitted to the probe (its second sample).
   A held-back second probe measures how much of a broad item a fix
   covers, not whether it was fitted, and would roll back root fixes; a
   heuristic on the fix's shape would be a symptom filter. Fitting stays
   with the held-back sets (rule 6) and the reading of the diff.

   Measured on the recorded diffs that motivated it (lane XC, leerie
   0.46.0), with the probe shown: N3 (barnacle 80e66fce item 4, a probe
   contradicting the report's F1) and G4-shown-2 (0d1c4033 item 29) each
   made the probe pass and broke cases in test files the run's base had
   and the run never changed (N3: 2 cases in
   `flow-runner.select-from-list-committed-control.test.ts`; G4-shown-2: 5
   cases in three files). Replayed on the runs' own final trees (the
   recorded diff as the group's commit, this rule's post-commit path, no
   model): the base-form check alone ran the run-changed test files the
   commit reaches (8 and 2) and found no changed case, because it runs
   only the test files a run changed, so on its own it stops neither. The
   near stage confirmed every one of those cases new under B\* (2 and 5),
   each in a test file the base had and the run left unchanged, and
   `_redrive_pinned_breaks` returned all of them, so with the probe passing
   both are contested. A group was already rolled back on those failures;
   what the conflict adds is the record and the end of the retries:
   before it, the rolled-back probe went to the next group again.

   After each
   group the orchestrator re-runs the sets and the repository's tests — a
   test command the task forbids replaced by the scoped run of the coupled
   tests, as at final and in the ratchet, never run raw; a
   result that is worse is rolled back to the group's start by the one
   restore (§8 *One restore*). Worse is counted in cases, the same unit as
   progress: any set case that passed before the group and fails after it
   — a newly failing case in a file that was already failing, or any case
   of a set file that passed before — or a control newly failing, or a
   test newly failing, each confirmed under B\*. Counted in files, a group
   that fixed one case of a failing file and broke three others in it read
   as progress and stood (review round 1 M4); and a group that fixed one
   set file by breaking another read as not worse, the file counts being
   equal. So is a group that
   had failing set cases and fixed **none** of them, even when nothing got
   worse: a change that measurably fixes nothing is speculative. Progress is
   counted in cases, not files — fixing one of a file's three failing cases
   is progress — wherever the runner's report names the cases; a file
   without that record counts as one case, and a newly failing case is
   counted by name where both sides name their cases. A set file that
   passed, or failed with named cases, and now fails as a whole — an
   import or collection error, no case list — is worse, counted as one
   case (the file): every case it had that passed is now failing, and
   reading the lost names as "no evidence" let a round that fixed one case
   elsewhere by making a file unimportable stand as progress (review round
   2 M4). A file failing as a whole on both sides, or turning from a whole
   failure to named cases, is not on its own worse. The cases a failing
   file names come from every run of its vote, never the first alone. A
   run with a resource signature contributes no case evidence: one that
   timed out, one killed by a signal with no report, or one whose every
   failing case's message carries a resource signature
   (`_RESOURCE_FAILURE_RE`, as in *A held case that fails again*). Every
   other failing run contributes the cases its report names, none when it
   names none (a collection error is evidence of a whole-file failure).
   The file names the cases every such run named, or all of them when no
   case was named by every run; it fails as a whole only when no such run
   named any case; and a file whose every run carried a resource signature
   has no case evidence at all. Such a file is failing but never a
   whole-file collapse, so it is not worse on that count. A file settled
   by a held case failing with no resource signature names that run's
   cases, and an intermittent file its held cases. Reading the first run
   alone, a first run that timed out followed by a confirming rerun that
   failed in the ordinary way, naming the same case as before, read as a
   collapse, and a round that fixed another set was rolled back as worse
   (review round 3 L1). In a
   replayed run (barnacle 7cc87f9a, pass 1) two repair rounds that fixed no
   failing case each added a defensive fallback the task explicitly
   forbade, and both shipped. A run that produces no verdict (a missing
   report) is `resource_affected`, never on its own a reason to roll back,
   and a set without a verdict cannot make a group zero-progress. A shown
   probe counts as a case here: a group handed one that, on its commit,
   still fails every probe it was handed and fixed no set case is
   zero-progress and rolled back, and a probe whose re-run gives no
   verdict is no evidence either way. Before this, progress read set
   notes only, so a group handed only a probe could never be
   zero-progress, and a commit that left its probe failing was kept. A group
   that survives all of that still goes through the delivery ratchet
   (*A repair that regresses met work is rolled back*): when it made an
   item that was met before it unmet, or turned a merge check that was
   green before it red (*A kept repair keeps the repository's merge
   checks green*), it is rolled back too. The item then
   goes to the remaining groups as a `control_regression` note, so a fix
   cannot hedge or remove what an earlier pass had already verified.
5. *A trade is not progress.* A group that fixes a case only by breaking a
   control or a passing test is rolled back, and the broken behaviour goes
   as a typed `control_regression` note to every remaining group and to the
   next round. Only when the same (fixed, broken) pair breaks again is the
   work declared a `conflict`: the re-drive stops, the run is
   `unconverged`, and the PR is a draft whose reason names both sides. When
   the broken side is a test already tracked in the repository, the pair
   is recorded as a contradiction with that test — typed PR evidence; the
   set is never dropped for it.
6. *Held-back names.* With four or more valid sets two are held back
   (*Held-out acceptance tests*). Once the shown sets pass, the held-back
   ones run; if any fail, one round names their failing cases — names
   only, never source or output, with "fitting these names will fail the
   recheck". It takes its round from the same counter.
7. *The last round may think harder — behind four gates.* A group whose
   members are on their last round and whose failing sets were all written
   by this run's own-start writer runs at effort `high` instead of the
   implementer's own, but only when every gate holds: (a) the set audit
   (three samples) did not type a case `contradicts_task` in a majority of
   them; (b) the round edits no tracked test so as to weaken it (fewer
   `expect`/assert calls, fewer cases, an added `skip`/`only`, a deleted
   file) — else the round is void and rolled back; (c) no new nullable or
   defaulted read of a required field (Prisma schema, zod object,
   interface member) appears on an added line — only patterns new in their
   hunk, with error branches and empty-collection defaults exempt — else
   rolled back; (d) a TypeScript-compiler AST check of every changed
   production file finds no removed null-guarded throw or error return
   (D1), no new success-shaped early return on a null branch (D2), and no
   new catch swallowing an error class thrown under a null guard (D3) —
   else rolled back. The AST check reads syntax only, so it loads the
   tree's own `typescript` when that package has the JS compiler API and
   the image's pinned 5.x otherwise (*Delivery detection* above): inside
   the image it can always run. Only where it cannot (no `node`, no
   compiler API from the tree or the bundled copy — a host run) is there
   no escalation.
8. *One budget.* Every group draws one round from each member's shared
   counter (§13 *One re-drive budget per subtask*) and its wall time from
   `redrive_budget_sec`, the hard stop.

After the last round the sets are measured once more on the tree that
ships, the merge checks re-run when the tree moved (read from the last
kept group's measurement when it holds every gate green), the failing-test-ID
diff (§9 *Which failures are new*) is measured again on that tree, and
each routed item is re-checked: re-judged by the cited judge, and an item
a falsifier proved unmet by re-running its saved probe on the new tree.
Every row's test-outcome part is then re-read from the diff of the tree
that ships. That verdict is what `_decide_outcome` reads.

**A re-check replaces a verdict only on a tree that changed, and only by
the vote that made it.** A routed item is re-judged only when the tree has
moved since the verdict it would replace: the commit the detection verdict
was measured on (`delivery_gate.final_sha`) until a re-check records its
own. And an item a 2-of-3 vote confirmed unmet is re-judged by all three
samples under the same majority: confirm-on-first-pass (one sample, two
more only when it flags something) is for a first look, where a clean
sample ends the vote, never for overturning a majority. Before this the
re-check's last-seen commit started empty, so the first round re-judged
even when its group changed nothing, and the re-judge's first sample,
saying met, ended its own vote. Measured on barnacle 48c48629: the
re-drive's one group made no change (`pre_sha == post_sha`, `no_change`),
and one sample on that same tree overturned the 2-of-3 unmet verdict on
"cookies from intermediate hops carried by the following request"; the
run shipped `done`.

The same rule covers the falsifier: an item reads met on a tree only by the
bar a met has at detection, the judge and the falsifier on that tree. The
re-check used to re-run a falsifier-confirmed item's saved probe and stop
there, so a sweep whose one demonstrated place was fixed read met with
nothing trying the others: on 4134b78c no falsifier ever ran on the tree
that shipped. So every re-checked item the re-check reads met is falsified
afresh on that commit (`falsifier_samples` samples, no leads); a confirmed
sample makes it unmet again, and its probe is the one the next re-check
re-runs.

**Every item the tree that ships reports met passed detection's bar on
it.** The re-check reaches only the items the re-drive routed. Every other
met item was read after a kept group by the delivery ratchet's judge alone
(*A repair that regresses met work is rolled back*), whose re-verification
carries no citation and runs no falsifier, so it is below detection's bar.
Measured (lane T9 bench 4, navegando 4134b78c sample 1): a group sent for a
base-form note was kept. While fixing that note it made the password
input's labels default to hard-coded Spanish. Item 0 had been met at
detection; one of its parts was "the entire site's user-facing strings are
present in the messages files". The item was routed nowhere. The ratchet's
judge ran three samples and kept the item met, its recorded evidence
repeating the round's own claim ("the component's Spanish defaults aren't
used on localized pages"). The sample's log has no falsifier line: nothing
tried the item on the tree that would ship.

**Invariant:** a kept change made after detection voids detection's
falsification of every item the change can reach. Leerie cannot soundly
tell which items those are from what it holds. The ratchet judge's
`evidence_files` are the files its own verdict cited. They sample an item's
reach, chosen by the judge whose verdict is in question, and a sweep item
reaches every file that renders a string. A diff names the files that
moved, not the items that read them. So the rule takes them all. When the
re-drive ends on a commit other than the one it started on, it collects
every item that meets three conditions (`_redrive_met_unread`):

- its row reads met, or every part of it other than its test outcome does;
- the falsifier is asked about it (`_falsifier_item`: never `external`,
  `test_id_diff` or `untouched_paths`, which code settles on the commit);
- no re-check read it on that commit.

Each one is re-checked there as a routed item is: re-judged by the cited
judge, then falsified afresh. A confirmed sample makes it unmet, with the
probe as its evidence. A judge that crashes leaves it unverified
(`unknown`, listed for a human, the verdict not re-keyed to that commit),
never met.

The rule runs once, on the tree that ships, and not after every kept
group. A confirm on one tree is detection's verdict, not a reason to roll
back: the ratchet's rollback rule was benched with its judge alone (N5),
and the falsifier's measured false unmet is 8.1% per item. A confirm that
one kept group demonstrably wrote is a different measurement, and it does
roll that group back (next rule). The cost was measured
over every recorded run under `~/.leerie/` (2026-11-09). Of 13 runs with a
re-drive, 10 kept at least one group and ended on a moved commit (12 kept
groups in all). Those 10 runs hold 23 met items that this rule reads,
2.3 per run. A met item's falsification at detection took 2.98 samples on
average (107 recorded rows), and 136 of those 319 samples were re-asked.
That is about 4.3 falsifier calls per item, or about 10 per affected run.
The 563 recorded falsifier calls had a median latency of 57 s and a mean of
107 s. Each affected run also pays one cited judge pass over those items.
A re-drive that keeps nothing pays nothing.

**A kept group that turns a met item's confirmed probe from passing to
failing is rolled back.** *Built 2026-11-10 (lane FL, barnacle 22a30525).*
**Invariant:** no kept re-drive group ships a failure of a met item that a
confirmed probe shows passing on the group's start and failing on its
commit under B\*.

**The rule it revises, and why that rule was right.** The rule above said
"A falsifier confirm is detection's verdict, not a reason to roll back".
For a confirm read on one tree that holds: bench Q2 F+ measured 12 of 148
met control items confirmed unmet (8.1%). The 12 include probes that read
the item more strictly than its words (two ask a payments route for a
card's brand and last four digits that the item never names), and rolling
a group back for one would undo good work for a probe that fails whatever
the group did.

**Why a flip differs.** A probe that over-reads its item fails on the
group's start as much as on its commit: the group did not write the
behaviour it pins. A flip conditions on more than one tree. The confirmed
case passes every B\* rerun on the group's start and fails every rerun on
its commit, interleaved (§9 *Which failures are new*: 0 of 88 clean trials
called new), so the group's own diff moved the behaviour the probe reads.
That is the ratchet's own question — did this repair regress met work —
answered by execution instead of a judge.

Measured (lane FL, every confirmed falsifier sample recorded after a kept
re-drive group or acceptance repair round under `~/.leerie/*/runs`, 15
probes in 7 runs, each re-run 3 interleaved pairs at every such group's
start and commit, confined, from the run's repository copy; pre-registered
`~/.cache/leerie-lanes/FL/PREREG.md`): 25 probe-group rows, 3 flips, 20
fail on both sides, 1 passes on both, and 1 fails before and passes after
(navegando 4134b78c item 0: its row kept detection's sample, which the
group fixed). The
two probes the audits call false (barnacle 22a30525 and 87580f62 item 8:
their markup drops what the report shows) fail on both sides of all 4
group rows. The flips: 22a30525 item 0 across round 1's group (the deleted
guard, a real regression); 87580f62 item 0 across round 2's group (`::0:5`
read as loopback, a true behaviour change the audit calls unreachable
through URL normalisation); 2dcb4cce item 8 across held-out repair round 1
(a bare `aria-expanded` combobox made a trigger, which broke a layered
widget of the item's own shape). Each flip names one group.

**The rule.** After the end-of-re-drive read (*Every item the tree that
ships reports met passed detection's bar on it*), each item it made unmet
with a confirmed sample is tried against every kept group in the order
they landed (`_redrive_flip_culprit`). The sample's saved probe runs as the
falsifier's gates ran it: in a held-out sandbox over a pristine installed
checkout of the group's commit and of its start, through the channel that
confirmed it, once each; a start whose report does not record the case as
passed (the probe does not load there, the case is skipped) is not a pass.
Only a case failing on the commit and passing on the start goes to B\*,
with the start as the base side. The first group B\* calls it new for is
the culprit. Staging goes back to the earliest culprit's start through the
one restore, which also takes every kept group after it, built on its
commit. The culprit records the flip (`flip_regressed`) and the reason
names the item and the probe's case. The item becomes a `control_regression`
note for the next groups, the ratchet's `met-item-<i>` note naming the case,
its assertion and its failure, as #355 does for a merge check. Then the
items that were open at the start, those the rolled-back groups drove and
the flipped items are read again on the restored commit by detection's
bar, and the round loop resumes. A member with a round left gets the note
and tries again; one with none leaves the item it was driving unmet, as it
was before the re-drive. The end of the pass then runs again, even on the
start commit, since its verdicts described a tree that no longer ships.

**What it costs.** Both re-drive flips in the replay rolled back a group
that had also fixed something real: 22a30525's round 1 fixed item 13's
gap (and round 2, built on it, part of item 10), 87580f62's round 2
widened item 10's match. In both runs the members had spent their two
rounds, so the note reaches no fixer and those fixes do not ship; the
items return to unmet, as on the base, with no regression the run wrote.
A run with no flip pays one probe run on each side of each kept group per
newly confirmed met item, plus B\* when one side passes.

**The rounds before detection.** Held-out repair rounds are kept before
detection, so detection's confirms are tried against them after it, by
this rule's measurement (2dcb4cce item 8: §8 *A held-out repair round that
turns a confirmed probe from passing to failing is rolled back*). The final
conformer, the other committing site before detection, is held to the
held-out sets it can break (§8 *A final-conformer round that turns a
passing held-out case failing is rolled back*).

**An unmet item reaches its owner, or is recorded as reaching none.**
Rule 2's "every claimer" includes a claimer that settled `unconverged`: it
is the subtask whose work the item is, and the confirmed finding is the
evidence it lacked. A claimer settled `blocked` (its blocker is typed
outside the tree, §13 *A blocked implementer says why, as a type*), one
the operator accepted, or one settled `accepted_external` is not driven.
An item no group drives — no subtask the re-drive may drive can take it,
or every group holding it was out of its members' re-drive rounds, or the
re-drive's time budget ran out first — is recorded as a typed
`unrouted_item` (`{item_index, item, reason: no_owner | budget |
unreproducible | no_code_target | after_last_round}`). So is an item rule 4 does not drive, with reason
`unreproducible` and the item words its probe tested (`probed`); the
outcome's reasons say for it that a confirmed falsifier probe of those
words fails under B\* and that the probe is held-out content no fixer
could see (its sample read a held-back set), so a reader knows why no
worker was handed it; once the run has ended the PR shows the probe
itself, its case, failing assertion and source (§6 *What is still unmet
when the run ends is shown as tests the reader can run*). It is never
dropped: it stays unmet, so the run is `unconverged`; the outcome's
reasons name it; and the next run on the task is handed it in its
residual. Measured on barnacle a192d275 (leerie 0.44.3): the falsifier
confirmed an item unmet whose only claimer, feat-001, had settled
`unconverged`; the re-drive excluded it, routed the item to nobody and
logged "done" one second after naming "1 unmet item(s)". The run's
outcome was `unconverged` on the unmet item, but nothing recorded that
the finding reached no worker. Under this rule the item would go to
feat-001, whose two re-drive rounds were spent before the falsifier ran,
so it would be recorded `unrouted_item` with reason `budget`; its only
evidence was a falsifier probe whose sample read every valid set, so
under rule 4 it is recorded with reason `unreproducible` before any
routing. A probe from shown-only leads would be shown, and the item
routed to feat-001 like any other.

**Invariant:** every confirmed finding on the tree that ships either was
handed to a worker who could act on it, or is recorded as an
`unrouted_item` with why, and the outcome's reasons, which the PR's draft
section lists, say it. Never silently neither. "Handed" is per finding,
not per item: an item is many findings over a run, because each re-check
confirms its own. Each source of an item's unmet evidence is a key: a
confirmed probe is the digest of its saved path and source, so a probe
confirmed later is another finding than one a group was handed, and the
same probe confirmed again is the same; any other source is its name (a
judge re-reading the item unmet again is the same finding). The re-drive
records every key a driven group's note carried
(`delivery_redrive.evidence_handed`), and at the end an open item with a
key never handed is recorded, with the first reason that holds: for a key
its note carries, `budget` (a group held it with no member left a round,
or the time budget stopped the re-drive), else `after_last_round` (the
key was confirmed after the last round began — by the re-check of the
tree that ships — so no round followed it), else `no_owner`; for a key no
note may carry, `unreproducible` (a probe no fixer may be shown) or
`no_code_target` (a process item's evidence that names no code a subtask
changed). Before this, an item counted as reached once any round had
driven it, whatever it was driven on. In 87580f62, item 8 was driven in
rounds 1 and 2, each on another probe; the re-check after round 2
confirmed a third, round 3's group was skipped for budget, and the item
was recorded only in `items_budget_skipped`, so neither the outcome nor
the next run said that its latest probe reached nobody. Across the 21
recorded runs with a re-drive (52 state files under `~/.leerie/`,
2026-11-10), six open items in four runs had a finding that reached no
worker and was recorded nowhere: four process items (two judge-only, two with a probe,
one of them shown) and two driven items whose latest probe never reached a
fixer (87580f62 item 8, and a2a825c2 item 4, whose probe read held-back
sets). Each is now an `unrouted_item`.

The diff is re-measured because nothing else is. Before review round 6
the re-drive re-applied the test-outcome verdict recorded at detection,
and `_decide_outcome` read detection's `new`, on a tree the diff never
measured. Driven on a real suite: a test confirmed new at detection, then
fixed by a re-drive group, left the row "unmet — new failing test(s)
confirmed against the base" and the run `unconverged` on a tree where the
test passes. The opposite direction is the one that matters more: a "no
regressions" verdict must describe the shipping tree. A group's own
ratchet confirms only that the group added no new failure against its own
start, and its unsettled candidates never roll it back (§9 step 4). When
the test axis cannot be measured on the shipping tree, the diff keeps its
old tree and is marked stale: with no `new` a test-outcome part reads
`unknown` ("not of the final tree"), never met; a `new` it carries still
counts — the item stays unmet and the run `unconverged`, the outcome
reason saying the failure was confirmed on an earlier tree.

**The final diff describes the tree that ships, whatever moved it.** The
re-drive's tail was the only place the diff was measured again, so it held
only when the re-drive itself moved HEAD. Review round 7 drove two more
ways the outcome came to describe a tree that does not ship. The final
conformance takes the diff only after a round's own post-measurement, and
a round that ends earlier — a worker error, a timeout, a malformed result,
a protected-path or clobber rollback — takes none: on a real suite a
regression the run introduced shipped `done` with an empty end-state
section when round 0's worker raised. And the held-out acceptance gate's
repair rounds commit to staging after the conformance: a kept repair left
the diff of the tree before it, so a test the repair fixed still made the
run `unconverged` ("newly failing on the final tree"), and a "no
regressions" item read unknown on every run whose repair kept a commit.

So the diff is a property of the shipping tree, not a side effect of a
conformer round. Right after the acceptance gate (so detection and the
re-drive route from the tree they judge) and again immediately before the
outcome is decided, it is measured again whenever it is missing or of
another tree than the one that ships; on the tree it already describes
this costs nothing. Every row's test-outcome part is then re-read from it,
as after a re-drive.

The tree that ships has one definition: the run branch's tree,
`refs/heads/leerie/runs/<id>^{tree}` (§6 *A delivery verdict counts only
on the tree it was measured on*) — finalize pushes that ref, and nothing
uncommitted reaches it. While staging is live, its `HEAD^{tree}` is that
same tree by construction, not by coincidence: every worker that runs
there passes I1's branch line (`_clean_tree_gate` requires `branch=`, and
every staging gate gives it the run branch, so a worker that leaves HEAD
detached or on another branch is re-asked or rolled back), and leerie's
own merges, rollbacks and resume resets all act on that branch. So the
measurements below carry the run ref's tree, and the decider, which
reads the ref once staging is gone, compares like with like.

**Every measurement reads the committed view.** The invariant: *what
leerie measures is exactly what ships, plus the environment* — the
dependencies installed into the tree. Staging is where workers work, and
I1 is what keeps their uncommitted files out of it; measured in staging,
a measurement is only as exact as I1's reading of it. Review round 17
drove the hole that cannot close from inside I1: a worker writes an
untracked `.gitignore` that ignores itself and a `helper.py` beside it.
I1 honours that `.gitignore` (git's standard rule, which every tool's own
cache relies on), so the tree reads clean; the build, lint, tests and
held-out sets run with `helper.py` present; the shipped commit lacks it.
The stricter rule — only committed `.gitignore` files count — breaks every
tool that writes a self-ignoring cache. Two ways were measured:

- *(b) I1 honours only committed ignore files.* Across the bench corpus
  under `~/.cache/leerie-bench-b3/` (every worker stream log), 537 of the
  3,735 sessions that ran Bash (14.4%) ran a package install. Both target
  repositories install husky v9 through `prepare`, which writes
  `.husky/_/.gitignore` containing `*`, and neither commits a rule for
  `.husky/_`; it was the only self-ignoring `.gitignore` found anywhere in
  the bench trees (157 copies). Under (b) every one of those sessions would
  leave I1 dirt and be re-asked, the only answer being to delete husky's
  hook shims or commit them; leerie's own installs would have I2 delete
  `.husky/_` after each one. 19 sessions ran pytest, mypy or ruff, whose
  caches are the same shape.
- *(a) Measurements run in a checkout of the commit.* A detached `git
  worktree add` of the branch tip costs a median 0.20 s on barnacle
  (1,369 files) and 0.44 s on funeralworks (2,845 files), seven runs each,
  once per commit measured; barnacle's test axis alone took 906 s and
  1,116 s in the two e2e runs that recorded it.

So (a): every command leerie runs to measure a worker's tree — the
measured build/lint/test axes, every test-ID run (B\*'s final side, the
intermittent-discovery repeats, the ratchet's and the re-drive's test
IDs, the integration gate's), settle by execution's verify commands and
the coverage settle's — runs in that tree's *committed view*
(`_committed_view`): a detached checkout of its branch tip (the run branch
for staging, the subtask branch for a subtask's worktree; never the
tree's HEAD, which a worker can move), kept while the tip stands and
replaced when it moves. The view is bracketed by I2 like any tree, so one
measurement's reports never reach the next.

Nothing a measurement reads comes from a tree a worker can write. Its
environment is installed by leerie into the view, from the view's own
committed manifests and lockfile: the provision recipe's `install` entries
(`_ensure_worktree_deps` on the view), so a `postinstall` generator (a
Prisma client) runs from the committed schema too; and its build outputs
are produced there by the recipe's `build` entries and the build axis,
from the committed sources. The first version shared the worker tree's
ignored paths into the view by symlink instead, and that carried two
holes: a worker that patched `node_modules/<lib>` in place had the patch
measured (green on code that fails in CI), and a symlinked build output
described whatever the worker last built, not the commit. The install
cost was measured before choosing (pnpm 10.4.1 with a store on the same
filesystem, as the state mount's store is, `--frozen-lockfile`, three
runs each): barnacle 9.0 s cold (empty store, 501 packages fetched),
4.3–4.5 s warm, plus 1.7 s for its second recipe entry
(`examples/plugins/hello-site`); funeralworks 23.2 s cold, 10.6–10.7 s
warm, its `prisma generate` included. A view is made once per branch tip
measured: the measurement memo of the four barnacle e2e runs held at most
7 distinct trees for any one command, so even 20 views (122 s warm) is 4%
of the shortest of those runs (3,051 s), against a test axis of 906 s and
more. The worker's own install stays where it was: a worker installs into
its own tree for its own runs, and leerie never measures through it.

*A view moves to the next tip when the install's inputs are unchanged*
(review round 18 L1). Making a view per tip measured 7.3 s (barnacle) and
15.8 s (funeralworks) per new tip with a warm store — a fresh checkout, the
removal of the old view's 0.6–1.4 GB of dependencies, and a full install —
and a run makes several views per subtask. So a view is kept per tree and,
when the tree's tip moves, moved rather than made again, if the install it
holds is one leerie made from the same inputs and is as that install left
it:
- the *install key* is the recipe's `install` entries (command, working
  directory, environment) and the git blob of every install input at the
  tip: every tracked file named as a manifest, lockfile or package-manager
  configuration (`_INSTALL_INPUT_NAMES`), everything under a `patches/`
  directory, and every path the dependency capture's `copy_inputs` names.
  The blobs are read from the run repository at the tip, never from a tree.
  The key is recorded with the view's install only when that install
  succeeded;
- the install's *outputs* are the ignored paths that appeared while leerie
  ran the recipe's `install` entries in the view. When the last of them is
  done, before any build runs, leerie records every entry under those paths
  with its state: a file's or link's inode, size, mode and change time — a
  time its owner cannot set back, moved by every write, rename, chmod or
  link — and a directory's inode and mode;
- when the key at the new tip is the key recorded, the view's `.git` is
  pointed back at its own administrative directory, found from the run
  repository's side; its measurement id there is removed, so to every
  measurement it is a new tree — a fresh measurement directory and empty
  stores of its own (DESIGN §6 *Leerie's runs of the repository's commands
  are confined too*), as a replaced view gets; it is checked out at the new
  tip (`checkout --detach --force`); everything untracked but the outputs
  is removed (`clean -x`);
  under the outputs, every entry the install did not make (a tool's cache, a
  report a measurement wrote) is removed; and every entry it made must be
  there in the state recorded, with no tracked path changed. Any failure,
  or a different key, and the view is removed and made afresh, as before;
- either way the recipe then runs again in the view in full — the store
  fetch, every `install` entry and every `build` entry. A moved view's
  install finds its own output in place, so the package manager does only
  what the tip needs, and the repository's own lifecycle scripts (a
  `prepare`, a `postinstall` generating from the sources) run against the
  new tip's files as they would in a fresh view. Builds are never reused.

So what a moved view holds is what a fresh view would: the install's output
reused is one leerie produced, under the same confinement as any repository
command it runs, from inputs identical at both tips, and verified untouched
since; no worker can write a view (I5), and whatever a measurement changed
under it sends the view back to a fresh one. A file the install reads that
the key does not name leaves no stale install either: the install runs
again on the new tip and reads it, over its own earlier output — the package
manager's incremental install, which is the residual difference from a fresh
view.

*A view lives no longer than its tree.* *Designed 2026-11-03 (the live
0.43.0 barnacle runs).* A view was replaced or moved only when its tree's
tip moved, so nothing removed it when its tree went: a subtask's tree is
pruned once its branch is integrated, and reset before a retry, and its
view — a full checkout with a copied install, about 650 MB on barnacle
(603 MB of it `node_modules`, link count 1 by the copy import of the
read-only-store design used through 0.44.3, *The stores a view installs
from are leerie's*) — stayed until the run ended. Counted on the
seven live runs: 43 views (37 of subtask trees, 6 of staging), about 27 GB
of the runs' 40 GB by `du`; one run held 9 subtask views beside 2
remaining subtask trees. And the in-process record of views
does not survive a resume, so a view made before one was reachable by
nothing for the rest of the run. Now the view of a tree, and the tree's
view stores, are removed wherever the tree is: when a subtask's tree is
pruned after integration (only once its branch is taken, as the tree
itself) and when it is reset for a retry (`_drop_view`). The view's path is
derived from the tree's name, never from the process's record, so a view a
process before a resume made goes the same way. A view goes sooner still
when nothing measures it again: as its subtask settles, and when a
coverage evaluation of it ends (§6 *A settled subtask's trees go when it
settles*); a later measurement makes it again from the branch tip, read
in the run repository when the tree itself is gone (`_view_repo`).

Measured with the confined install, copy import, the store fetch and the
stores emptied on a move (review round 19), a new tip with unchanged install
inputs: barnacle 14.6–16.1 s moved against 28.8–34.6 s remade (three of
each, idle host), funeralworks 24.4–25.6 s against 47.0–47.2 s (two of
each, load under 9). What a move still pays is the install run again in
place and the two walks of the install's output (and, through 0.44.3, the
store fetch).

What this removes: the measurement no longer depends on I1's reading of
staging, so the assertion every staging reader made — that staging was
clean, or the run stopped — is gone; each reader stamps the branch's tree
(`_view_tree_sha`: the run branch's tree, for staging), which is what
its view measured. I1 still
holds every worker to a clean tree: it is what keeps uncommitted work out
of the commits that ship and out of the next worker's way. No worker
reaches a view: it lies under the run directory, of which a worker's
processes may read and write only their own grant, and no grant names a
view (§6 *A worker writes only where it is granted (I5)*); nothing names a
view to a worker either. Each tip's view is a fresh checkout, or one
moved there whose install is verified as leerie made it (*A view moves to
the next tip when the install's inputs are unchanged*, above).

Staging is restored at every resume all the same: an interrupted run's
cleanup removes it, but a SIGKILL (Fly's `machine stop`, an OOM kill of
the container) skips cleanup and leaves staging as the killed worker left
it — partial edits, a merge half
resolved, or a HEAD a worker detached or moved to another branch. So
`setup-run.sh`, which every process runs once before it reads staging,
restores a staging that survived with the one restore primitive (*One
restore*, §8 below): it checks out the run branch itself — `git reset
--hard HEAD` alone kept a detached HEAD, review round 15 H2 — ends any
merge, and removes what is untracked, ignored files and so the installed
dependencies kept. Nothing uncommitted in
it is anything leerie may keep: I1 never commits a worker's leftovers,
and the run branch — every integrated commit — is untouched. The same
holds for every subtask worktree the process will reuse: a SIGKILL leaves
each as its implementer or conformer stopped, and `new-worktree.sh`
reattaches to a registered worktree as it is, so a resumed subtask's
first measurement, or its next worker, would start on the killed
worker's half-made edits (a measurement through I2 leaves them; the next
worker's I1 gate holds it to files it never made). `setup-run.sh` restores
every subtask worktree of this run the same way onto its own
`leerie/subtasks/<run-id>/<sid>` branch, before any wave runs, and keeps
the branch's commits. It finds them by path — the run's worktree
directory, a name whose subtask branch exists — never by the branch git
reports as checked out there: a worktree a worker detached reports none,
and was skipped (review round 15 H2). That is exactly what a
Ctrl-C's cleanup, which removes the worktree and keeps the branch, leaves
the resume. This runs once per process; within a process the per-attempt
rules govern a subtask's worktree (I1 after every attempt — `complete`,
`blocked` or `failed` — and before an in-place retry; a handoff
commits its partial work and leaves its checkpoint in the run
directory). A restore that still leaves dirt stops setup, naming it. A killed
integrator's half resolution goes with it, as it already did under a
Ctrl-C's cleanup.

**What ships is what was measured, once per change that can affect it.**
*Designed 2026-11-07 (the barnacle runs, where a run spent nearly ten hours in
near-whole test runs on a task that forbade the full suite).* The invariant: *a
test's result is measured once per change that can affect it, and the tree that
ships has every test's result traceable to a measurement on a tree that the
later diff could not affect.*

Measured on six barnacle runs (about 1,092 test files; every run ≥200 files
attributed to the code that started it). A summary-counting
reading of the logs saw 1,008 minutes; the real figure is 1,776, because a report
run prints no summary (four of the six were still running when read):

| Run | Runs ≥200 files | Minutes, summaries only | Minutes, all | Same tree again: runs / min | Unreachable in a final round: min | Per-subtask closure: min | Minutes left | Saved |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| a2a825c2 | 25 | 293 | 581 | 6 / 258 | 25 | 143 | 155 | 73% |
| 73751002 | 13 | 218 | 381 | 6 / 154 | 0 | 51 | 176 | 54% |
| b24806a1 | 10 | 143 | 249 | 3 / 91 | 1 | 51 | 106 | 57% |
| a79384a4 | 8 | 111 | 235 | 2 / 81 | 0 | 42 | 113 | 52% |
| 8aa14a04 | 13 | 131 | 177 | 2 / 31 | 0 | 101 | 45 | 75% |
| a41a09fd | 12 | 112 | 153 | 2 / 41 | 0 | 70 | 42 | 72% |
| all six | 81 | 1,008 | 1,776 | 21 / 656 (37%) | 26 (1%) | 457 (26%) | 637 | 64% |

(A selection's time is its files' share of the recorded per-file durations, applied to the run's wall time: an estimate. The wall of a silent run that shares a log gap with B\* discovery is an estimate too.)

Three defects, by the time they cost:

1. *The same tree, measured again.* 21 of the 81 runs measured a tree already
   measured, 656 minutes, 37% of the time. A failing axis ran twice, verdict
   then report (the rule was that a verdict is never measured with altered
   flags: on a2a825c2 that second run took 36 minutes on a tree the first
   had just measured); the delivery ratchet and the re-drive measured outside
   the memo, so a tree the final conformer had just finished was run again (25
   minutes) and phase 5 ran a repaired tree the ratchet had already run. The
   verdict and the report now come from one run (§9 *Which failures are new*),
   and every reader of a tree that ships goes through one memo.
2. *Impact analysis on every subtask round.* 457 minutes, 26%. On a repo with
   a hub file the tests a one-line change "affects" are most of the suite
   (`vitest related` 400–890 of 1,092 files, about 400 of them importing the hub
   directly), so a subtask's rounds measured what the whole-tree pass measures
   anyway, under load: of the 593 failures that vanished from one per-subtask
   measurement to the next, 359 did so across a diff that could not reach them.
   A subtask now runs the tests it names; the closure runs once, on the
   integrated tree (§9 *Per-subtask scope*).
3. *A final round re-running what its diff cannot reach.* 26 minutes, 1%, on
   these runs, because the rounds there nearly always edit a hub, which is
   correct saturation; over the 83 later final-tree measurements of 40 recorded
   runs it removes 12% of their time (12,110 of 97,360 s). It matters more for what it stops: a run
   under load fails tests nothing touched (one round on 107cd8a3 failed 76
   files after editing one test file), and each of those costs B\* budget.

What is left after all three is 637 of the 1,776 minutes: the first measurement
of the integrated tree, and each change that really reaches most of the suite.

**How a result is carried.** Every measurement of the tree that ships
(`_measure_axes` with `carry`: the final conformer, the acceptance gate's
pre/post check, the delivery ratchet and re-drive, phase 5's refresh) enters
per-file results in a ledger: test file → the tree it was measured on, and
whether it passed. A later tree re-runs:

- a file that failed there — a carried failure is always re-run, so it is never
  a stale red, and a flake stays B\*'s to judge;
- a file the diff from *that file's own measured tree* to this one can reach;
- a file with no entry (a new test, one a crashed run did not report).

The key is content: the diff is read from git between the two trees at every
use, so a rollback, a re-integration or a revert cannot leave a stale entry
standing, and no round counter is involved. A tree the ledger's trees differ
from by nothing is a memo hit. The whole command is what the memo and the result
answer for (`whole_command`); `command` says what ran and `carried` what did
not. A forbidden command stays forbidden: the whole command there is its scoped
replacement, the narrowed form passes the same gate, and a narrowing the task
forbids is no narrowing.

**A change's reach is never guessed.** `_change_reach` walks the import graph
(through test helpers too, which the coupling for a forbidden command does not),
and adds any test file or helper whose text names a changed file's basename (a
test that reads a source as text, or spawns it). Nothing else counts as "cannot
reach". The whole command runs when any changed path is one no graph holds — a
manifest, lockfile, config, fixture, document, a deleted file, every path of a
language leerie has no graph for, so a Go or Rust repository keeps running
whole on every tree that differs — or a runner's configuration, or a file that reaches no test at
all, since a `conftest.py` or `setupFiles` entry is reached through the runner,
never an import. A run whose report does not account for its verdict (a red exit
with no failing case, a failing case with no file) empties the ledger. What this
cannot see is a test that finds a source file by directory walk without naming
it: the replay below found none, and the first measurement of the integrated
tree is whole regardless.

**The replay**, mechanical and with no worker call, of the selection over the
actual commits and failures of the 40 recorded runs with two or more measurements
(36 on barnacle, 4 on `web`). 83 later final-tree measurements; 8 run whole for a
path nobody can scope (a stylesheet, `eslint.config.mjs`, message catalogues, a
document). 98 test files failed at a later measurement outside what the selection
would have run. Each was examined: 87 passed again by the next measurement, and
11, all on 107cd8a3, failed once more on the next, which is the load storm above,
B\* calling all of them resource-affected; none is named new by B\*. All 8 IDs B\*
confirmed new on a shipped tree are inside the selection. So nothing is missed on
the final tree, and the 98 are noise this stops chasing. Delayed, not missed: the
per-subtask failures counted in §9 *A subtask runs the tests it names*.

**A round's near tests are measured first.** *Designed 2026-11-07, after 0.46.0
removed the repeats: a round that edits a hub still re-ran nearly everything, and
was then often rolled back for a test beside its own edit.* The invariant: *the
tree that ships has every coupled test's result, once, and a round does not pay
for the whole closure before its nearest tests have passed.*

Measured over the 41 recorded runs with a shipping-tree verdict (`barnacle` and
`web`, 526 hours of wall time with pauses removed) and the 114 rounds among them
that committed and measured a large set: final conformer, acceptance repair,
re-drive. Worker time is 39% of that wall. Discovery repeats cost 66 hours (133
of them), against 26 for the closures of those 114 rounds at 0.46.0's rule. Of
the 26 rounds with a verdict of a new failure:

| Where the failing tests were | Rounds | IDs |
|---|---:|---:|
| At least one carried from the round's start (133 IDs), its own test (5) or a direct importer (16) | 24 | 154 |
| None near: distance 2 (one round, one ID), distance 2–4 (one round, 53 IDs) | 2 | 54 |
| Distance 2, in a round also rejected by a near ID | (3 of the 24) | 6 |

(IDs a verdict's stored text does not list, past its first ten, are not counted;
web 6f147a0c's 18 IDs have no measurement to place them against and are in
neither row.) So a test beside the edit decides nearly every rejection, at about
half the files of the closure (median 56%, by file; 38% by recorded duration).

*The stage.* A round measures first the tests nearest its diff from its own
start (`_near_test_files`: a changed test case; a test case importing a changed
file itself, a test helper included), everything the ledger holds failed, and
any test it was named (a control an earlier re-drive group broke). If one of them
is confirmed new under B\*, the round is rejected there: a rollback for the
acceptance repair and the re-drive, the next round for the final conformer,
which starts from the tree as measured and does not pay for its closure either.
If none is, the closure follows, and runs only what the stage did not settle:
the ledger holds what the stage measured, on this tree, so a keeper pays for no
test twice. One red run decides nothing: a near failure B\* does not confirm goes
on to the closure like any other.

A stage is never a tree's answer. Its result goes in no memo, says `near_stage`,
and is recorded as the tree's failing-test-ID diff only when it rejects the
round, marked the same way, which phase 5's refresh will not take for the tree's
(*The final diff describes the tree that ships*): it measures, and with the
ledger that runs the closure the rejected tree never had. The ledger is why
nothing else had to change: each file answers to the diff from its own measured
tree, so a far test skipped on a rejected tree is reached by the next change
from where it was last measured.

No stage is taken when nothing is nearer than the rest: a changed path of unknown
reach (a lockfile, a config, a fixture), a stage that would be the closure, a
scoped command the task forbids, or no ledger yet, so the first measurement of
the integrated tree is whole as before.

*Closure once was tried and is not done.* Measuring only near tests per round
and the closure once on the final candidate would save 3.8 to 6.7 hours more over
those runs (35 keeper closures that were not the run's last). Two rounds were
rejected only by far tests: barnacle 83674caf's acceptance round 1 (an edit of
`capture-filters.ts`, near set 16 files, 53 IDs at distance 2 to 4) and c33bef9e's
round 2. Kept until the end, 83674caf's second round is built on the first and
edits the same file, so finding the guilty round by bisection then undoes both,
and the fix the second one made. A closure before a round is kept is what keeps
that from being a late, expensive catch.

**The replay**, with the shipping `_near_test_files` and `_change_reach`, over
the recorded commits and failures of the 114 rounds. 101 take a stage. 19 are
rejected on it (13 final conformer, 4 acceptance repair, 2 re-drive). On all 41
shipping trees every confirmed-new ID was measured, and no failure stands
carried from a tree the diff could not reach: **no regression missed on the
final tree.** Three rounds are rejected with a far ID the closure would also have
named: c33bef9e's acceptance round 1 (2 IDs) and re-drive group r1g0 (1), both
rolled back, so those IDs leave with the round and only their naming to the next
attempt is lost, at worst one more attempt; d8aff199's final conformer round 1 (2
IDs, not rolled back), measured at the next round's closure, so a round later, at
the cost of one more conformer round if they still fail. Those are all the late
catches. One shipping tree (of 41) was last measured by a rejecting stage, so
phase 5 runs its closure there: 189 file-runs that 0.46.0 had paid inside the
round. Over the replay, file-runs drop from 65,205 to 62,125 (5%), recorded test
seconds from 495,874 to 457,644 (8%). The closures of those rounds drop from 26.4 hours to 24.2 (23.6 by
recorded durations), and the near B\* passes are smaller: 2.3 hours of confirm
reruns of far candidates on rejected rounds, estimated from each phase's median
confirm wall. A near failure B\* does not confirm can be confirmed a second time,
if it fails again in the closure: 18 of the 80 rounds with both ID lists carry
one, at most 4.6 hours, and of the 288 `resource_affected` IDs recorded 30 (10%) failed again on a rerun. A
hub-edit round rejected near, a79384a4's round 1: closure 25 minutes, discovery 25
(the "50 minutes of discovery" in its log's gap held both), B\* 5 today; about 10
and 3.

Most of what this saves is discovery (§9 *Discovery on a tree that may not
ship*): together, the closures and discoveries of these runs go from 92.7 hours
to 46.1, half.

*What the recordings cannot say.* A real run's rounds may roll back differently
once their worker hears only the near IDs of a mixed failure, and a kept round's
near and far passes cost a second runner start-up. Near wall time is an estimate:
each file's share of the run's wall, by count (conservative) and by recorded
duration. And the replay's distances are over the import graphs of recorded
trees, so a test reached only by a mention of a changed file's name counts as far
(none of the verdicts here was).

**Every post-execution verdict is of the committed tree.** The invariant:
*a verdict becomes `met` only on a read of a commit, or on a measurement
the orchestrator itself made of the committed tree.* Review round 9
asked whether the delivery judges, and the held-out re-measure, judge
the wrong tree when staging holds what does not ship. Every check that
can make a verdict *met* reads a commit, and a check that fails to read
one makes nothing *met*:

- the delivery judges — every item verdict, the DEFECT CONTRACT verdict,
  and the delivery ratchet's judged re-verification of the items a
  re-drive group did not route (its execution-typed items are read from
  the failing-test-ID diff of the commit, below) — read exactly the
  commit: a detached checkout of staging's HEAD (`git worktree add
  --detach`), with no dependency install, made for each judge pass and
  removed after it. A judge runs nothing — its tools read files and git —
  so it needs no environment, and gets none. A checkout that cannot be
  made fails the judge like a crash (it reads nothing, so it settles
  nothing *met*), never falls back to staging.

  Why not staging, which I1 and I2 keep at HEAD plus ignored files: the
  ignored files are exactly what a judge must not read. Its tools include
  `grep -r`, `cat` and `ls`, which (unlike `rg`) read ignored paths, and
  two of its verdicts carry no citation — the DEFECT CONTRACT verdict and
  the ratchet's re-verification — so nothing checks what they rested on
  against `HEAD`. And ignored output in staging is stale by construction
  once HEAD moves: the final conformance builds staging (`dist/`, `.next/`,
  generated clients), then the acceptance repair and the re-drive commit
  on top without rebuilding, and a worker's own build reflects whatever
  its tree held then. A `grep -rn` for the fixed symbol then finds it in
  the stale build of a fix that was rolled back (pinned by
  `tests/test_judges_read_the_committed_tree.py`). Review round 12 drove
  the uncited half (an untracked helper held the contract up), and round
  13 L2 the ignored half (a worker's uncommitted `dist/` build). A test
  run is the opposite case — it needs the installed dependencies and
  regenerates its own output — which is why measurements run in staging
  and judges do not;
- a judge's `met` counts only when each part cites a quote found in
  `git show HEAD:<path>` (`_verify_delivery_cite`), and an `ABSENT` cite
