`nothing_to_change` three times, each time listing the eight sites and the
arguments each already passed. Its claim was most likely true. Nothing
had integrated on its surface, so the settle returned before any command
or probe ran; it was re-driven twice and settled `unconverged`, and its
dependents `bugfix-005-3` (the parity test that would have checked the
claim) and `bugfix-006` settled `unconverged` without running. The
sibling check was the `e33` guard (above), but it guarded by refusing
every claim nothing had landed under, true or false. The guard now comes
from evidence about the claim itself, and a claim with nothing landed
under it is settled the same way as one a sibling delivered:

1. **(a) Run the commands.** The subtask's `verify` argvs run on HEAD,
   exactly as settle-by-execution runs them. A failure re-drives, with the
   failing command and its output tail in the note — once: a no-op claim
   its commands still refute after that re-drive settles `unconverged`
   (`no_op_refuted`), because a worker that reads the failure and still
   claims there is nothing to change will not be moved by a third round.
   An environment limit settles `unconverged`, as before.
2. **(b) Ask the probe, with the implementer's evidence.** When nothing
   failed, the HEAD `satisfied_probe` judges the criteria as before, and
   is now also shown the implementer's typed per-criterion evidence:
   `criteria_results` with the `locations` (file, start and end line) it
   read for each. The probe is told this is a claim to check, never a
   finding: it reads every location cited, then looks past them for what
   the criterion asks that they do not show. Code filters the locations
   mechanically (a relative path to a file on the tree, positive line
   numbers) and never reads the text. `satisfied` settles `complete`,
   recorded as `satisfied_on_base` — or `satisfied_by_sibling`, with the
   `satisfied_by` merges, when a sibling did change its surface: check 1
   above is now provenance, not a gate. `cannot_verify` that leerie's own
   passing commands answer in full settles too, as above. A gap re-drives,
   with the probe's typed `gaps` (criterion id, file, lines, what is
   missing) in the note.
3. **`cannot_verify` with no command covering it settles `unconverged` at
   once,** typed `undecidable_no_op`, and spends no re-drive round. The
   probe could not decide a criterion by reading, and no passing command
   decides it; a re-driven worker reports the same tree, and nothing in
   another round changes what can be read or run. A round spent there buys
   nothing but the delay of the dependents.

**A dependent of an `undecidable_no_op` runs.** Every other `unconverged`
predecessor keeps its dependents from running, because they would be
built on unfinished work that never reaches the run branch. An
`undecidable_no_op` settles only with zero commits ahead of the run
branch, so there is no unfinished work: the dependent starts from exactly
the tree it would have had had the claim settled `complete`. Running it is
the one way left to test the claim: in `2a663a3e` the dependent was the
parity test over every audited site, which passes only if the audit's
claim holds. If the claim was false, the dependent's own checks fail and
it is re-driven or settles `unconverged` on its own evidence. Nothing is
presented as done: the predecessor stays `unconverged`, so the run's
outcome is `unconverged` and its PR opens as a draft. Skipping the
dependent instead discards the cheapest available evidence about the
claim and leaves its work undone for a reason that is not on the tree.

**Split children carry `verify`.** The `e33` guard and both checks above
lean on `verify`, and a split used to drop it: the splitter's schema had no
`verify`, and code-built children copied every other field but that one.
In `2a663a3e` the planner gave `bugfix-005` a `verify` (the parity and
bypass-site acceptance tests) and neither child had one, so
`bugfix-005-1` could not be settled by execution at all. The splitter now
emits `verify` per child, from the parent's commands narrowed to the
child's criteria — but not `verification_only`, which stays planner-only
(code drops one a splitter child carries). A child code builds — a region,
peel or migration-chunk child whose criteria are the parent's seed
verbatim plus a scope clause — inherits the parent's `verify`; a chunk the
label-only splitter re-wrote keeps the `verify` it gave, else the
parent's. `verification_only` is never inherited either: a child of a
split subtask has work to do, and absence means false. A splitter-made child with no `verify`
under a parent that had one is logged as a plan defect
(`SPLIT_CHILD_NO_VERIFY`) and not repaired: which of the parent's
commands decides a child's own criterion is a reading the splitter makes.

**The `e33` guard holds on the evidence.** A no-op whose commands pass but
whose criterion the probe, shown the implementer's evidence, finds not met
does not settle `complete`: it is re-driven with the gap. The probe's input
changed, so the rule ships behind a bench, not on reasoning: the 22 E4/d4
cases plus every live no-op settled `unconverged` for want of a sibling,
with zero false settles required (`e33` among them) and at least the four
E4/d4 misses and `bugfix-005-1` settled. *Measured 2026-11-06* (3
samples per case; arm 4 is this rule, arm 1 the sibling-only rule before
it): zero false settles on every arm, `e33` settled 0/3; true settles 41
(arm 1: 10) at 17 re-drive rounds (arm 1: 124); `e163`, `e78`, `e90` and
`bugfix-005-1` settled 3/3. `e165` settled 0/3 on every arm, measured only
on a stand-in tree: its own tree and spec were pruned, so the bench ran it
on its run's start commit, where the artifact is genuinely absent and the
probe rightly says so; it is unmeasurable here, not a miss. The splitter,
re-run on 14 past split parents that had `verify`, gave 16 children over 42
samples, all carrying `verify`, none `verification_only`.

**Probing a flagged subtask before it spends.** Settling a no-op only after
its implementer has run is wasteful in ordering: `_warn_provider_subset_subtasks` (§5
*Provider-subset subtasks*) already flags, at plan time, every subtask whose
entire `files_likely_touched` surface belongs to an ordered predecessor —
measured always right and inert (a run's three flagged subtasks all ran a
full implementer and committed nothing; twelve corpus-wide reached the
post-execution settle only after their whole spend). So the flagged sids are persisted
(`provider_subset_sids`) and `_settle_subtask` runs the satisfied-probe on
HEAD against staging *before* spawning the implementer — staging sits at
run-branch HEAD, and a provider-subset predecessor is by construction
already merged there. A hit settles on one read-only probe instead of a
full implementer (one run's three cost ≈18 worker-minutes/≈$2.6 combined). A
miss costs one probe. This does **not** become a drop — the plan-time signal
stays advisory (a subtask may make a genuinely distinct edit to a shared
file) and the decision stays the probe's, judged against a real tree; only
*when* it's asked changes.

**A settle without an implementer still owes the wave a branch.**
`integrate_wave` filters only on `status == "complete"`, never on whether
`leerie/subtasks/<run-id>/<sid>` exists. A post-execution settle
(settled by execution, above) is safe because its implementer ran and created the branch (zero commits, a true
`git merge --no-ff` no-op). The pre-spawn probe returns *before*
`_run_implementer`, so no branch exists and `integrate.sh` exits 2 on every
probe hit. So the pre-spawn path creates the branch itself, at the
run-branch tip, before settling — the general invariant: **any path that
marks a subtask complete must leave behind the branch integration will look
for.** If the branch cannot be created, the subtask falls through to its
implementer.

**The sibling-invalidation case.** A third, opposite hazard: a subtask whose
criteria are met on the base tree *now*, but which a **surviving sibling in
the same plan will invalidate** — e.g. a coverage-floor test passes on the
seeded base and gets soft-dropped, but a surviving feature subtask later
adds the keys the test guards, turning it red, with no survivor owning that
file. The base-tree-only discipline is exactly what makes the probe blind to
this. The resolution keeps the base-tree rule but hands the probe the
**surviving siblings' declared surface** (`provides` and
`files_likely_touched`) as context, and asks it whether any surviving
sibling's work would invalidate the criteria it just judged met — declining
the drop (defaulting to *not satisfied*) if so. A mechanical
file-overlap rule was considered and rejected: the motivating case has
disjoint file sets (`nav-parity.test.ts` vs `messages/*.json`) whose
dependency lives only in intent, which a file-overlap predicate would miss
entirely — the judgment is left to the worker as the sole mechanism.

**Why this is §12-compliant.** `check_branch_has_commits` fires first and
unchanged; the probe can only *rescue*, never turn a committed subtask into
a failure, and fails safe to *not satisfied* on any crash or uncertainty.
"Are these success criteria semantically met on this tree" is exactly the
judgment §12's complementary half assigns to a worker — no new carve-out.

The structural contract of the §8 disciplines is mechanically enforced: the
worker's output schema requires the falsification, reconciliation, and gap
fields present, so a worker that skipped them fails its own JSON gate before
the orchestrator reads it. Their *quality* is model-judged; their *presence*
is not.

**Self-graded confidence is advisory; an independent verifier gates.** A
self-report has a structural ceiling no adversarial-falsification instruction
can raise — you cannot disprove a failure mode you cannot conceive, and the
mind that produced an incomplete solution bounds the failure modes it can
imagine. A real subtask scored itself `solution 9.5` with every falsifier it
"tested" about its own test plumbing, and shipped three latent behavioral
defects a later re-run had to fix — despite the prompt already commanding
maximal adversarial falsification. The fix is to change *who* runs the check,
generalizing the `fit_judge` precedent below: an independent judge finds cuts
the self-grader was blind to *because it did not produce the artifact*. So the
load-bearing gate for each self-graded axis becomes an **independent
adversarial verifier**, and the self-score is demoted to advisory.

Tests passing, lint clean, build green, and per-criterion satisfaction
remain **best-effort signals**, surfaced as warnings, never gating — any
code-enforced "tests must pass" gate invites a stuck model to weaken the
test instead (§9). Independence dissolves the gaming incentive without
reintroducing that bar.

#### Independent adversarial verification

The planner demonstrated the pattern first: `decomposition_quality`
self-score is retained as advisory, while the independent `fit_judge` is the
authoritative decomposition-quality gate (§5½), and `plan_overlap_judge` /
`adherence_judge` gate other planner dimensions the same way — `fit_judge`
works because it is a separate worker that did not produce the
decomposition, so it sees cuts the planner was blind to.

The same discipline now covers every ungated self-grader. Each remaining
self-graded axis gets an independent verifier that (a) did not produce the
artifact, (b) is handed only the artifact plus the task, and (c) is told to
**attack** it — enumerate concrete unhandled inputs, paths, cases, or
mis-wirings:

- **implementer `solution`** → verified by the **conformer's `solution_defects`
  axis**. The conformer already runs independently after the implementer's
  success path and reviews its committed diff (it did not write that diff —
  its own conformance edits are a separate, later layer), attacking it for
  behavioral gaps the self-grade missed. Gates in `_settle_subtask`; the
  conformer's existing build/lint/test and drift/docs/rule work stays
  advisory (below).
- **classifier** → an independent verifier of the category set against the
  task + codebase. A miscategorization here is not cosmetic — the same task
  classified one way produced ten subtasks, another way zero, and a "landing
  page feature" classified as documentation shipped only markdown. Gates on
  a found miscategorization.
- **reconciler / plan wiring** → the deterministic `check_plan_wiring` plus the
  independent `wiring_judge` described in §5 *A wiring re-check on the
  fully-merged plan*.
- **provision** → an independent verifier of the detected recipe against the
  actual image/runtime — e.g. does a `pip install` recipe carry
  `--break-system-packages` on the externally-managed Debian image, does the
  package manager match the lockfiles present. A recipe self-graded 9.3
  that omitted `--break-system-packages` caused twelve real install
  failures. Gates on a recipe that would fail.
- **planner `task_understanding`** → an independent `task_coverage_judge`,
  handed only the task plus the reconciled subtask set: does the union of
  subtasks actually *cover the task* — any required work missing entirely,
  any subtask off-task? Distinct from `fit_judge` (is each subtask
  sized/scoped correctly) and `wiring_judge` (are subtasks correctly wired to
  each other). A planner can self-report high `task_understanding` while a
  whole required piece of work never became a subtask, since a decomposition
  self-review is anchored to the decomposition already committed to, not the
  task independently re-read. It was first built to gate on a non-empty
  array of concretely-named coverage gaps and re-drive `phase_plan`. Since
  2026-08-04 it is advisory (below), and the gate re-plans only on the
  typed item accounting, never on a judge finding. A re-plan runs one
  planner per category with no cross-category visibility, so it can
  reintroduce the cross-domain tag drift `phase_reconcile` already
  resolved and the surface collisions the overlap judge merged. The gate's
  re-plan is therefore followed by reconcile, the overlap judge and the
  adherence gate (§5 *A re-plan invalidates every phase that already
  ran*). This doesn't reopen the earlier falsified attempt at gating
  `task_understanding` directly (§12 *Instruction adherence is
  code-enforced*): that finding was specific to an *understanding*-framed
  judge, which can't distinguish "understood and disobeyed" from "understood
  and obeyed." `task_coverage_judge` scores neither — only whether the
  subtask union is complete against the task, since a plan can honor every
  prescribed instruction and still omit unprescribed required work.

  `task_coverage_judge` originally had no deterministic PRIMARY check, only
  this SECONDARY judge. A floor, `check_required_items_coverage`, was tried
  and **deleted on 2026-08-04**: measured across every run that ever carried
  `required_items`, it passed 0 of 102 items — a 100% false-positive rate —
  and violated the *Language-to-JSON* rule (token-matching LLM-written
  sentences against subtask titles).

  The judge itself is retained but **advisory**: re-invoked on identical
  input it returned a different finding set 85% of the time (n=20), with an
  empty intersection across repeated samples — not a stable property of the
  input, so it cannot justify discarding a plan. The principle: **a judge's
  terminal authority must be proportional to its measured reproducibility,
  and a judgment layer with no mechanical backstop should not be terminal at
  all.** `wiring_judge` keeps its authority (99% of findings verify true,
  69/70) and `plan_overlap_judge` keeps its (impossible-assertion catches).

  That demotion was right for what was measured: a token floor and a
  judge, which both read prose. It was never evidence against a plan-time
  coverage gate. The mechanical check the gate lacked exists now. Each
  subtask names the required items it delivers by a code-assigned integer
  (`claims.items`); the only item a plan may leave unclaimed is one
  another category's planner delivers (`items_not_needed`,
  `other_domain`). The gate's authority rests on set
  arithmetic over those fields, which gives the same answer on the same
  plan every time (§5 *Required items are claimed too, and the plan
  accounts for every one*). The judge does not gain authority. It runs as
  before, and its findings are recorded and logged.

  `phase_plan` hands every planner the `required_items` (only when
  non-empty), each with its code-assigned `item_index`, mirroring the
  instruction-adherence gate's `prescribed_procedure` injection. The
  coverage judge gets the same items with the same numbers.
- **integrator `resolution`** → an independent `integration_judge` that did
  not perform the merge, handed the merged result plus both parent diffs and
  the conflicting subtasks' intents: did the merge actually resolve the
  conflict *behaviorally*, not just remove `<<<<<<<` markers? The existing
  conflict-marker scan plus `check_merge_committed` catch the mechanical
  failure; they cannot see a syntactically clean merge that silently drops
  one side's behavior — e.g. a merge that keeps side A's function signature
  but side B's call sites, compiling but breaking at runtime. Gates on a
  non-empty array of
  concretely-named behavioral defects in the merged result. A finding is
  handed back to the integrator as typed data and the repaired tree is
  re-judged whole, up to `integration_repair_rounds`; a typed
  `intent_conflict` (both sides' intents quoted, no merged tree can keep
  both) or a merge that does not converge backs the subtask out as
  `unconverged` instead of killing the run (§6 *When integration cannot
  succeed*).

  **Location is not coverage.** A merge that drops a *duplicate* is textually
  indistinguishable from one that drops the only copy — both remove content
  present in a parent — so reasoning from the parent diffs alone can't tell
  them apart. A `dropped_change` is therefore only behavioral if the behavior
  is absent from the **merged tree**, not merely from the side the merge
  chose. The judge holds inspection tools, so it's asked to search the merged
  tree for equivalent coverage and cite it concretely (file + assertion). A
  defect carrying a specific citation is advisory; one without still gates —
  judge by *coverage*, not *location*, the same correction applied to the
  on-HEAD satisfied-probe.

  The citation is **asked for and never required**: requiring a field on a
  judge's schema has repeatedly produced a worker that emits no schema-valid
  output at all, and a gate that never runs catches nothing (§8 *Findings
  carry a severity* — the default is gating). Absence therefore gates.
- **`plan_overlap_judge`'s own `judgment` self-score is dropped, with no new
  independent verifier.** This worker is already the independent adversarial
  check for cross-planner surface collisions — layering a second judge on top
  of a judge would be self-scoring one level removed. Its existing
  deterministic validators — `PHANTOM_ARTIFACT`, `NO_FILE_OVERLAP`,
  `DROP_BREAKS_GRAPH`, `DUPLICATE_PAIR` (`check_overlap_judge_output`, §5
  *Cross-domain surface overlap*), and `_validate_overlap_judge_output`'s
  `merge_feasibility`-presence backstop — already catch the concrete,
  checkable failure modes. What remains ungated by dropping the self-score is
  purely a *quality-of-judgment* concern with no mechanically-attackable
  "artifact" for a second worker to find defects in — the same reason the
  implementer's `solution` axis is verified by a *different-role* worker (the
  conformer) rather than a second implementer grading the first. The
  deterministic validators become this worker's sole gate; `confidence` stays
  an advisory record only.

**Why this does not reintroduce the gameable bar §9 removed.** The old
criteria-lock / "tests must pass" gate was gameable because the *same* worker
controlled the bar. Independence dissolves that incentive: a verifier that
(a) did not write the artifact and (b) gates on "here is a concrete input
this artifact mishandles" — never "a test passed" or "the criteria say met"
— presents no bar for the graded worker to lower, and can't be defeated by
weakening a test, because it constructs *new* adversarial inputs the graded
worker never anticipated. A verdict is a list of concrete found defects, not
a score crossing a threshold — the invariant every new verifier must
preserve.

### Existing tests the run changed are listed in the PR

A run can make its task pass by changing a test the repository already had:
an expected value rewritten, an assertion dropped, a case deleted, a skip
marker added, a file removed. Sometimes that is the task (the behaviour
changed, so the old expectation is wrong); sometimes it is a weakening. The
two look the same to code. At finalize, once, leerie measures the run
branch's final tree against the run's own start (`_diff_base`) and lists
every such change in the PR under `## Existing tests changed by this run`
(§6 *The PR's end-state section*): per file, the assertions and cases the
base had that the final tree lacks, then the ones it added, a skip count, a
deleted file. The section says plainly that nothing verified these against
the task and that the reviewer should read each before merging. It renders
on every PR, a draft (`unconverged`) one included, and from the same
`pr_end_state` text on the pr_writer path and the launcher's fallback.

**It is report-only.** A flag changes no outcome, verdict, gate, retry or
rollback, and a worker is not asked about it. What does change the outcome is
measured, not read: the existing tests' base forms (*What an existing test
pins on the base holds on the tree that ships*, below). Escalation gate (b) of the
delivery re-drive (`_redrive_weakened_tests`: fewer expect/assert call sites,
fewer cases, more skips, on the escalated round only) is a separate check
and is unchanged.

A rewritten setup lists too. A test can stop testing what it did without one
assertion string changing: the call that drives the code under test is
replaced, a fixture is reshaped, a `settle:` option dropped. So a file also
gets a count line, `setup or other lines changed: N removed, M added`, when
the final tree removes more non-blank, non-comment lines than the removed
assertions and cases account for (each counted as one line). The count is
over the file's lines with comments blanked (`_tt_mask`) and each line's
whitespace collapsed, blank lines dropped, compared as multisets against
the base: a deleted or added blank line or comment, a reindented or
reflowed-in-place line and a moved line count nothing, a changed line counts
one removed and one added. Nothing characterises those lines; the reviewer
reads the diff. It over-reports on purpose (a removed case's body counts
beyond its one line); a false positive costs a glance. A file only added to
(0 removed lines) stays unlisted.

Why not more. A branch built the stronger form: the same detector on every
code-writing round, voiding a round that altered a tracked test unless the
worker declared it with a quote of the task. A confined bench of that
declaration failed: legitimate updates were declared correctly 6 of 12, and
real weakenings evaded with a weak quote 4 of 6. A gate that voids honest
rounds and passes dishonest ones is worse than a list. The detector itself
held up: replayed over recorded runs it found real weakenings in 3 of 17
hand-classified flagged rounds, one of which (run 73751002) had shipped.

What it measures (mechanical, on test source with strings, comments and JS
regex literals masked): an assertion statement (`expect(`, `assert(`,
`assert.<m>(`, Python `assert`, `.assert<X>(`, `pytest.raises(`), compared
whitespace- and trailing-comma-free; a case (`it(`/`test(` by title,
`def test_*` by name); skip/only/todo/xfail markers; the file. Only a file
present at the base counts, and only a change that survives to the final
tree: a change a later commit reverted is not listed.

What it does not do. It does not say which commit or round made a change
(one comparison, base to final tree). It does not judge: a legitimate update
and a weakening are listed alike, and so is a known false-positive shape,
an assertion whose subject moved into a local variable, which reads as one
removed and one added assertion. It sees only test-shaped paths. It lists at
most `_TRACKED_TEST_ITEMS_MAX` items per list and `_TRACKED_TEST_FILES_MAX`
files in state, and `_PR_TRACKED_TEST_SHOWN` entries in the PR, counting
the rest.

### What an existing test pins on the base holds on the tree that ships

*Designed 2026-11-07, after run a79384a4.* The invariant: *the behaviour an
existing test pins on the run's base keeps holding on the tree the run ships,
unless a person decides otherwise.* Run a79384a4 ended `done` and its PR undid
an earlier merged fix: acceptance repair round 2 (`4d80a79`) changed
`click-settle.ts` and deleted the two cases of
`flow-runner.post-click-settle.test.ts` that pinned the fix, because the run's
two held-out sets asked for the opposite. Nothing stopped it. The failing-test-ID
diff and B\* look for tests that newly fail, and a deleted case never runs; the
ratchet read required items, not existing tests; escalation gate (b) runs on the
re-drive's last round only; the list above is report-only. The task had said
"We must ensure that any new changes NEVER INTRODUCE REGRESSIONS in current
functionality."

**The check is a run, not a reading.** Every test-case file the base had that a
tree modified or deleted is run *in its base form* — the base's own content —
against that tree, and every case that fails there is confirmed under B\*
against the same base form on the tree's start. A deleted case still runs. A
loosened assertion still asserts the old value. A deleted file is run from its
base blob. A file that no longer loads (a removed export it imports) is a
failing case of its own (`(file failed to load)`), as it is in every report
leerie reads. No prompt, judge or text rule takes part: nothing here asks a
worker or reads an assertion.

*Where the base form runs.* In place of the final form, at its own path, in
a disposable copy of the tree: the held-out sandbox over the committed view
(§6 *A held-out evaluation runs alone*), an overlay whose writes vanish with
it. Every test-case file the check runs is replaced there by its base blob (a
deleted one is restored), and every test-case file the base did not have is
removed, so the runner sees the base's test-case files and the tree's code,
and nothing is written to a tree. A JS file's base snapshot replaces its final
one, and a final snapshot the base did not have is removed with it. A test
helper, fixture or `conftest.py` keeps its final form; it is reached through
the cases that use it.

It was first placed beside the final form under a tagged name
(`a.test.ts` -> `a.leerie-base.test.ts`). That cannot work wherever a runner
builds a package or a directory together. A Go package declares each test
function once. A Ruby class reopened by a second copy merges its methods. A
JVM or .NET test source set compiles every copy. Those files were listed as
unchecked. A tagged name is also not the file's own name, and a test that
reads a fixture or a snapshot named after its own file then finds none.
Replacing the file works for every runner, so it is the one mechanism. The
removal is what a runner that compiles a package together needs. Without it,
a helper the run added to a changed file and used from a new one, or moved
from a changed file into a new one, no longer compiles beside the base form,
and every case of the package would fail as if the run had changed it.

The check costs what it cost when the copy sat beside the final form. The
sandbox lies over the view the measurement already installed. A fresh git
checkout of the tree with the file replaced would need an install of its own
for every check, on top of the one B\*'s base side already pays when a case
fails (at most 38 s for a `web` view in 6f147a0c's re-drive, the log's whole gap
around it, pnpm from the run's store). A path that is a
link or a directory, or has a link or a non-directory on its way, in either
tree, is never written through: the file is unmeasured. A test file whose
runner gives no report leerie reads (a JVM, .NET, PHP, Swift or Elixir test;
§9 *Which failures are new*) is listed under "Regression checks the run could
not settle", not run, as its failing-test-ID diff is.

*Where it runs.* After every acceptance repair round and every delivery re-drive
group that commits, inside the ratchet's execution route: the files the round
touched or reaches (`_change_reach`; all of them when its reach is unknown), the
round's own start as the base side. A case that fails only after the round
rolls it back (`_roll_back_round`), the reason naming the case. A case an
earlier round already broke is not this round's. And once more on the tree
that ships, after the last refresh of the failing-test-ID diff and before the
outcome, every file, against the run's base. There a failing case makes the run
`unconverged` with a typed `existing_behaviour_changed` reason naming each case,
and the PR's `## Existing tests changed by this run` lists it first under its
file. A check that could not run (no report, a taken path, another tree than
the one that ships, a raise) is unmeasured, which `done` does not rest on (§6
*`done` rests on measurements that ran*).

**Measured: the replay.** Every recorded run (barnacle and `web`) whose run
branch modified or deleted a test-case file its base had: 41 runs, 157 files.
For each, the base and final trees were extracted from the run's own
repository, installed from their lockfiles, and every such file was run in its
base form on both, under leerie's own Landlock shim; a case failing on the
final tree and passing on the base was rerun in three interleaved base/final
pairs (B\*'s rule). Read only, no worker call. The 4 `web` runs could not be
measured (their install's `prisma generate` was refused under the replay's
grant); 37 barnacle runs were. The base-form run on the final tree took a
median 24 s, at most 58 s. 138 cases were confirmed changed in 17 runs; no case
was mixed evidence, and none was a load failure.

| `done` runs (13 measured) | stopped | real regression | task-required change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| a79384a4 | 4 cases | yes: the #696 fix the task said must not regress | |
| 2e382c2f | 1 | | yes |
| 7c1f0bfe | 2 | | yes |
| b009c575 | 5 | | yes |
| 43bd4671 | 12 | | yes |
| ef425976 | 3 | | yes |
| the other 7 | 0 | | |

The five task-required rows change what their report calls the defect. 2e382c2f,
7c1f0bfe and b009c575 carry the required item "Generated response schema for a
recon:generate run must accept valid responses of sibling entities served by
the same endpoint", and their failing base-form cases assert the strict
one-entity schema (a "no WARN" case, `tags: z.array(z.string())` required, a
lone sample strict); b009c575's other four are the generated contract's text,
reshaped by the same change, not checked one by one. 43bd4671 and ef425976 fix
"recon-generate-rest-get-hardcodes-path-segment-and-query-params-so-the-plugin-can-only-replay-the-recording",
and their cases assert the hard-coded `/items/1` and the constant query keys.
73751002, the run the tracked-test replay found had shipped a real weakening,
is not stopped: its final conformer (`edc5083`) restored the behaviour, and the
base form passes on the tree that shipped.

So the check stops 6 of 13 measured `done` runs: 1 real regression, 5 changes
the task asked for. Among the other 24, 11 carry changed cases. One is a second
live case, a2a825c2 (it ended `unconverged` for other reasons): its final
conformer (`aea6d06`) inverted #358's case "drops a same-host, non-mutation
capture that passes isAllowedFixtureHost and the fold-return matcher but is
structurally unrelated to the flow's mutation family", to satisfy the report's
section C16, which asks for the one-line exemption. The base form fails
(`expected [ 'PromotionsWidgetSearch', … ] to deeply equal [ 'SubmitBookingavailVas' ]`).
A fix exists that satisfies both: exempt a declared fold-return capture only
when it is joined to the flow's items.

On a79384a4 the round check would have acted where it mattered: at round 2's
start (`4a48b8c`, where the final conformer had restored the budget) all 67
base-form cases pass; after it, the 4 above fail, 11 s a side.

**Why a person decides, after two rounds that try to keep both.** A failing
base form is either a regression (a79384a4) or the task asking for the change
(five of the six). Code cannot tell them apart by reading: that is the task's
meaning, and every reading tried failed its bench — the declaration path (§8
*Existing tests the run changed are listed in the PR*: weak quotes passed 4 of
6 weakenings), and an independent judge with verified quotes and a majority
of three (T9 bench 1: it accepted a2a825c2's inverted #358 case 6 of 6,
because report C16 names #358's pinned behaviour as the defect word for
word). What does tell them apart is constructive: a regression is a change a
fix could have avoided. So before the run stops, the delivery re-drive tries
to build that fix (*A fix that keeps both, on opus when sonnet could not*,
below); what it cannot build stops the run and shows the conflict: the case
that fails in its base form, its failure, and, beside it in the PR, what the
run changed in that test. One read settles it. Nothing is accepted by
reading the task. The one exception is not a reading of the task: a pinned
case that a required item's confirmed, shown probe contradicts — no
implementation passes both, a fact verified against the two tests' quoted
assertions and the code — is task-required (§8 *Delivery re-drive* rule 4,
*A pinned case a required item's probe contradicts is task-required*). The
cost is convergence on a task whose required change IS the
tested behaviour (a sweep that moves literals into message files): no fix
keeps both, so such a run ends `unconverged` and opens a draft.

### A fix that keeps both, on opus when sonnet could not

*Designed 2026-11-09, lane T9.* Before the tree that ships is checked, the
existing tests' base forms are run on the tree the delivery re-drive starts
from (`_check_existing_behaviour`), and each test file with failing cases is
a typed `base_form_case` note of the re-drive (§8 *Delivery re-drive*): its
cases, their failures, and the command that shows the original test. The
note asks for the change that keeps both — the cases pass as the original
test wrote them while every required item stays met, the pinned behaviour
restored wherever the task does not need it changed — and never for undoing
what the task asks. It is routed like a control, on the shared re-drive
budget, and judged by the re-drive's own checks: the base-form run against
the run's base (did its cases pass?), the round's own base-form check (did it
break another pinned case?), the shown held-out sets, the delivery ratchet
(did a met item go unmet?), the clean-tree gate; a round that fixed none of
its cases is zero progress. Each is rolled back like any other group.

**Two attempts, the second on opus.** A file's note is driven once on the
implementer's own model and effort (sonnet, `low`). The cases still failing
after that attempt get exactly one more, on `MODEL_BASE_FORM_ESCALATION`
(`opus`) at `EFFORT_BASE_FORM_ESCALATION` (`high`), with the same note for
those cases only, driven alone (no other note in its group), with the same
checks and rollback. A per-call override of that one round: no worker's
default model changes. Why opus there and nowhere else: the cases that reach
it are the ones sonnet at low effort could not keep, which is where a
stronger model is worth its cost, and only there — as the delivery re-drive
raises effort only on its last round (`EFFORT_REDRIVE_ESCALATION`). Measured
(T9 bench 7b, 3 samples per run, 2026-11-10, on 0.55.2 — before
#365's flip rollback):
- A responsive grid the task did not need changed: sonnet put it back in all
  3 samples (3/3 cases each).
- An existing test the run had inverted: sonnet kept nothing in any sample.
  Opus kept the fix that holds both in 2 of 3; the third stays blocking.
- A run whose base-form cases cannot pass without undoing its own late-body
  test: blocking 3/3, every round rolled back.

No kept round's harm ended a run with the harmed item reported met. In one
sample, the #352 re-check judged a required item unmet after the opus round
was kept, and that run ended `unconverged`. #365's flip rollback would now
roll such a group back when the item's confirmed probe passed on its start;
its base-form attempt then reads `rolled_back`, like any other group's.

**A round changes what the test is run against, never the test.** A base-form
case asks whether the base's test, in its original form, passes on the new
code — and the test's form includes what it runs with. So a round driving
base-form notes may change only files outside its cases' **test closure**
(`_base_form_closure`): the case files, every test-side file they import
transitively (test files, the import graph's test-support modules,
`__mocks__`), the runner's configuration and the setup or support files it
names, and a Python case's `conftest.py` chain. A closure file may be
written back exactly as it is at the run's base — that is putting the
original test back — and nothing else; and a test file the run added may not
be changed or deleted at all (`_base_form_closure_breach`). A round that
does otherwise is void and rolled back. The rule needs no attribution: in
T9 bench 4 the two harmful kept rounds changed the test's support (e0d101e3:
the global message mock rewritten so old literal assertions pass, and a
test the run added changed) and would have been rolled back by it, which a
check of which cases still pass could not see, because the round's own mock
change is what made the run's deleted cases fail.

**And it may not drop a case that still holds.** Putting an original test
file back exactly is allowed, and with it every case the run had added to
that file goes. A case the restored behaviour contradicts may go; one that
still passes may not: the round's commit is measured for the cases of each
test file it modified whose form at the round's start passes on its commit
but that the commit's own form no longer has (`_redrive_dropped_cases`); any
such case, or a measurement with no report, voids the round. The closure
rule does not catch this: in T9 bench 3 a kept round wrote a79384a4's
original `flow-runner.post-click-settle.test.ts` back exactly (no breach) and
dropped 10 of the 32 run-start cases still passing there, the task's own
guards among them.

**A case pinning a moved literal gets no round.** Some base-form cases
cannot be satisfied without harm. When a task moves UI text into message
files, a base test that finds or asserts that literal text passes only if
production holds the literal again. In T9 benches 4-6, opus took exactly
that path on navegando 4134b78c in 3 runs of 3, and every check passed it.
Reading the task cannot tell such a case apart (T9 bench 1). Code facts can
(`_base_form_moved_literals`, in `_check_existing_behaviour`). A case is
classified `pins_moved_literal` when a string or plain regex literal of its
base form's reachable code (from `scripts/test-case-facts.cjs`) meets all
three of:

- (a) a production source file at the base holds it;
- (b) that file on the run's tree no longer holds it;
- (c) a message file the run added or changed holds it as a value.

Presence is read from the file's code with its comments blanked: a doc
comment that still names the old text is not the text (4134b78c's
`campaign-list.tsx` kept one). A message file is
`(messages|locales?|i18n|translations|langs?)/*.json`. Such a case gets no
round: it stays `existing_behaviour_changed`, never accepted. The PR lists it
as "existing test pins text the run moved to the message files", with the
literal and the key it moved to, so the person updates that test. The run
ends `unconverged`, which is the honest verdict.

Known limits: a moved text inside a larger literal (a CSS selector) or with
its case changed (`includes("transferir")`) is not classified, so such a case
still gets its rounds.

**What neither catches.** A round that undoes a required item in production
code while keeping every test green: in T9 bench 4 an opus round on
4134b78c restored the original password-input cases by giving the
component hard-coded Spanish label defaults. The item stays covered only by
the delivery ratchet, which re-verifies a met item after a kept round with
its judge alone (`_ratchet_judge`); the falsifier that a met needs at
detection, and that a re-check runs again (`_redrive_falsify_met`), never
runs on a ratchet's tree. That is a delivery-detection gap, not this
section's.

### Held-out acceptance tests

Every verification layer above grades the fix against tests the fixing
run wrote itself. On both v0.36.0 repeat runs the first run's fix failed
on the report's own quoted input, and none of the 44 review calls across
those two runs (fit judges, conformers, delivery judges) flagged it: the
tests had been written around the implementation, not the report. The
automated-program-repair literature names this *overfitting*: a patch
that passes the tests its author saw and fails the behaviour those tests
stood for (Smith et al., FSE 2015; on SWE-bench, 29.6% of "plausible"
patches disagree with the reference fix on fresh tests — Wang, Pradel et
al., ICSE 2026). The measured remedy that recurs across that work is the
same: tests the patch author never saw (DiffTGen, Opad, UTBoost), and
ImpossibleBench (ICLR 2026) shows that test visibility is exactly what
drives special-casing to a test's inputs.

So after the defect-scope audit, an `acceptance_writer` worker — an
acting worker in a disposable checkout at the **validity base**, which is
the run's **own start** (the HEAD the run started from) — writes tests
from the report alone. It sees the report, the audited `defect_shape` and
the report's `inline_examples`; it never sees the plan or any code the run
will write. It writes several
independent *sets*, each split into **defect files** (must fail on the
validity base) and **control files** (correct behaviour that must keep
passing), driving the behaviour through the module's stable entry points
rather than internal helpers whose signatures a fix may change. Python
validates each set mechanically, **per case** — from the runner's
structured report of what ran (below), and by exit code only where the
runner can write none, never by reading runner prose: a set is valid when
it has at least one control case, every control case passes, and at least
one defect case fails; a defect file none of whose cases fails cannot
discriminate and is dropped. A set with no control cannot show an
over-broad fix, so it is not valid however its defect cases fail — the rule
the C1 bench validated with (every one of its 11 own-start-valid sets
carried passing controls, and ground truth called 9 of the 10 it could
resolve valid).

**The validity tree is the run's own start, not the report's.** It used
to be the tree the report was filed against — the earliest same-task
run's starting HEAD — so a chain's later runs validated against a tree
the chain had long since changed. Measured (Q6, 6/7 sets of one failing
cluster): those sets were written at a base where the production probe
the report concerns did not exist yet, while at the run's own start both
the probe and the repository's own helper that answers it (imported by
59 tests) did; the sets then demanded a shape no later tree had. Written
and validated at own start, a set says what is still wrong *now*, on the
tree this run will change: a defect the chain already fixed yields no
failing defect case and so no set. The earliest same-task base is still
looked up, but only as information: each valid set records
`report_reproduced` — whether it also fails there — and nothing filters
on it. Sets from earlier runs are never carried forward or re-validated;
each run writes its own. (A `done` run's *settled bar*, below, is not a
set: it is a record of cases that passed on a tree carrying the fix, re-run
but never re-validated, rewritten or shown to a writer — *Done is a fixed
bar per task, not re-sampled each run*.) The writer's checkout is a clone whose only
reachable commit is the own start — no branch, tag or run branch — so
neither a later commit nor an earlier run's fix can steer the tests, and
everything the writer runs runs on that base tree (fail-open to a plain
worktree, logged, when the clone cannot be made).

**Written whenever the defect-scope audit ran.** The sets used to be
written only when the audit said `applicable`. Measured over 152
historical audits, 18 said `applicable: false`, and on those runs no set
was ever written — including runs whose task was a real, still-open
defect (Q5/N1: of 9 such strict-decoding cases labelled *needs*, 8 had a
false first sample). Ungated (Q7/N1-L), the writer put adjudicated
right-reason work on 14 of 16 *needs* tasks, and on the not-needed side
0 of 22 lever-covered sets created false work (CI 0–15); on a task that
is already done, own-start validity discards the sets by itself, because
no defect case fails. So every run whose classification triggered the
audit gets sets, whatever the audit returned — its fail-open
`{"applicable": false}` included — and a set left failing feeds the
run-outcome decider (§6 *The run outcome is decided once*) like any other
unfinished work. When the audit is not applicable the writer's payload
simply carries no contract and no examples.
A set carries what its validation ran on: a writer that
edited an existing file loses the set, and every other new file it left
(a helper or fixture beside the tests, even one the repo's ignore rules
match — though an ignored file elsewhere, likely build output from the
unfixed tree, does not) travels with the set — minus what the dependency install made
and the runner's caches and bytecode, which would only collide with the
target tree's own. Without its helper, a correct fix fails the set. Measured: on the page-advance report, five sets written this way
classified all 8 trees correctly (40/40: run 1's broken fix, two other
example-shaped or test-skipping fixes, four correct ones); on the
generate report all sets failed every broken tree including barnacle's
HEAD, which leerie had declared "no work required"; on a Python repo
with a planted defect, 3/3 sets were valid, passed the fixed code and
flagged an example-shaped patch.

**The gate runs after the run's own final conformance.** Each valid set
runs against staging's committed HEAD in a disposable worktree of its
own — never in staging itself, where a crash mid-run (which no cleanup
survives) would leave hidden tests for the next fixer to read or commit.
Judging a fix, the verdict is the exit code: a command the shell could
not run, one the container's limits killed (a fork-exhaustion message in
the output's tail), or any set run where a dependency install failed is
no verdict (a failing build step is not: a fix that breaks the build is
evidence against it — at the cost that a transient build failure reads as
the fix failing). Every other non-zero exit fails, including a
missing-file defect whose failure prints "No such file or directory", and
including a file that no longer loads: it ran on the base, so the fix is
what stopped it. A set that cannot even be placed is no verdict, never an
error that skips the rollback check below.

Validating a set on the base asks more, because a defect file that never
ran must not count as failing. Exit codes cannot say whether a file ran:
jest and vitest exit 1 alike for "no tests", "could not load" and "a test
failed"; cargo exits 101 for a build or a test failure; and `go test`
exits 0 when nothing ran. So where the runner can write a structured
report of the run — pytest's JUnit XML, the jest-compatible JSON of jest
and vitest — validation asks for one and reads how many tests executed (a
test whose fixture failed to set up counts as executed: it ran and failed)
and whether the file loaded — pytest marks a file it could not collect
with a fixed "collection failure" message, which no report option
renames. The same report carries each case's own status, and that, not
the exit code, is the verdict: a defect file fails on the base when one
of its cases failed, and a control passes when none of its cases failed
— so a coverage threshold or a teardown error that turns the exit code
red no longer discards a set whose cases all passed, and a failing
case sitting in an otherwise-passing file still counts. The reports read
are pytest's JUnit XML, the jest-compatible JSON, rspec's JSON formatter,
a minitest reporter leerie supplies (a plugin found through `RUBYLIB`,
writing one record per case), `go test -json` and libtest's JSON events
(`cargo test`, through `RUSTC_BOOTSTRAP=1`).

Asking means appending report flags to the test command (or, for pytest,
setting `PYTEST_ADDOPTS`, unless the command names its own JUnit path,
which would override it). What runs is the template as written with the
flags appended, and only when the appended words would land as the last
arguments of the runner's own simple command. The command is split into
words and operators by a close reading of bash's rules — quotes kept in
mind (a quoted `"("` is a word, not a paren; an escaped quote inside
`${…}` opens nothing; a backtick body is read as bash reads it, as a
command of its own once its backslashes are undone), a line continuation
joining lines, a comment starting only at a word, a newline ending a
command as `;` does — noting how deep in command substitutions each token
sits. It is a reading, not bash: the tests pin it against bash's own argv.
The file under test never counts as the runner, even when named like one.
There is no report when, from the runner on, anything but words follows at
the top level (a separator, pipe, redirect, or a `)` closing a subshell
the runner runs in — a `$(…)` among its arguments is not that), when a
`--` after it would make the flags file arguments, when the appended word
would fall into a trailing comment or be joined by a trailing backslash,
when the command has a heredoc (its body is text, not commands), when the
runner runs inside a substitution, or when a shell comes before it in its
command, or `eval`, `source` or `.` is that command (found as bash finds
it: past redirects and their fds, assignments, and the `!`, `time`,
`command`, `builtin` and `coproc` prefixes with their options) or a
command word an expansion or a brace expansion builds (`$E jest` and
`{eval,} jest` could be `eval`; a `/` in the word outside the expansion
rules that out, `$VENV/bin/python`, while `$NPX jest` loses its report
rather than risk it) — each takes what follows as text or as a script, not
as a program and its arguments (`sh -c jest`, `timeout 60 sh -c jest`,
`fish run.fish jest`, `bash run.sh jest`, `eval jest`), while a bare `.`
argument is just a path (`npx --prefix . jest`). Operators are read as
bash reads them, longest first, so a redirect (`2>&1`, `<in.txt`, `>|out`)
belongs to its command and ends nothing, and neither this nor the
container check below can be hidden behind one. The placement is
syntactic: the flags reach the runner when its command is the runner or a
wrapper that passes arguments on (`npx jest`, `uv run pytest`). A command
that merely names the runner as an argument (`./run.sh jest`) is not told
apart and receives the flags itself, as it has since reports were
introduced. A runner started through a container or remote CLI, or as
another user — `docker`, `podman`, `nerdctl`, `kubectl`, `oc`, `lima`,
`finch`, `apptainer`, `ssh`, `su`, `sudo` and the rest of
`_CONTAINER_CLIS`, or a brace expansion that could build one (never a
`NAME=` value, which bash does not brace-expand) — earlier in the simple
command of any occurrence of the runner, not a container started by an
earlier command nor one queried inside a `$(…)` for a value — is not asked
at all: it cannot see the orchestrator's environment, and a report path it
cannot create would fail a run whose tests pass. Matching is by name, so a
package or folder named like one of these before the runner (`yarn
workspace toolbox jest`) also loses the report.

A file that ran no test, or could not be loaded, is no verdict and
discards its set (the gate then has less to check, never a false failure)
— with one exception. When the report's
defect is itself that loading fails (a missing entry point, a module that
raises on import), the writer says so for that file, and a file that
cannot load on the base is then the defect showing — provided the file,
and every other Python file the writer wrote (a broken helper would fail
every fix just the same), parses under the project's own interpreter: a
throwaway compile check, named to fit the repository's own test-file
convention where any candidate name does, run through its own test
command, so its interpreter version
decides, not the orchestrator's. The check marks when its own body is
reached and when every file compiled, because only a failure between
the two is about parsing: one before it (a conftest or package that
cannot import — perhaps the very entry point the defect lacks — or a
runner that collected or selected no test) or after it (a teardown, a
coverage threshold) says nothing about it. A check that
did not reach its body proves nothing, and the declaration is not
honoured either; the log says which, with the exit code where the
command ran.
That is checked only where it can be checked reliably, in Python; a
declared import defect in any other language is dropped on its own,
leaving the rest of its set (`node
--check` was measured accepting a syntax error in an ES-module test file
run through babel, and TypeScript has no parser check short of a build).
Reading the report to know which case applies is the writer's job, never
Python's (§12); the price is that a writer who declares a guessed import
produces a test no fix can pass, which costs two repair rounds and a
residual, never the run. Without a readable report (a runner with none
known, a report that was not written, or a runner the test command starts
inside another container, which is never asked for one) validation falls
back to the runner's own "ran no test" exits where they exist (pytest's), and
otherwise to the exit code alone — so on `go test`, a file that ran
nothing reads as passing: it cannot become a defect file (it does not
fail on the base), but it can be accepted as a control that proves
nothing. **Every failing validated set is repaired** — not only when a
majority fails. Under the old majority rule a minority of failing sets
was shipped as a residual with no repair round at all (G1: a failing
validated set left unrepaired because the majority passed). A set
failure is a verdict like a new test failure and is confirmed the same
way (§9 *Which failures are new*) — with one asymmetry, below: a set file
that fails on the tree is rerun serially behind the host-pressure gate,
`confirm_pairs` times (or `confirm_pairs_escalated` after a gate timeout)
inside `confirm_budget_sec`, and it stays failing only if it failed on
every rerun that produced a verdict. A rerun the budget cuts short is not
a run (§9 *Which failures are new*, step 4): when the budget alone stopped
the vote short and every rerun that finished failed the file, it stays
failing — a budget cut is never evidence that a failure went away. The
exception is a file whose first run failed only by timing out or dying of
a signal: that is a resource signature, not the assertion the file was
written to make, so with no finished rerun it is unsettled
(`budget_short_unsettled_files`) — the set is unmeasured unless another
file fails, never failing on the timeout alone. Measured (review round 6):
such a file, every rerun cut, was confirmed failing and the run
`unconverged`.
Anything else is `resource_affected`,
and a set whose only failures were resource-affected and touched no held
case is no evidence either way — so a load flake never forces a repair
round, nor a residual.

**A held-out set the final tree leaves unmeasured is never silent.** The
sets exist to show the task's own scenario works; one that ends with no
verdict on the tree that ships is verification the run did not finish, so it makes the run `unconverged`
(§6 *The run outcome is decided once*, "`done` rests on measurements that
ran"; before review round 19 it did not: no evidence was taken as no
failure). It is always listed under the PR's "Needs human
verification", one line per set naming its files and why each could not
be measured, from a fixed vocabulary the evaluation records on the set's
result (`unmeasured_reason` for the whole set, `unmeasured_files` per
file): the evaluation could not be set up, the commit or the worktree
could not be made, the dependency install failed, the files could not be
placed, a file's path is already used by the tree, the runner gave no
verdict, a file timed out (or was killed by a signal) on its first run
and the budget cut every rerun, no rerun produced a verdict, or the
reruns disagreed. Two whole-gate shapes are listed the same way: valid
sets with no final verdict at all (the gate raised or never ran), and a
final verdict of an earlier commit because re-measuring the commit that
ships measured nothing. A set typed broken, and a variant set of a
report-pointer task (no counted case), are left out: neither could be
work. Measured (review round 7, M3): a vote file that only timed out,
every rerun cut, left its set unmeasured — the run `done` and the PR's
end-state section empty, the file named nowhere.

*A timeout is not read as failing, even on a file that ran to a verdict
at the own start* (every valid set file did, by construction). A
deterministic hang the change introduced looks exactly like this, and
that reading would end fewer such runs `done`; it is rejected because the
evidence cannot tell the hang from load. The first run's timeout is one
observation, recorded the same way as a signal death — the out-of-memory
kill that is the commonest load signature. A rerun the budget cut is a
second non-finish only if it was given time the file needed, and the own
start's duration is not recorded, so a cut after two seconds of a shared
budget would count the same as one after thirty minutes; any threshold
would be an unbenched constant. And round 6 measured the failing reading
directly: a file confirmed failing on a timeout alone sends repair
rounds at a failure with no case to name and ends the run `unconverged`.
This is the same trade §9 *Which failures are new* (step 4) makes for a
base-paired candidate too slow for one pair: unsettled, `done`, named for
a human. What this rule adds is that the human always sees it, with a
timeout called out as the hang it may be.

**A held case that fails again is a failure, not a flake.** A set's
*held* cases are the defect cases validation saw fail at the run's own
start (`base_failing_cases`; in a set the scope judge bounded, only its
counted cases). Each failed there by construction, so on the tree under
test the vote is the wrong question for them: the rerun vote exists to
tell a load flake from a regression, and a held case failing again for a
non-resource reason is the reported defect showing, however rarely. So:

1. *No vote for the defect showing.* A held case failing on the tree,
   whose runner-report message carries no resource signature — a timeout,
   a worker crash or exit signal, an out-of-memory kill
   (`_RESOURCE_FAILURE_RE`, the same mechanical match on fixed runner
   output as §9's intermittent typing) — makes its file failing outright.
   Only the rest goes to the vote: a held case failing with a resource
   signature or with no message to read, a failure whose report names no
   case, a control. A vote rerun that shows a held case failing with no
   resource signature also settles its file as failing.
2. *Discovery.* Every set measured with confirmation whose defect files
   did not end failing — it passed, or the vote typed its failures
   `resource_affected` — has those files rerun up to
   `acceptance_intermittent_repeats` (10, never more than 10) more times,
   serially behind the gate and inside `confirm_budget_sec` counted from
   when the gate returns, each rerun's timeout what is left of it (§9
   *Which failures are new*, step 2), stopping at
   the first rerun that shows a held case failing with no resource
   signature, which makes the file failing. Discovery always leaves a
   record on the set's result when it had files to rerun, found or not,
   with how many rounds ran of how many required and, when it stopped
   short, why (the budget ran out): "held cases rerun ten times clean"
   must never read the same as "held cases never rerun". A set whose
   discovery stopped short is logged `discovery_incomplete` and listed in
   the PR's advisory section. Discovery the operator turned off
   (`acceptance_intermittent_repeats` = 0) is recorded `disabled`, not
   incomplete: nothing stopped short of what was asked, and listing every
   set with held cases under a deliberate setting was noise (review round
   5 L4). A record that requires 0 rounds is never read as stopped short,
   whatever else it says: run state saved before that change carries
   `incomplete` (reason `repeats_disabled`) for the same setting, and a
   resumed run finalizing over it would otherwise still list it.
3. *A held case that failed is never unmeasured.* A set whose held case
   failed at least once, but only with resource signatures (or none
   readable), and that neither rule settled, is not "no evidence": it is
   typed **intermittent** (`intermittent_cases`) and counts as a failing
   set — the repair rounds and the delivery re-drive take it like any
   failing set, the gate's residual names it (`residual.intermittent`),
   and left unresolved it makes the run `unconverged`. A set unmeasured
   with no held-case failure is not a failing set, but it is not a passing
   one either: it makes the run `unconverged` as unmeasured (§6 *The run
   outcome is decided once*), and the gate never logs that the held-out
   sets pass while any set is unmeasured: it logs how many were.

Measured (barnacle 7cc87f9a, early replay, pass 1): the shipped generator
drew its one guaranteed special from an alphabet that included `-` and
`_`, which the report's sites do not count. Two sets' counted case ("every
sample contains a special other than `-`/`_`", 2000 samples) failed per
run with p = 0.546; the vote confirmed it only when all four runs failed,
0.546⁴ = 8.9%. In 45.7% of first passes it was seen failing on an
`AssertionError`, typed `resource_affected`, the set went unmeasured and
the gate logged that the held-out sets pass — about 91% of first passes
shipped the defect with a green verdict, and the chain took three passes.
Rule 1 catches it whenever the first run fails (54.6%); with discovery's
ten reruns a set misses it with probability 0.454¹¹ < 0.02%.

The asymmetry is deliberately confined to held cases. Elsewhere a B\*
verdict has no own-start failure to lean on, and each place keeps its
symmetric rule:

- *The final ID diff (E3) and the delivery ratchet's execution route
  (N5's `_ratchet_exec`).* A candidate there passed on the base: it is an
  expected-to-pass case, and an expected-to-pass case failing now and then
  is exactly what a pre-existing flaky test looks like, which a few base
  reruns bound but cannot exclude. So a non-resource intermittent failure
  stays typed `intermittent_regression` — evidence, not a trigger (§9 *An
  intermittent failure the run introduced is evidence*). What these routes
  must not do is go silent: the ratchet records the execution-shaped items
  it could not check (`exec_unchecked`) when its ID diff measured nothing,
  rather than keeping the round as if they had held.
- *The delivery re-drive (B2's `_redrive_verdict`).* Its set verdicts come
  from the same evaluation, so rules 1–3 reach it unchanged; a set with no
  verdict keeps its earlier one (`_redrive_carry`), never a pass.
- *The falsifier's confirm.* A probe is written against the final tree and
  never failed at an own start; an unconfirmed probe leaves the item at the
  judge's verdict and is recorded in the sample's gates. It stays a vote:
  a probe that fails one run in four may be the probe's own nondeterminism,
  and a confirmed probe drives a re-drive.

A failing
set triggers **at most two repair rounds**: the conformer is
given the task text and its typed required items, with each item's
classifier-typed parts verbatim — neither is held-out data, and a round
shown neither repairs blind: in the replayed barnacle 7cc87f9a pass 1 both
rounds, never told that the task forbade defensive code, guessed that the
hidden tests stub the crypto source and added a fallback for it — and is
told which declared cases failed and the defect contract — cases whose
file was SEEN failing to load against the unfixed tree (declared an
import defect by the writer and confirmed by the runner's report) listed
apart, as a fact about that tree, which a case name alone does not say;
a declaration the base run did not confirm is recorded as an ordinary
failure — never the
runner output or the test source, because a conformer shown the failing
output special-cased it (one shown runner output patched the visible
redirect parameter; failing names plus the contract got 2/4 page fixes
at the root against 1/4). The repair note stays **names-only** even when
richer evidence is at hand: measured as P1, the held-back sets of 9
repairs passed 7 times when the note named the failing cases and only 4
when it also carried the failure evidence — the evidence taught the
repair the shown cases, not the defect. When four or more sets are valid, the two
highest-indexed are never shown at all; every round is re-judged on all
sets, so a fix fitted to the shown names still fails the hidden ones.
When only hidden sets fail, the round is told exactly that — every failing
test is one it is not shown — and works from the contract alone, rather
than being promised a list of failing cases that is empty; when a shown set
fails but names no cases, it is told that instead, never that tests are
hidden; and when named and unnamed failures mix, the names are followed by
a note that other failing tests declared none. The sets are evaluated on a
given commit once per invocation (a resume measures afresh): the no-work
settle, the pre-sweep protection check and the already-fixed check all
read the same HEAD during planning, so the later ones reuse the first
measurement. A
round whose verdict measures nothing where the one before it measured is
measured once more before the rounds stop on it: every evaluation installs
afresh, and a one-off install failure would otherwise end the repair with
a round left. With
fewer valid sets every failing set is shown and nothing is held back — a
weaker check, logged as such, and the repair is not told of hidden tests
that do not exist. A set whose files could not all be run (a
missing runner, a path the target tree already uses) and none of whose
run files was confirmed failing is no evidence either way: it is left out
of the vote rather than counted as passing (a confirmed failing file
still makes it failing), and when
no set can be run the gate records no evidence instead of a pass. Repair rounds run the conformer at **high
effort**, regardless of the operator's `--effort`/`--effort-conformer`
settings — the rounds exist only on failing runs, and effort is the
measured lever: on the multi-mechanism generate report the low-effort
pinned conformer fixed the contract from HEAD 1/2 times, medium 2/3,
high every time it finished (6/6) — effort, not turn budget, was the
lever, and only failing runs pay for it.

**Nothing a held-out evaluation produces reaches a fixer but its verdict
and leerie's own identifiers.** (I3, its relay half: the rule above keeps
a set out of a fixer's tree, this one keeps what the set yields out of a
fixer's input.) What may leave an evaluation of a held-out set for any
worker's input — a prompt, a file a worker reads, a record a judge cites
and a fixer then reads in the judge's evidence — is the set's index, its
verdict (passed, failed, unmeasured), and, for a set a repair round is
shown, the paths and case names its writer declared. Never runner output:
the code under evaluation is a worker's, so whatever the runner prints is
chosen by it, and an assertion diff prints the test's expected values.
Runner output is read in code only, for its resource signature
(`_RESOURCE_FAILURE_RE`, a fixed runner string). Never a held-back set's
paths or names either, except in the delivery re-drive's one held-back
round (*Delivery re-drive* rule 6). The audit for this rule found four
relays, each closed where it relayed:

- *The next run's planner.* The residual handed to the next same-task
  run named the failing cases of every set, held-back ones included. The
  previous run's sets never run again, but the next run's writer writes
  its own from the same report and the same prompt, so those names
  describe its held-back tests, and the planner's words reach its
  implementers — the reason the no-work dispute already took names from
  shown sets only (*No work is declared on executed evidence*). The residual names the shown sets' cases and
  counts the failing held-back sets apart (`held_back_failing_sets`), and
  a residual recorded before this rule is re-derived when it is read.
- *The delivery judge's record.* `_orchestrator_results_digest` named
  every failing set's files and cases. The judge's evidence reaches the
  final conformer, the re-drive's implementers and the next run's
  planner, so a held-back set's line gives its verdict only. A shown
  set's line names its failing cases, never every case its writer
  declared in a failing file: a declared case that passed, listed under
  "failed", is false evidence (*Delivery re-drive* rule 1).
- *The logs the record reads.* The record took every `logs/*.log` for a
  worker's transcript: the acceptance writer's included, whose runs of
  its own tests carry their output, and leerie's runs of set files, whose
  output the evaluated code writes — a printed line shaped like a tool
  call is read as one. Every log of the held-out side is now written under
  `logs/held-out/` (`HELD_OUT_LOGS_DIRNAME`): leerie's runs of set files
  and of falsifier probes, and, in its `transcripts/`, the transcripts of
  the workers that read a set or run one (`HELD_OUT_LOG_WORKERS`: the
  acceptance writer, the set auditor, the scope judge and the falsifier,
  which stays on this side although its leads are now the shown sets
  only: its transcripts of older runs read every valid set, and its runs
  of the final commit's harness keep their cache apart all the same). Nothing that builds a worker's input
  reads that directory.
- *The falsifier's evidence.* A confirmed sample put its probe's case
  title and its own prose into `unmet_final`, which the re-drive's
  implementers read; both came from a worker that read the held-back
  sets. The evidence became the span of the item the probe tests, which
  code checks is verbatim in the item, and the fact that it fails under
  B\*. The relay is now closed at its source instead: the falsifier's
  leads are the shown sets only (§6 *A falsifier reads only what a fixer
  may read*), so its probe, case title and prose carry nothing held back,
  and the re-drive hands them on through the note and the self-check.
  `unmet_final`'s evidence stays the span (a probe of a sample that read
  every valid set, recorded before this rule, is still never shown), and
  what a note adds is read from the sample record only when its
  `lead_sets` names shown sets alone.
- *The caches* (review round 21 R2). Every worker's processes wrote one
  cache set per run, `<run-dir>/worktrees/.stores/cache/` (`XDG_CACHE_HOME`,
  `GOCACHE`, `CARGO_HOME`, …), the held-out side's included, so whatever
  a held-out-side worker's processes left there a later fixer read: `go
  test` alone keeps a run's compiled test package, string constants
  included, in `GOCACHE`, and the falsifier runs the final commit's own
  harness — a fixer's code — with the probe on disk. The rule is over
  every store a held-out-side worker can write, not only what it returns:
  that side (`HELD_OUT_LOG_WORKERS`) has a cache set of its own,
  `<run-dir>/worktrees/.stores/cache-held-out/`, granted to it in place of the
  fixers' and named by no fixer's grant (`_worker_cache_dir`; the
  environment follows the grant, `_granted_cache_dir`). Its cost is one
  cold set per run for that side.

Workers on the held-out side — the writer, the set auditor, the scope
judge, the surrogate fixer's witness run — read set source or runner
output by design; what they return feeds only the held-out side (a
rewrite of the set, which cases count) or a typed verdict code reads.

**Non-blocking, with a mechanical safety net.** Held-out tests can be
wrong: on a report that states no expected behaviour (a diagnostic
report) or needs a heavily mocked harness, all three sets failed a task
the operator had confirmed finished. So a residual after two rounds
never blocks the PR; it is recorded and handed to the next same-task
run's planner (`prior_delivery_residual`), where a full plan-and-
implement cycle settled the generate residual 2/3 times. And a repair
round must not trade the report for a regression: if the repo's test
axis goes from passing to failing across the repair rounds, and the
failure is confirmed, their commits are reset away and the residual is
recorded instead. Confirmed means what it means everywhere else (§9
*Which failures are new*): the IDs failing on the repaired tree are
confirmed under B\* against the pre-repair tree, which passed, and only a
confirmed new failure resets; when the red run produced no per-test report
at all (the suite could not run — a broken import or build), the axis is
run once more, unmemoised, and a second red resets; a confirmation that
itself fails falls back to the red run. Unconfirmed, one red
run of one flaky test reset every round's work, the fixes included. The
per-round ratchet does not make this rule redundant: it is the same B\*
check per round, but it is blind exactly where the suite stops reporting
(no IDs on one side is no verdict), and a ratchet that raises keeps its
round; this rule, over the whole repair, is the net under both. The
commits are likewise reset if the repair turned measurable held-out sets unmeasurable (a broken
dependency manifest, which the staging test axis, installed long before,
would not notice) — but only after the repaired tree is measured once
more and the pre-repair tree measures where it does not, since every
evaluation installs afresh and a one-off failure looks the same. The
reset is confirmed, never assumed: a failed one is recorded as such, the
record then describes the repair's tree, which is what ships, and the
next run's planner is told the repair it should not have inherited is
still on the branch. With no readable HEAD to reset to, no repair starts. The
pre-repair verdict and HEAD are persisted before the first round and
every round after it runs, each verdict pinned to the commit it was
measured on (a round whose worker failed is measured again whenever HEAD
is not that commit — whether its worker committed before failing or an
interrupted earlier attempt at the round did, before a resume; when the shipped tree cannot be measured at all — usually an
environment failure, since a repair that made the sets unmeasurable is
rolled back below, unless that rollback itself fails — the last measured
failing verdict is the residual, marked as such), and the rollback decision
before the reset
it orders, so a resumed gate always reaches this check and never records
the repaired tree's verdict for the reset one: re-measured on resume,
the verdict would read the already-repaired tree and skip it. Measured
on the finished task with wrong held-out tests: the repair conformer
changed code in 3/3 trials, but 0 of the task's 247 regression tests
and 0 attributable scraper tests (of 1,605) regressed.

**A repair round that fixes nothing, or makes the verdict worse, is rolled
back.** Each round is also
judged on its own, against the verdict before it: a round that committed
and fixed **none** of the failing held-out cases — counted per case where
the runner's report names them, over the sets measured on both sides,
variant sets included since the rounds repair them too — is reset to that
round's own start (recorded before its worker runs), whatever the test
axis says. So is a round that made any held-out case that passed before it
fail — in a set that was already failing or in one that passed — by the
same per-case count as the delivery re-drive's rule 4 (*Delivery
re-drive*). Without it a round that fixed one case of a failing set and
broke a passing set kept its commits: the held-out verdict got strictly
worse and the round stood. A blind change that measurably fixes nothing is speculative by
construction. In the replayed barnacle 7cc87f9a pass 1 both repair rounds
left every failing set failing, and each added code the task forbade (the
second a defensive `Math.random` fallback); both shipped, because the only
rollback rules were a test axis turning red (the axis was not even
measured) and sets turning unmeasurable. The decision is on disk before
the reset, so a resume finishes it; a rolled-back round's verdict never
describes the tree again, and the next round starts from the tree before
it. A failed reset is recorded and stops the rounds, like the gate's own.
The price: when every set still failing is one no correct fix can pass (a
set the audit below would type broken), a correct repair fixes no case and
is reset too. With several valid sets a correct fix shows up as progress on
the sound ones; the set audit and rewrite after the rounds then deal with
the broken one, and its residual reaches the next run.

**A final-conformer round that turns a passing held-out case failing is
rolled back.** *Built 2026-11-11 (lane FC, barnacle 39c4c5ad).*
**Invariant:** no final-conformer round ships a held-out case that passes
on the round's start and fails, confirmed, on its commit. The final
conformer commits to staging before the gate's first measurement, so the
rule above, which compares each repair round with the verdict before it,
had no verdict before the conformer: its `initial` was measured on the
conformer's commit, and a case the conformer broke was read as a case the
run never fixed. In barnacle 39c4c5ad (leerie 0.60.0) the conformer's
round 0 (`9712d56`, "keep replay success as transport verdict") turned
held-out sets 2–5 from passing on its start (`7be9b18`) to failing; the
gate recorded "5 of 5 measured held-out set(s) fail on the integrated
tree" and spent its repair rounds getting back what the conformer had
taken (repair round 1 restored sets 2–5).

The rule is the repair round's, with the conformer's rounds as the rounds:
the same worker writing to the same tree, read by the same measurement.
`_run_final_conformance` records each round's start and the pass's end
(`_final.round_starts`, `_final.end_sha`). When the gate's `initial` is of
that end, still staging's HEAD, and fails a case, the sets are evaluated on
