the pass's start; a case failing on the end that passed there
(`_acceptance_broken_cases`, the repair round's count) makes the pass a
suspect. Its rounds that committed are then tried in order, each round's
commit evaluated against its start, and the first one that broke a case is
the culprit (`_conformer_flip_culprit`); with no step showing it (a set
unmeasured on an intermediate commit), the pass's first committing round
is. Staging goes back to the culprit's start through the one restore,
which also takes every round after it, built on its commit — #365's
"earliest culprit" shape. The decision (`acceptance.gate.conformer_flip`)
is on disk before the reset, so a resume finishes it; the culprit's start
verdict becomes the gate's `initial`, and the repair rounds then start from
the tree the conformer started from. A failing case is already confirmed
under B\* by the evaluation itself (every rerun failed); passing on the
start is a pass, as in the repair round's rule.

It is a rollback, not a note handed back, because nothing after the
conformer could take a note: its loop has ended, and the next fixer is the
gate's own repair, which is shown only the shown sets' failing names, never
what broke them (I3). Rolled back, the cases pass again on the tree the
repair starts from, and only what still fails is repaired. What it costs:
the culprit's other work in that round and the rounds after it — fixes to
merge checks, or to the unmet items and solution defects it was handed.
Those come back to the run through the routes that already own them: the
delivery re-drive drives the conformer's `residual_defects` and every unmet
item detection confirms on the tree that ships. A pass whose failing cases
also fail on its start pays one more evaluation, on the start; a culprit
search pays one per committing round after the first; a pass whose sets
all pass at its end pays nothing.

Held-out repair rounds that regress a met item are a different rule (the
next one): the probe that shows it does not exist when the round runs —
detection writes it afterwards — so the flip is found by trying a later
probe against an earlier round, a measurement of another kind at another
time. Here both sides of the trade are held-out cases, already ranked by
the repair round's rule (a round that fixed one case by breaking another
is not progress).

**A held-out repair round that turns a confirmed probe from passing to
failing is rolled back.** *Built 2026-11-11 (lane HR, barnacle 2dcb4cce,
issue 42).* **Invariant:** no kept acceptance repair round ships the
failure of a required item's confirmed probe that passes on the round's
start and fails on its commit under B\*.

**Root cause.** The delivery ratchet below reads the met items again after
each repair round, by its judge, below detection's bar, and said no more
was needed "because final detection runs after it". Detection does run
after it, but its confirms were routed to the re-drive as unmet items and
never tried against the round that wrote them. In barnacle 2dcb4cce
(leerie 0.49.0) repair round 1 (`3dffb039` → `fa80ed17`) fixed the held-out
frame-locator case and, in the same commit, made a bare
`[role='combobox'][aria-expanded]` a prompt trigger. The ratchet's judge
kept item 8 (layered dropdown widgets) met: "the layered collapse logic is
untouched". Final detection's falsifier then confirmed item 8 unmet with a
layered widget of the item's own shape, whose anchor carries the
`aria-expanded` the round's selector matches. The run ended `unconverged`
with the regression it wrote on its branch.

**What a repair round can turn from passing to failing, and what catches
it.**
- A held-out case: the round's own rule above (`broken_cases`), measured
  against the verdict before it.
- A repository merge check: *A kept repair keeps the repository's merge
  checks green*, in the ratchet.
- An existing test: the ratchet's execution route (the failing-test-ID diff
  under B\*).
- A required item: the ratchet's judge on the round's commit; and, for an
  item detection then confirms with a probe, this rule.

**The rule.** After final detection, each item its verdict of staging's
HEAD holds unmet with a confirmed, saved falsifier sample is tried against
every kept repair round in the order they landed, by #365's measurement
and culprit search: the saved probe in a held-out sandbox over a pristine
installed checkout of the round's commit and of its start, through the
channel that confirmed it; a start where the case did not run and pass is
not a pass; a case failing on the commit and passing on the start goes to
B\*, the start as the base side. The first round B\* calls it new for is
the item's culprit. The decision is on disk before the reset
(`acceptance.gate.item_flips`), so a resume finishes it. Staging goes back
to the earliest culprit's start through the one restore, which also takes
every kept round after it, built on its commit. Each round goes out with
a reason naming the item and the probe's case. Each flipped item becomes
the ratchet's `met-item-<i>` `control_regression` note, pending for the
delivery re-drive. Then everything measured on the tree that no longer
ships is measured again on the restored commit: the held-out sets (the
gate's `final` and residual), the shipping diff and detection. The check
repeats over the rounds left; each pass takes at least one, so it ends.
A probe that fails on the round's start too (one that over-reads its item)
flips nothing: it stays detection's verdict, as in #365.

**Why a rollback, though the round also fixed held-out cases.** The trade
was already decided: the ratchet rolls back a repair round that fixes a
failing case and undoes a met item (*A repair that regresses met work is
rolled back*). Only the measurement was missing, because the judge reads
the round's own claim. The cases the round fixed are not lost to the run.
They fail again on the restored tree, and the delivery re-drive drives
failing held-out sets, so they go to the next fixer with the item's note.
A group must then fix the case and keep the item: a group that breaks a
passing case is rolled back (*Delivery re-drive* rule 4), and one that
flips the item again is rolled back by #365. That is #365's shape:
rollback, and a note for the next fixer. #369 has no note, because no fixer
runs after the final conformer that could take one. If the re-drive
cannot keep both, the run ships the case failing, which the run never
fixed before the round, and no regression it wrote.

Measured: lane HR's replay of every confirmed, saved falsifier probe
recorded in a run with a kept repair round under `~/.leerie/*/runs`, as
lane FL's replay ran them: 13 probes in 6 runs, each run as 3
interleaved pairs on the kept round's start and commit, in a clone of the
run's repository copy, confined, the case read from the runner's report.
One flips: 2dcb4cce item 8 across round 1 (3/3 pass on `3dffb039`, 3/3 fail
on `fa80ed17`), the only rollback. 10 fail on both sides, among them the
two probes the audits call false (22a30525 and 87580f62 item 8), 2dcb4cce
items 0 and 13 and a2a825c2's four, and 2 pass on both. Most probes were
recorded after later re-drive groups, a stricter test than detection's
own probes on the round's commit: none of them fires.

**What it costs.** The culprit's other work, and every round after it:
2dcb4cce's round 1 also fixed the frame-locator case, which then fails again
and is driven by the re-drive. A run with no kept repair round, or no
confirmed probe, pays nothing. Otherwise it pays one probe run on each side
of each kept round per confirmed item, plus B\* when one side passes, once
per detected commit. A flip pays one evaluation of the sets and one
detection on the restored commit.

**A repair that regresses met work is rolled back (the delivery ratchet).**
A repair writer runs after the judges that verified the run's required
items. A round that fixes a failing case can still undo an item that was
met before it: drop a guard, hedge a path the task said to fix at the root,
delete a test. Nothing judged that tree again. In the replayed barnacle
7cc87f9a pass 1 the only delivery judge ran before either repair round, and
a re-drive group's commits were re-judged only for the items it was sent to
fix. So after **every** acceptance-repair round and every delivery
re-drive group that commits and survives its own rules, the items the latest
delivery verdict holds met are verified again, on the tree after it, by
route:

- An item that only says paths stay untouched is settled in code, as
  everywhere else.
- An item the coverage classifier typed `execution` / `check:
  test_id_diff` is `execution` here without asking; a judge part typed
  `test_outcome` is dropped from the ratchet judge's verdict, as at final.
- A verifiability classifier types every other item, once per run, by its
  own text: `in_tree` (a reader of the repository can cite whether it holds)
  or `execution` (only running something shows it: "no regressions", "the
  suite passes"). An `execution` item is never judged by reading. It is
  flagged when the repair's failing-test-ID diff confirms a new failure
  under B\* (§9 *Which failures are new*). The test axis therefore always
  runs after a repair: its start is measured before the worker, its tree
  after it. A command the task forbids is replaced by the scoped run of the
  coupled tests, as at final. The tests that import a file the repair
  changed are rerun first, as at final, so an intermittent regression the
  repair introduced is found and typed. Like the final one, it is evidence,
  not a trigger: it goes to the ratchet's judge and to the PR.
- An `in_tree` item goes to the delivery judge. Its input is the item, the
  evidence it was verified on and the repair's diff. Each verdict also types
  `evidence_files`, the files it relies on. One sample runs. Two more run
  only when it marks an item unmet, or when an item's evidence files meet
  the files the diff changed. An item in that set is confirmed regressed on
  2 of 3 unmet votes.

A confirmed regressed item, or a test confirmed newly failing, resets the
repair to its own start, using the sha recorded for that round or group.
In a re-drive, the regressed item then goes to the next groups as a
`control_regression` note. A kept repair's verdicts become the prior
evidence of the next one. The ratchet's read is below detection's bar, since
its judge carries no citation and no falsifier runs. So the items it keeps
met after a re-drive group are read again on the tree that ships, by the
judge and the falsifier (*Every item the tree that ships reports met passed
detection's bar on it*), and a confirm there whose probe passed on a kept
group's start and fails on its commit rolls that group back (*A kept group
that turns a met item's confirmed probe from passing to failing is rolled
back*). An acceptance repair round needs no such read of its own:
final detection runs after it, on the tree it leaves, and a confirm there
whose probe passed on a kept round's start and fails on its commit rolls
that round back (*A held-out repair round that turns a confirmed probe from
passing to failing is rolled back*).

Measured (bench Q4 N5, frozen design): 49 natural repair rounds and
cross-run pairs, 517 met items re-verified. 2 runs false-alarmed (4.1%,
Wilson 95% 1.1–13.7%), on 2 of the 517 items. One was a defect already
present before the change; the other was an execution-shaped item typed
`in_tree`. The judge confirmed 2 real regressions and the execution route
2 more. On 17 freshly generated repair rounds, scored against a
ground truth by execution, the ratchet caught all 3 rounds that regressed
an item and raised nothing on the other 14. The judge confirmed 5 of their
7 regressed items. The execution route caught the third round, whose 2 items
only a test showed.

**A kept repair keeps the repository's merge checks green.** *Built
2026-11-10 (lane CK, barnacle 87580f62).* **Invariant:** a kept repair
round never makes a gating merge check red that was green before it. The
merge checks (§9 *The repository's own merge checks run too*) gate every
round the ratchet gates, as the tests do: measured on the round's commit,
confirmed under B\* against the round's start, and rolled back with the
round.

**Root cause.** The rollback rules read new test failures, base-form
changes and met items that regressed, never a merge check. Inside the
re-drive the checks re-ran only after a round that was routed a red
check's note. In barnacle 87580f62 (leerie 0.55.2) all four gates (build,
typecheck, prepush-typecheck, smoke-load-dist) were green at the base and
on the tree the re-drive started from (04:35). Re-drive round 1's
commit `5c0f667` introduced `TS2345` at `recon-http.ts:536`: its fixer
self-checked with the test runner only. No rule measured the checks, so
the round was kept. Round 2 was built on it. The checks were next run after
the loop (05:47), red 3 of 3 against the base's 0 of 3, and the run
shipped red and ended `unconverged`.

**The rule.** After every acceptance-repair round and every re-drive group
that commits and survives its own rules, the ratchet runs every gating
check and ratchet on the round's commit, in a fresh worktree of it
(`_ci_round_regressions`). It runs them in their recorded order, in one
tree, as the final pass does: a check may read what an earlier one built.
B\*'s reruns keep that order (§9 *A merge check's rerun sees what its
measurement saw*).
A gate red there is confirmed by the final pass's B\* (interleaved reruns,
same budget), against the round's start instead of the run's base. Only
a gate that fails every rerun on the commit and passes every rerun on the
start is the round's. A gate red on the start too is `pre_existing` and
not the round's, so a round sent for something else is not rolled back for
a check that was already red. A strict lint that ratchets per diagnostic
is the round's when a diagnostic's count rose from the start in a file the
round changed. A coverage threshold is the round's when it fires on the
commit and did not fire on the start. Either way the start's values come
from its kept measurement, or are measured when none is kept. A check
the round broke resets the round to its own start through the one
restore, with a reason naming each check and its first error line.
In a re-drive the group's later groups get a typed `control_regression`
note: the check, its command, and the first error lines of its red run.
That is the kind for behaviour an earlier attempt broke and was reverted,
so the note says to keep the check passing. A round its tests already
reject runs no check, and a round rolled back for a check runs no item
judge, since the tree will not stand. A measurement that raises, or a
worktree that cannot be made, decides nothing and the round is kept, as an
unsettled test candidate is kept (§9 *Which failures are new*, step 4).
The tree that ships is still measured before the outcome.

The rule sits in the ratchet, so the two callers that keep rounds share
it: the acceptance gate's repair rounds and the re-drive's groups. The
acceptance rounds had the same gap. 87580f62's kept acceptance round 2
happened to leave the checks green, and nothing measured them until the
final pass at 04:35. The
other places a commit lands are not kept rounds. Per-subtask integration
and the final conformer have no rollback rule that reads tests either, and
the final pass measures the tree they leave. A check they broke is red
there and goes to the re-drive as a `ci_check` note (§9). That is
measured once and routed, as before.

**Cost, and what makes it cheaper.** Each commit's raw measurement is kept
(`ci_parity.measured`, the last four commits). The next round's start and
the final pass read it. When the final pass's commit was measured by the
last kept round with every gate green, nothing runs again: green is green
against any reference. Only a red gate needs the base reruns. Measured
over the 22 recorded runs with gating checks (barnacle, navegando, web;
`~/.cache/leerie-lanes/CK/cost/`), there were 24 kept rounds and 23 green
final-pass measurements. Their median wall was 217 s (39 s to 722 s,
install included). At each run's own median, measuring every kept round
would cost 8,190 s across the 22 runs. With the final pass reading the
last kept round's measurement, 1,680 s are added, in 3 runs: 87580f62
41 s, navegando a70fb4a6 1,292 s, web 6f147a0c 348 s. The rest pay nothing
extra. B\* runs only on a red gate, which is when the round is rolled
back.

Running only the checks a round's diff can reach was not adopted, because
it cannot be decided soundly. A typecheck's or a build's reach is the
whole program. Barnacle's `smoke-load-dist` loads the `dist/` that its
`build` writes, so it has no files of its own. A check names no inputs,
and its reach would be guessed.

**A set that keeps failing is audited, and rewritten once.** A held-out
set can be wrong in ways validity at the own start cannot see: it fails
there for the reported reason, and then fails every correct fix too,
because it was built on how the code happens to work rather than on what
the report asks for. Measured on Q6's 58 own-start-valid sets: 33 still
failed on a tree where the run's original sets passed, and a blind
second labeller (hand-checked where it disagreed) found 19 of those 33
were sets no correct fix could pass. Leaving such a set as a residual sends
the next run after a contract the set itself got wrong. So after the
repair rounds, each measured set that still fails goes through three
triggers, in order, and **any trigger leads to exactly one rewrite at the
run's own start** (`acceptance_rewrite_rounds`, a per-set counter); no
trigger ever drops a case, a set or a residual on its own:

- **Mechanical checks M1 and M2**, on code identifiers only (Q6/R5): M1,
  a set file reads a recorded mock call by position (`.mock.calls[0]`,
  `toHaveBeenNthCalledWith`), so it depends on which calls the test's own
  setup or the implementation makes; M2, a set file imports a named symbol
  from a production module that no other production module uses at the
  own start, an internal helper whose place a fix may change. Measured on
  the 58 fresh sets before the rule was frozen, M1 flagged a set later
  labelled broken 3 times of 9 and M2 8 of 16 — too imprecise to type a
  set broken, enough to buy one rewrite, whose harm was then measured:
  on the 6 fairly-failing sets M1/M2 trigger, every rewrite was valid at
  the own start and still failed the run's tree (Q6/R6, first sample) —
  the real gap stayed caught.
- **The c+ set audit**: a judgment worker, `set_auditor`, reads the set
  staged in a fresh worktree of the integrated tree, the report, the
  audited contract and every failing case with its runner failure message,
  and types each failing case `implementation_gap` (the default) or
  `set_defect` with a `defect_kind` (`harness_unreachable`, `coupling`,
  `contradicts_task`, `overspecified_mechanism`, `environment`,
  `test_bug`). Its payload carries a REPOSITORY TEST HARNESS section built
  by code from the import graph and `git log`: the newest existing tests
  that drive the production modules the set imports, the test-helper
  modules they import with their exported names, and the five newest as
  exemplars. Its rule for them: a set fake that does not answer a request
  production makes on this tree — so production takes an error or
  fallback path before reaching the reported behaviour — is `coupling`.
  Every typed `set_defect` must quote the set file (`test_quote`) and, by
  kind, the production line, the task or the failure message; code checks
  each quote is a verbatim substring of the file it names, and a case
  whose quotes do not check counts as `implementation_gap`. The audit is
  run `set_audit_samples` (3) times independently and the union of the
  counted cases is the verdict — one sample is unstable (Q6 R2: one set
  typed 9/9 cases broken in one run and 0/9 on the re-run). On the 33
  labelled sets (Q6 R3, the first three runs per set) one sample flagged
  13, all correctly, but found only 13 of the 19 broken sets; the union of
  three flagged 18, 16 of them correctly (recall 16/19). The writers
  almost never use the repository's own test helpers (S1: 4 of 44 writes
  imported one); the harness section is how the audit sees what they
  should have used.

  *Identical assertions get one verdict.* Every still-failing set is
  audited before any audit is acted on. Code then reconciles the verdicts
  across sets. It matches failing cases mechanically by their **assertion
  key**: the normalised `expect(...)` / `assert` statements of the case's
  own test block in the set file (located by its title or function name),
  plus its **target**, the repository modules that set file imports. When
  one key is typed `set_defect` in one place and `implementation_gap` in
  another, the verdict that keeps the case wins (`implementation_gap`).
  The `set_defect` finding is withdrawn from its set, so it no longer
  triggers a rewrite or marks the set broken, and the conflict is recorded.
  A set rewritten later is re-audited against the other sets' recorded
  verdicts in the same way. Measured (barnacle 7cc87f9a, pass 1): two sets
  held the identical assertion `expect(samples().filter((p) =>
  /[\s$]/.test(p))).toEqual([])` against `src/lib/random.ts`. Set 1's audit
  typed it `contradicts_task` in 3 of 3 samples and the rewrite removed
  it, while set 5's audit typed it `implementation_gap` in 3 of 3. The
  rewrite removed the only signal the repair loop could see (set 5 was
  held back), and the run ended `unconverged` on set 5. Case titles differ
  between sets ("dollar signs" vs "template interpolation characters"),
  so the titles are not the key; the assertion and its target are.
- **The surrogate witness**, only when neither of the above fired: one
  independent `surrogate_fixer` per gate fixes the report in a ref-less
  clone of the own start (the writer's checkout) without ever seeing a set
  — its `Read` denies cover them as they cover the fixers — and each
  remaining failing set is run on its tree, confirmed under B*. A set that
  still fails on an independent fix is a trigger and nothing more: the
  surrogate is one fix, not the contract, so a failure there never drops a
  case, never types a set broken and never stops the residual. The set is
  then audited on the surrogate's tree, and its typed cases (if any) go
  into the note. Q6/R7 ran the witness on 11 failing sets: all 6
  broken ones failed on the independent fix (both held-out sets the other
  triggers missed among them), and so did 4 of the 5 sets that were
  failing fairly — which is why a surrogate failure buys a rewrite, whose
  no-harm R6 measured, and nothing else.

The rewrite is the `acceptance_writer` again, at the own start, in the
same ref-less clone, with its original payload, its set's files put back
where it wrote them, and a typed note: every trigger that fired with its
evidence (the counted cases and their quotes, the M1 lines, the M2 symbol
and module, the cases failing on the independent fix), and the closing
instruction benched for each kind — check the report's contract through
the public entry point, model the world the code talks to rather than the
implementation's private protocol, keep cases the note does not name. It
is validated exactly like a first write. Two guards keep a bad rewrite
from costing the set: **a rewrite that declares no defect file is asked
once more with the identical prompt** (Q6/R8: of the 5 surrogate-triggered
rewrites, 2 came back with no defect file; one retry recovered one of
them), **and the original set is kept whenever the rewrite is not valid**
(no defect file after the retry, none failing at the own start, a failing
control, an edited tracked file). A replaced set is judged again on the
same integrated tree, under B*. A set still failing after its rewrite is
audited once more; **a set the audit still types broken after its rewrite
is marked `broken: true`** — so is a set the audit typed broken whose
rewrite was not kept. A broken set is not chased again: no further
rewrite, it does not count as unfinished work in the run outcome (§6 *The
run outcome is decided once*), and it is kept out of the next run's
residual (below). Only the audit types a set broken; M1/M2 and the
surrogate are triggers only.

**The writer gets one more try when nothing fails at the own start.**
When every declared defect file ran and passed on the own start — the set
cannot discriminate as written — the writer is asked once more in the
same checkout, its files still there, with the runner's per-case result
for its defect files: rewrite them to fail for the reported reason if the
defect still reproduces here, or say in `notes` that it does not and
return the files unchanged (C1's writer, Fix A.3). Still nothing failing
discards the set, as before; a done task still yields no sets. The note
carries only what the runner reported of the writer's own tests.

**Prisma repositories get a real database.** On a repository whose
schema lives in Prisma (a tracked `schema.prisma` whose nearest
`package.json` declares `prisma` or `@prisma/client`, with a PostgreSQL
datasource — read mechanically), a writer working from fakes hand-rolls
the persistence layer, and a hand-rolled fake that does not answer a query
a correct fix makes fails that fix (the `coupling` kind above; 10 of Q6's
broken sets were on such a repository). So the writer, the rewrite and
every set run use the repository's real Prisma client against a throwaway
database. Each command that needs one — a set run, the writer's session
in its checkout, an evaluation, the audit, the surrogate's clone, a
delivery-detection falsifier's (§8 *Delivery detection*), a CI-parity
check that `require`s a database (§9 *The repository's own merge checks
run too*) — gets a private PostgreSQL cluster of its own, from the server
binaries leerie's base image ships (§6½ *A database server in the base
image*), started inside that command's own confinement and isolation and
gone with it, listening only on a socket in that command's own `/tmp`,
with a database named `leerie_<hash>_test` and the tree's schema pushed by
`prisma db push` inside the same confinement: the push loads the tree's
`prisma.config.ts`, which a worker wrote, and the cluster the orchestrator
used to start unconfined ran any query's `COPY … TO PROGRAM` outside every
grant (§6 *No database server leerie starts is ever unconfined*). A falsifier and a CI check are the same case as a set run: a
probe or a database-backed check that runs against no database fails for
the missing database, not the defect, so without one the falsifier could
not demonstrate a persistence-layer item and every database-backed CI
check went red at the baseline and dropped out of the gate. A falsifier
lane is reset between samples, and its database is a new one per
command, so one sample's rows never reach the next; the confirm checkout
the probe is re-run in has its own. A CI check's prerequisites that would
themselves push to or reset a database (matched by the same rule list the
worker deny reads) are not run: the push `scripts/sandbox-db.sh` makes
inside the command's own confinement is the only push. The set runs still
go through the repository's own test command; a test-database wrapper
script there (one that starts its own cluster when DATABASE_URL is unset)
defers to the database it is handed. **Before every command that pushes,
code checks the target the wrapper will push to**: a postgres URL whose host is the command's own socket directory
in its `/tmp`, a database name starting `leerie_` and ending `_test`, and
DIRECT_URL equal to DATABASE_URL (Prisma configs commonly push to
`DIRECT_URL ?? DATABASE_URL`); anything else is refused. Prisma's AI-agent
consent variable is set on that push subprocess alone — never in a
worker's environment, which is scrubbed of it — and the user's consent
covers exactly this: pushes to throwaway test databases. The writer's
payload gets a REAL DATABASE section (the client module, the five newest
database-backed tests that import it unmocked, the helpers they import:
all from the import graph), and a set file that mocks the client module
earns one fix-up call (Q6/R4). **The section is a promise, so it follows a
database that is there, never the repository's shape.** Before composing
it, code runs the wrapper once in the writer's checkout, confined as a
measurement, over a check that the command was handed the URL the wrapper
composes (`_test_db_present`): the section is added only when that check
passes. The writer's own session then requires its database the same way
— the check runs between the wrapper and the worker, and the worker
never starts without it — so the prompt never names a database its
session lacks. It used to be added for any Prisma/PostgreSQL repository
whose URL leerie accepts, while the wrapper falls back to running the
command without a database whenever a step fails: the writer was told to
build unmocked tests on a database that did not exist, they failed on the
base for want of one, and read as discriminating defect files (review
round 21, execution L2, measured with `DATABASE_URL` empty). Every worker in such a repository carries
Bash deny rules for the commands that push to or reset a database
(`prisma db push`, `prisma migrate reset`, `prisma migrate dev`, the
package scripts that run them, and setting the consent variable), paired
with an orchestrator notice, as the whole-suite deny is (#292: deny alone
ended 2/2 replayed workers `blocked`). Without server binaries, as root,
or when a step fails, the sets run as before, without a database, logged
once. Q6/R4 measured 0 database-path errors across the 22 database
rewrites and their evaluations.

**A set typed broken is not handed on.** The residual records which sets
still failed, by index. A set the set audit types `broken` after its rewrite
(its `broken` field — a test no correct fix could pass) is left out of the next run's `prior_delivery_residual`: the next
planner is not sent after a contract the set itself got wrong. The filter
is applied when the residual is read, so a set typed after its run
finished is excluded all the same.

**A task that points at a report is bounded by the report's own
scenarios.** A writer told to break the fix writes variants — a later
retry, the last step instead of a middle one, a delay outside the range
the report states — and every variant left failing used to be unfinished
work, so a chain re-ran until the variants ran out. The user's rule (option
a): a report-pointer task — one naming a report file the repository does
not track (`_d1_report_sources`) — is finished once the report's own
scenarios pass. An independent `scope_judge` reads, per defect file with a
case failing at the own start, the task, the report, the test source and
each case's own-start outcome, and reports typed facts only: the numeric
ranges the report states (`{param, min, max, unit, span_quote}`) and, per
case, its `origin` (`report_example`, `report_regression_test`,
`report_symptom` or `other_scenario`), the values it sets for those ranges
and the report passage it comes from. Code decides: a case **counts** when
it failed at the own start, its origin is not `other_scenario`, every value
it sets lies inside its range (milliseconds and seconds compared in one
unit; overlapping verified ranges for one unit merge), and its
`span_quote` — like every range's — is a substring of the task or report
after NFC and whitespace normalisation. A failing case the judge leaves out
of its answer counts: an omission is the judge's, never evidence of a
variant. It used to be dropped silently: in a2a825c2 (0.45.0) two of the
judge's answers typed 5 of 10 and 1 of 10 cases, and the 14 failing cases
they left out never counted. A set with no counted case is a
**variant set**: it is still repaired in the same pass, but it never
creates a run — the no-work settle, the already-fixed check, the
satisfied-probe protection, the delivery re-drive and the run outcome read
only failing cases that are counted ones, and the next run's residual
leaves variant sets out like broken ones. The decision is **per case, not
per file**: the evaluation asks the runner for the same structured report
validation reads and records which cases of each failing file failed, so a
variant case left failing in a file whose counted case now passes is not
work. Decided per file, it was: in a replayed run (barnacle 7cc87f9a, pass
1) the scope judge typed the one case still failing `other_scenario`, but
its file also held a counted case — passing by then — and the run ended
`unconverged` on a variant. A file whose run produced no readable report
still counts as a whole. A judge that fails leaves the set unbounded (every
failing file counts, as before). A set whose defect cases all pass at the
own start even after the writer's one retry is recorded with the reason
`fixed_on_head_by_execution` — assigned by code from the runner's
per-case report, never by a worker. Benched as P2 (v3b, frozen; 15 sets
from the C1/D1 corpora, three samples each, every failing case hand-labelled
under option a): 242 of 246 in-scope failing cases counted and 102 of 102
out-of-scope ones dropped; per set-sample, 15 of 15 with an in-scope case
kept and 30 of 30 without one dropped; and the late runs of the two replayed
chains (12 and 4) all converged, in every sample.

**Done is a fixed bar per task, not re-sampled each run.** Own-start
writing (above) re-decides "done" on every run from a fresh, stochastic
sample of tests, and nothing tied that sample to what an earlier run of the
same task had already accepted. So finished tasks kept reopening. On one
report's lineage (barnacle, REST GET), 43bd4671 and 396c84e3 each overturned a
confirmed no-work on counted failures with none genuine (8 of 8 and 9 of 9
over-reach or test error), and 43bd4671's change introduced a real regression
that the next run, 673a0cc6, spent itself fixing.

The invariant: **a task that ended `done` stays done as long as the tests that
passed when it finished still pass. A later run's new failures
are reported as advisory and create no work; a failure of those recorded tests
reopens the task. No LLM takes part in this decision.** It is deliberately not
a judgement of which fresh failures are real. Three benched attempts to have a
worker make that judgement failed: the `set_auditor` dropped 2 of 17 bad cases,
and `scope_judge` v4 and a structural version of it each lost genuine recall on
held-out cases. So the judgement is removed, and what it costs is stated below.

*The bar.* When a run ends `done`, its counted cases that pass
on the tree it ships, with the control files of their sets, are recorded as the
task's **settled bar**: copies of the passed test files and the IDs of the
cases, under the state root (`settled-bars/`), never inside one run's
directory. So is the run's **change** (below): its diff from its own start to
the tree it ships, and the test files that diff added or changed, in the form
it shipped them.

The key is the stripped task text and the path and content hash of each report
the task points at, as the run read them at its start. A task that points at no
report is keyed by its text alone: it asks exactly what it says. "The task" for this rule
means what was asked, and a task that points at a report asks what the report
says, so a new finding in the same report is a new question, not a fresh failure
to withhold. So a run whose task text or report changed has no bar and is
swallowed by none: rewording the task or editing the report starts a new bar. The
trade-off is that even a trivial report edit, a typo fixed, resets it: the next
run behaves as a task with no bar, and fresh sets may reopen it until a `done`
run records a new one. Content cannot be told trivial from substantive without a
judgement, and a false reset costs a run where a false match would hide a finding.
A report that cannot be read leaves nothing to key on, so no bar applies, and
that is logged. The key is the bar's alone: the same-task lookups for the prior
residual and the dispute bound keep matching on the task text.

The bar is a record of
tests that passed, not a set: it is never validated, rewritten or shown to a
writer or a fixer, and it carries no fix (I3). It reconciles with own-start
writing and Q6 because what Q6 measured were sets written at an old base that
never passed anywhere; a bar case passed on a tree that holds the fix.

*The bar does not grow.* Once recorded it is fixed: a later `done` run adds
nothing. The ratchet this replaces appended each `done` run's cases, which
could only add what the rule now withholds, and it broke the check itself: a
later run whose PR was never merged would leave its own cases failing beside
older passing ones, which reads as a regression. Under this rule a later `done`
run exists only after a regression, or after a bar found unlanded. A bar found
unlanded is replaced by the `done` run that found it, since nothing of it ever
reached the tree.

*At each later run's own start*, after the fresh sets are written and typed and
before planning or any no-work settle, the bar is re-run per case in the
held-out sandbox. A failing file runs once more and a case counts as failed
only when it failed both times, so one flake does not reopen a done task. Then:

- A bar case that can no longer run — the runner reports that its file does
  not load or holds no test, or the case is gone — is dropped for good, and
  logged. Q6's lesson holds: no case is kept that demands a shape no later code
  has. A file the environment could not run says nothing of its cases: they are
  kept, and the bar is not applied in this run, which goes on as if it had none.
- When every bar case from the report's own scenarios that ran fails again, as
  it did before the run that settled it, the fix the bar records is not on this
  tree (its PR was never merged, or the tree moved back). The bar is ignored,
  logged: today's behaviour. This cannot be told from a regression of every
  case, so a one-case bar's regression, or a total one, is ignored too and left
  to the fresh sets, which still count here.
- When some bar case fails and another passes, accepted work has regressed and
  the task is reopened. The failing cases join the run as a held-out set of
  their own, whose failing cases count. Its names are always shown: they are the
  run's work and not new to anyone. It overturns a held no-work confirmation
  without the dispute bound, which exists to stop re-sampled tests, and it is
  never audited or rewritten, since no worker may type a regression away. Its
  names reach the planners as the no-work dispute does. A run that then changes
  nothing is `unconverged`, not `no_work`. The fresh sets stand as typed in this
  run: the task is no longer done, so the rule that withholds them has lapsed.
- When every bar case passes, the bar **holds**. Every fresh counted failing
  case is withdrawn from its set's counted cases and recorded as advisory, with
  no auditor call and no contradiction check, and the run ends `no_work` before
  planning.

*Nothing else starts work while a bar holds.* The rule is decided by the
invariant, so it is not "no other work" in the sense of asking who else has an
opinion. The classifier marking required items unmet with no held-out failure,
the `no_work_judge` disputing the classifier's claim, a prior run's recorded
residual, and a classifier that this time does not type the task `bug-fixing`
(the bar is still run, with no fresh sets) all give way: a bar that holds ends
the run. What bypasses the rule is what cannot measure it. An operator's
`--skip-acceptance-check` runs no held-out test at all, a repository with no
scoped test command has no way to run one, and a bar that could not be measured
or errored fails open to the run having no bar.

*The user sees what was withheld.* The advisory cases are the rule's whole cost,
so they are listed in the run's final log, its no-work reasons and `run.json`,
each with its set, file and name, with the plain statement that the task stays
done on its recorded tests and that editing the report or rewording the task
starts a new bar. A PR would
carry the same list in its advisory section; no run that withholds a case makes
one today, since a held bar ends with no commits. They never reach the next
run's residual: the run has no gate, so nothing is handed on.

*A done run's change on the base settles the task.* The held-out half of the
bar is narrow (one counted case in REST-GET's) and exists only for runs that
ended `done` with sets. The user's statement of the rule is wider: when the
change a `done` run shipped is on a later run's base, the task is finished, and
a run that reverses it is the opposite of what leerie is for. Barnacle 73751002
ended `done`, its PR (#696) was squash-merged, and the next run of the same task,
a79384a4, started on a base holding it, found the symptom no longer reproduced,
was overturned by two fresh held-out sets demanding the opposite, deleted #696's
tests and opened a PR (#702, closed) that reversed it. So at each later run's own
start, beside the held-out entries:

- *Is the change on this base?* Decided by git alone: every hunk the `done` run's
  diff made to a non-test file, each taken on its own, reverse-applies to the own
  start (`git apply --cached --check -R`; a diff touching only tests uses its test
  hunks). A squash merge leaves no ancestry, so ancestry cannot answer, and a
  later commit to another part of the same file must not hide it. A hunk a later
  commit rewrote does not reverse-apply, so the answer is then "not on the base",
  and the run goes on as the held-out entries alone decide — today's behaviour.
  An unsure answer never settles.
- *Has it regressed?* When it is on the base, the test files the change added or
  changed are run, in the form it shipped them, at the own start in the held-out
  sandbox, per case. They are the repository's own committed tests, not held-out
  ones, and the base usually has them, so they are written onto the bar's
  disposable tree, after its held-out entries ran, rather than placed in the
  sandbox, which never places a file over a path the tree has (I3); a failing file run once more as for the held-out entries.
  A case that already failed on the tree the `done` run shipped (its recorded
  final failing IDs) is not a regression. A file that no longer loads or holds no
  test is dropped for good. With the change on the base, a failure of every case
  reads as the regression it is, not as unlanded: the git answer has told the
  two apart.
- Then the bar holds, regresses or is not measured exactly as for the held-out
  entries, and a holding bar ends the run `no_work` before planning with every
  fresh counted case listed as advisory. A change on the base whose test files
  have all been dropped, or that changed no test, holds on the git answer alone.
  A regressed change test's names reach the planners as a regressed bar case's
  do, through the no-work dispute, and a run that then changes nothing is
  `unconverged`; no held-out set carries them, since they are not held out and
  their paths are the tree's. A change that is not on the base is
  `unlanded`, and the next `done` run replaces the bar.

The three signals measured over every recorded lineage, for each `done` run with
its PR and every later recorded base (167 pairs; truth: the PR's merge commit is
an ancestor of the base), on barnacle and web:

| signal | on base, said so | on base, missed | not on base, said on base |
|---|---|---|---|
| each file's content equals the run's shipped tree | 5 | 135 | 0 |
| the whole diff reverse-applies | 32 | 108 | 0 |
| every non-test hunk reverse-applies on its own (chosen) | 61 | 79 | 0 |

The misses are bases where later commits rewrote the change's own lines, or
where the PR that merged was not the run's tip (43bd4671's #685 was edited before
merge: 2 of its 8 non-test hunks differ). On the twelve pairs of a `done` run and
the next run of its task, the chosen signal says "on base" on ten, among them
73751002 → a79384a4 (15 of 15 non-test hunks; the whole diff does not
reverse-apply, for #694's and #695's hunks in the same file and an import reorder
in a test).

*Prior runs, backfilled at run time.* A task with no change in its bar takes it,
at the own start, from the latest run of the same task that ended `done` and
whose directory is still under the state root: its task text equal; its key equal
when it recorded one, or, for a run from before keys, every report the task
points at unmodified since that run started (the file's mtime earlier than the
run's start); its own start, and its branch in its own repository. A bar that
already has held-out entries takes the change of the run that recorded them. A
`done` run whose directory was pruned, whose repository is gone, or that recorded
no own start cannot be backfilled, and its task behaves as before. Nothing outside
leerie's own run writes it.

*Rewording starts fresh.* A task that legitimately has more to do after a `done`
run whose change is on the base is not reopened by its fresh sets. The user's
rule is that a re-run finding work means something is wrong; the way to ask for
more is to reword the task or edit the report, which is a new key. This is an
accepted cost, and the replay below shows it is not zero.

**What was measured.** A mechanical replay of the recorded barnacle runs through
`_record_settled_bar` and `_settled_bar_withdraw`, with no worker and no
repository code run; the bar's status at each own start was read from the
commits. REST-GET's bar is 107cd8a3's one counted case and its set's control
file. At 43bd4671's own start, which has #682 merged, it holds, so 43bd4671's 8
hand-labelled over-reach cases are withheld and the run ends `no_work`. That
removes the 8 of 17 bad cases that started the churn, and #685 with them. The
runs after it then do not exist on these trees: the 8 genuine cases of 673a0cc6
all trace to `isInstanceSlug`, which #685 added and which is absent from
107cd8a3's end tree and #682's merge. Read on the recorded trees those runs did
have, the bar is `regressed`, not held: its control file asserts `["lang", "en"]`
and `/venues/time-machine/slots`, which #685 changed and every later tree keeps.
So on those trees the rule withholds nothing: 673a0cc6's 8 genuine cases stay
work, and so do 396c84e3's 2 test errors and 7 over-reach, which fresh sets may
count on a reopened task. No hand-labelled genuine case is withheld in either
view. a41a09fd's one counted case (compact date-window keys) has no hand label.
Not covered, because no earlier run of the task ended `done`: 73751002 (3
over-reach), 80e66fce, d7c06fe3, 0d1c4033 and a2a825c2.

The report did not change across this lineage: the report text in the scope
judge's prompts hashes the same in all six REST-GET runs, so the content key
leaves these decisions as they are.

**Known limits.**

- *A real gap on a held tree creates no work. This is the accepted cost, and the
  user chose it.* A real gap in a fresh sample, on a tree whose bar holds, is
  listed as advisory and nothing more, until someone rewords the task or edits
  the report. Its size is unmeasured: under the rule those samples are never
  acted on, and no recorded run sampled a held tree after 43bd4671.
- *A regression of every report case reads as unlanded.* Squash merges leave no
  ancestry to tell the two apart, so a one-case bar's regression, or a total one,
  is ignored and left to the fresh sets. REST-GET's bar has one counted case.
  A bar that holds a `done` run's change on the base is the exception: there git
  tells the two apart, and a total failure is a regression.
- *A reopened task's fresh sets count.* On a regressed bar nothing is withheld, so
  over-reach can come back into a reopened run: on their recorded trees,
  396c84e3's 9 bad cases stay work. Withholding them too would also withhold
  673a0cc6's 8 genuine ones there, so they stand.
- *The bar is narrower than everything that passed.* It holds counted cases and
  their sets' control files, not every case passing at the finish: 1 of the 24
  cases in 107cd8a3's sets is counted. REST-GET's bar sees #685's regression only
  through its control file, so a set with a less specific control sees less.

**The change half, replayed.** Every run after a `done` run of the same task in
the recorded barnacle, web and navegando runs (17), with the latest earlier
`done` run as the prior one, mechanically and with no worker or repository code
run: the git answer computed on the recorded commits; the test half read from
the record, every prior change test unchanged on the base or the base suite
green apart from unrelated scale tests. "Hunks" is non-test hunks that
reverse-apply.

So of the eleven runs it settles, three are the reopenings this rule exists to
stop, two change nothing, two are a task the user re-ran for more, and four did
work the user merged after a `done` that was premature: on leerie 0.43.0–0.44.3
the earlier run ended `done` with part of a multi-issue report, or one emission
path of one symptom, still open. The rule cannot tell those apart from a done
task without a judgement, and it trusts `done`. That is the accepted cost above,
and its measured size: on these lineages, 4 of 11 settles hid real work, all
behind a `done` leerie should not have reached. Each is recovered by editing the
report or rewording the task.

**Not measured:** the bar's re-run at the own start in a real run, which runs
repository code and so stays inside leerie's confinement; the statuses above are
read, not executed. The re-run, its statuses and the no-work exit are exercised
only by the test suite, on small real repositories.

**A case has one name in every tree.** A set runs in several trees: its
validation and its scope judge in its own (`acceptance-N`,
`acceptance-rewrite-N`), the evaluation in another (`acceptance-eval`), the
audit and the surrogate witness in others still. Some runners name a case by
its file's absolute path — vitest's jest-compatible JSON does — so one case
read in two trees had two names, and every per-case comparison across trees
(the counted cases against the failing ones, the held cases against a
rerun's) found nothing in common. Measured on barnacle 48c48629 (leerie
0.43.0, replayed under 0.44.3's functions on 2026-11-04): set 5 still failed
at ship on its counted cases, the per-case test found none of them failing,
the run ended `done`, and the residual read back as nothing, so the next run
on the task (a192d275) was handed no `acceptance_unmet`; 0.44.3 runs
237ea25c, 7cff429a and ddd383ea recorded the same absolute names. A case's
name is therefore made relative to the tree it ran in when the runner's
report is read, so every reader compares like with like. Names a run
recorded before this rule are made relative when its state is read — on
resume, and when a later run reads it for its residual — against the set's
own file paths, never by guessing at a tree.

**Scoped runners for every runner leerie can read.** A set runs only
through a scoped test template — the canonical command over the set's own
files, in the runner's direct form (`vitest run`, `jest --runTestsByPath`,
never the impact-analysis form; §9 *Operands that are already test files
take the runner's direct form*) — so a repo with no template got no sets
at all, silently. The
template is inferred, when the repo declares none, from a canonical test
command that is a bare runner invocation (only options after the runner,
read from its argv, never from prose): `pytest` (also `python -m pytest`
under any `python<version>`, and behind an environment wrapper — `uv
run`, `poetry run`, `pipenv run`, `pdm run`, `rye run`, `hatch run`, with
the wrapper's own options — which the template keeps; its path positionals,
such as `pytest -q tests`, are replaced by the set's files rather than
disqualifying it, while a node id, a selecting option such as `-k`/`-m`/
`--lf`, or a word after a long option leerie cannot tell is a flag still
does; which pytest options take a value is one table derived from real
pytest 9's parser with its common plugins, not written by hand — a
hand-written one listed the flag `--cov-branch` as value-taking, so
`pytest --cov=src --cov-branch tests` kept `tests` as the option's
"value" and ran the whole suite beside every set; and a suite-level
threshold is dropped from it, because a set is judged by exit code and
one file of tests is below any threshold set for the whole suite —
`--cov-fail-under` and `--max-warnings`, the junit report options whose
file nobody reads, and, when the command shows pytest-cov is installed
(any `--cov` option), every coverage option, replaced by `--no-cov`,
which also disables a `fail_under` the coverage config sets. Measured
with pytest 9.2 and pytest-cov 7.1: `--cov=src --cov-fail-under=90` over
one passing file exits 1 with every case passing, as does `--cov=src`
under a `.coveragerc` `fail_under = 90`, and `--no-cov` over the same
file exits 0. A threshold reached only through the repo's own `addopts`
is not seen — the command does not say pytest-cov is there, so
`--no-cov` could be an unknown option), `rspec` (also `bundle exec rspec`, `bin/rspec`) and
minitest's `rails test` take `{test_files}` as written; `rake test`, which
takes one path, becomes a `ruby -Itest -Ilib` loader over `{test_files}`;
`go test` takes the test files' packages (`{test_packages}`, with a
`-run` selector naming the set's own test functions, read from the Go
source, so a package's existing tests stay out of the set's verdict); and
`cargo test` takes `--test <name>` per integration-test file
(`{test_targets}`, `--no-fail-fast`). Benched as C9 on one fixture per
runner (pytest, rspec, minitest through the loader and `bin/rails test`,
go, cargo): every derived command ran exactly the set's files and the
per-case report gave the expected verdict, 6/6, and the minitest pair
matched on the rootful runtime. When no scoped runner applies — `npm test`,
`make test`, a runner invocation with its own selectors, a cargo file that
is not an integration test — the skip is typed (`no_scoped_runner`, with
the command) and logged as a warning, never silent.

**Hidden from the fixers.** The sets live under the run's state root,
and no fixer's grant (I5, §6 *A worker writes only where it is granted*)
names that directory or any run-directory file that records them — the
evaluation worktree, the logs (the writers' transcripts carry the test
source), the orchestrator log, the captured-call log, the run state (case
names and paths) and every other worker's configuration (its session
transcripts). The fixers — implementer, conformer, the surrogate
witness's fixer and the falsifier — read nothing of the state root but
their own directories, their subtask specs, criteria and checkpoints, and
the kernel refuses the rest to the Read tool and a shell `cat` alike.
Their own configuration holds only their own sessions, and the home
directory's `~/.claude/projects` holds none: every CLI leerie starts in
the container is given its own configuration directory. Evaluation output
is never echoed, and nothing of a set reaches staging at all (above).
The CLI `Read` denies that hid these paths before Landlock covered them
are gone: they added nothing the grant does not refuse, and any `Read()`
deny makes the CLI refuse ordinary `cd <dir>; grep …` compounds — the
refusal naming `acceptance/` appears on 45 log lines of the seven live
0.43.0 barnacle runs.

### Mechanical-feedback loops (the CRITIC pattern)

Research shows that LLMs cannot self-correct reasoning without external
feedback (Huang et al., ICLR 2024), and that self-correction WITH
tool-verified feedback works (the CRITIC framework, ICLR 2024).

Leerie applies this: every worker (except the PR writer) runs inside a
code-enforced loop (`_run_checked_loop`) where the orchestrator computes
**deterministic structural checks** on the worker's output — file-existence,
dependency-graph cycles, lockfile consistency, protected-path violations,
**confidence-axis gates** — and re-invokes the worker with the check results
as external feedback if issues are found. The feedback is mechanically
derived (no LLM). Confidence gating (threshold 9.0 on every worker's
schema-defined axes) is code-enforced for all workers, not just the
implementer.

The conformer loop (`_run_conformance_phase`) is the original instance of
this pattern — it loops on observable build/lint/test signals. The generic
`_run_checked_loop` extends it to all workers.

#### Findings carry a severity; only gating findings re-invoke

A check function's findings are not all the same kind of thing. Some name a
defect that makes the output **unusable** — a dependency on a subtask that
does not exist, a cycle, a subtask with no success criteria. Others are
**advice** about a judgement call that is frequently correct as it stands.

Treating both as retry triggers is a mistake with two distinct costs:

- **Advice cannot converge, so it burns the whole retry budget.**
  `INTRA_DOMAIN_OVERLAP`'s own text is *"consider merging or splitting"* — it
  never reliably reaches zero, because there is frequently nothing wrong to
  fix.
- **Per-subtask advice turns the retry count into a proxy for plan size.**
  Findings like `PHANTOM_PATH` fire once per offending subtask, so a large
  plan must be flawless to beat a small plan with one flaw, and an *empty*
  plan scores a perfect zero — the same defect the sample validity gate
  addresses at its extreme.

So each finding declares a severity. `_run_checked_loop` re-invokes only on
**gating** findings; **advisory** findings are surfaced once, in the returned
warnings, without costing a round. Multi-sample selection likewise ranks on
gating findings only, so plan size stops being a scoring penalty.

**The default is gating.** A finding whose severity nobody declared keeps
today's behaviour, so the classification can be incomplete without silently
weakening a real gate — the advisory set is an explicit allowlist.

**A mechanical floor is not thereby an independent one.** A pure-Python
check can still gate on a planner self-report field the planner is free to
omit (`check_prescribed_command_coverage` on `runs_commands`, measured
populated on under 5% of subtasks) — being deterministic is not the same as
being independent, the same trap documented for `migration_targets` in §8. A
floor must either read something the planner cannot omit — the repository,
the diff, the dependency graph — or repair the omission itself rather than
re-driving the worker that made it.

**Repairing an omitted self-report beats re-driving for it.** The floor
above *is* satisfiable — told explicitly, planners fill the field — but a
full re-plan to fix it once cost roughly the entire first planning pass and
the run then died of budget exhaustion having written no code. leerie
already holds the prescribed commands as structured classifier output, so
`_repair_prescribed_commands` synthesises a subtask that runs them, at zero
worker cost, before the floor is evaluated. A repairable gap therefore never
reaches the re-plan path.

The repair **synthesises rather than picking an owner**: attaching the
commands to "the subtask that owns verification" was prototyped and
rejected, since a verification-shaped matcher hits most subtasks in a real
plan, making an exactly-one-owner rule never fire and a looser one attach
arbitrarily. A dedicated subtask whose entire content is running the
prescribed commands cannot be wrong about intent, depends on the plan's
current sinks (acyclic by construction), and schedules alone in the final
wave.

**A declared command must also have been executed — the settle-time half.**
The floor above only proves some subtask *declares* each prescribed
command; nothing verified the declaring subtask ever *ran* it. Measured
(barnacle, 2026-09-22): a subtask declared `runs_commands` naming the
task's one empirical acceptance command, its worker never issued it (the
input the command needed was unreachable from the sandbox), and the
subtask settled `complete` on tests the same wave had authored — across
ten runs of that task, the declared command was executed zero times while
every run finalized green. The settle-time half closes this: the
orchestrator already holds every Bash invocation the worker actually made
as structured `tool_use` JSON in the per-worker log (`_iter_log_tool_use`
— JSON→JSON, no prose is read), so `_settle_subtask` requires every
`runs_commands` entry on a `complete` result — except one the whole-suite
deny refuses (§9 *The whole suite is orchestrator-owned*) — to match some
executed invocation under normalized token matching, per shell segment
(segments split first, so a match inside a pipeline or a `cd … && …`
prefix still counts — but never a cross-segment token union, which would
credit `pnpm install && ls test` for a declared "pnpm test"). Matching
accepts either direction, because `runs_commands` legitimately takes two
shapes: a *literal* entry (declared token set ⊆ executed segment's) and
a *paraphrase* entry that wraps the command's tokens in extra words (the
plan-level floor's one corpus sample, "barnacle recon browser" for
`recon browser`, plus `prompts/planner.md`'s exact-commands instruction
are the whole evidence base for that shape — a tail-position assumption
was briefly shipped on no evidence and withdrawn). For the paraphrase
shape the executed segment's salient token list must appear as a
length-≥2 **contiguous ordered sublist** anywhere in the declared
entry's salient token list. Contiguity is the settled endpoint of a
measured three-round oscillation whose neighbors are both known-bad: a
bare-SUBSET reverse rule let any ≥2-token fragment of a wordy paraphrase
count as executed ("pnpm run", "make test" — non-adjacent words
reassembled); a SUFFIX-only rule then false-alarmed on every paraphrase
with words *after* the command ("run pnpm test to verify" vs an
exactly-executed `pnpm test`), looping the re-drive deterministically
into the blocked terminal — where `accept-blocked` silently drops a
correct subtask's commits, strictly worse than any near-miss pass. No
token rule can separate "ran the command mid-paraphrase" from "ran an
adjacent fragment of the paraphrase"; contiguity resolves the
undecidable remainder toward keeping work. The gate's honest contract is
therefore: it catches **"never touched the declared command"**, not
"ran a variant of it". Accepted near-miss residual class, in full: a
parent sub-command (`barnacle recon` for "barnacle recon browser"), a
flag-dropped variant (`pnpm lint` for "pnpm lint --fix" — its mirror,
adding `--dry-run`, already passes the literal direction), a `--help`
probe of a declared literal, and a deliberately-typed adjacent word pair
("test suite") — the same §9 concession that declines to gate on test
content a stuck worker could weaken, because the check verifies
invocation, not success or intent: gating on the command's outcome is
the code-enforced "tests must pass" bar §9 rejects, and the command's
*output* reaching the worker is what the re-drive prompt asks for, not
what the gate can honestly measure. The false-alarm residual that
remains is glued punctuation (a declared entry quoting the command,
"run \`pnpm test\`"), genuinely non-contiguous paraphrases, and a
declared entry with fewer than one salient token (all-stopword or
separator-only strings, e.g. "&&", are deterministically unsatisfiable
— separators never survive segment splitting); the worst
case for each is the re-drive round then the blocked terminal,
adjudicated by the operator via `accept-blocked`. A miss first re-drives
the implementer through the existing mechanical-check feedback loop —
forgetting to run a declared command is exactly the "retryable mistake"
shape that loop exists for. When the confidence-retry budget exhausts
with the command still unexecuted, and the subtask has its own commits or
is verification-only, the orchestrator runs the subtask's typed `verify`
argvs itself (§8 *Settled by execution*): a pass settles the claim on the
orchestrator's own execution, not the worker's word. Otherwise — no
`verify` argv, a failing execution, or neither commits nor
verification-only — the subtask settles **`blocked`**, naming the
command, and the wave-end re-drive takes it from the shared budget (§13),
ending `unconverged` when that is spent. The one thing the run must never
do is what it measurably did — settle `complete` on a verification it
*silently* skipped. A result rescued from `empty_handoff` (§6 *Detecting
memory OOM* — the worker was reaped mid-turn with committed work) used to
settle complete with only a warning, because blocking it stranded its
commits behind `accept-blocked`. It has commits by construction, so it is
now settled the same way: a passing execution settles it complete; an
unsettled one is re-driven as a continuation, which keeps the branch and
its commits, and a spent budget ends it `unconverged` — reported, never
silently merged as done. The warning record that rescue wrote
(`declared_unrun_warnings`) is therefore no longer written; finalize still
surfaces one a run recorded before this change. The check binds only
where the field is populated (under 5% of subtasks), but
`_repair_prescribed_commands` above makes prescribed commands
always-declared, so the two halves together close the loop: plan-level
"someone declares it," settle-level "the declarer ran it."

### Task-referenced file extraction

When the task string references files (detectable by globbing), the
orchestrator mechanically resolves the paths (`_glob_task_references`) and
names them for the planner, which reads them itself; whether the plan
covers what they require is the `task_coverage_judge`'s call (§8). This is
deliberately just a list of paths — naming the files is mechanical, but
judging whether a document's requirements are met is a judgment about
meaning, which is a worker's job, not Python's.

An earlier version harvested the referenced files' headings with regex,
classified the harvested prose with another regex, and gated on substring
overlap between the result and the plan text — three layers of prose
parsing over one mechanism, and the source of a real freeze incident
(identical feedback rounds on a ratio no planner could move, because
backtick+MUST convention headings cannot appear verbatim in a subtask by
construction). It is deleted; `task_coverage_judge` reads the referenced
files itself and judges substance rather than string overlap.

The classifier is the one worker handed a referenced file's text: a
markdown report the task names that is not tracked at HEAD is inlined,
cut at its headings, so requirement coverage (§8) can anchor items on
its sections. That cut assigns IDs only (§12 *Delimiter-only cutting is
not the deleted heading harvest*); the planner's section above stays a
list of paths.

### Multi-sample planning

Multiple independent planner invocations per domain, each a fresh
`claude -p` session (Cross-Context Review, arxiv 2603.12123, 2026: context
separation is the mechanism). Mechanical selection by issue count and
subtask count avoids self-bias (a novel extension beyond the paper, which
tested single fresh-session review only). Controlled by the
`planner_samples` cap (default 3).

---

## 9. Success criteria (informational; historical lock)

Each implementer's first step is to turn its assigned seed into a brief
success-criteria file describing what success looks like for the subtask —
the explicit success condition plus any regression guards worth naming. The
file is **informational**: written for the implementer's own clarity, read
by the conformance phase for context, and useful for human reviewers. The
orchestrator does not gate on whether the file's individual criteria are
satisfied; that is what the confidence gate at §8 is for. The implementer
may update the file freely — there is no lock.

This is a reversal of an earlier discipline that locked the criteria file by
sha256 hash on first write and threaded any later edit through orchestrator
approval, to guard against a stuck model lowering its own bar. With the
confidence gate as the sole load-bearing signal (§8), the bar is the model's
*anchored confidence in the solution*, not the contents of a text file —
there is no longer a fixed bar to lower. The lock and its proposal channel
were removed in the same change that consolidated build/lint/test under the
conformance phase.

A worker that wants to record "this criterion isn't met" does so via
`criteria_results[].met: false` in its result — recorded and surfaced as a
warning, but it does not change the subtask's terminal status.

### Post-work conformance

The §8 confidence gate says whether the work landed; the implementer's
criteria notes describe what it was aimed at. Neither says whether the
*change* is in good standing with the repo it lives in: whether documentation
that describes the touched surface is still accurate, whether tests for the
touched code were updated, whether the change still honors whatever rules the
repo declares for itself (CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, `.cursorrules`, a section of
the README, a `docs/` file). These are real obligations of a finished change,
but the wrong thing to bake into the assigned criteria: criteria are scoped
to the subtask, and the repo's rules are an environmental fact that survives
across subtasks.

So a separate phase runs once a subtask's work has settled: the
**conformer**. It triggers only on the success path — implementer reports
`status: "complete"`, commits are present, the worktree is clean, no
protected path was written. It reads the diff just produced, reads whatever
rules files the orchestrator located in the repo, and is empowered to commit
fixes to the same worktree branch — updating documentation, adding or
amending tests, repairing a rule violation it spotted.

Where the rule files live varies, so location discovery is code, not the
worker's problem: a fixed, capped allowlist of paths in the repo root and
`docs/` is checked for existence, and the surviving paths are handed to the
conformer as inputs. If discovery finds nothing, the phase still runs — the
conformer focuses on whether the diff touched a surface the README or a
`docs/` file describes, and whether tests were updated — and silently skips
the rule-conformance axis.

The same discovered set is surfaced to the *implementer* at write time too,
not only to the conformer post-hoc: convention drift is cheaper to prevent
than to catch, since a conformer that only reads the diff afterward can flag
a rule violation but can't re-derive an unwritten visual convention. The
implementer's prompt names the discovered convention docs as paths, and its
evidence gate asks it to reconcile the pattern it followed against them —
advisory, since matching an existing design is judgment, but discovery itself
is code so the doc list can't silently drift. The allowlist therefore
includes the repo's design-system doc (e.g. `docs/DESIGN-SYSTEM.md`).

Two further disciplines sit at the §12 axis:

- **Highest effort, never required.** Building, linting, and the test suite
  passing are *desired* outcomes but never gating ones: each of build, lint,
  and tests resolves to *ran and passed*, *ran and failed*, or *not
  applicable*, and a failure surfaces only as an advisory warning. Making
  "tests pass" a hard requirement here invites the conformer to weaken a
  test or skip a lint rule to clear the bar — the same failure mode §9
  guards against from the other side.
- **The one gating axis: solution completeness.** The conformer carries a
  single gating axis, `solution_defects` — gating for the exact reason
  build/lint/test are not: it is not a self-assertable bar the conformer can
  lower, but an adversarial attack on an artifact the conformer did not
  write (§8 *Independent adversarial verification*). It enumerates concrete
  behavioral gaps — an unhandled input, a missing guard, a decoy shortcut, a
  sibling call site left unedited, a behavior keyed on an undocumented
  external-interface detail, a check-then-act sequence whose precondition
  is never revalidated at the act. A non-empty set of concretely-named
  defects gates the subtask: the found gaps become mandatory additional
  criteria and the subtask retries the implementer with them folded in
  (bounded by `completeness_retry_rounds`; on exhaustion the subtask blocks
  with the residual defects named, fix + `resume`). This is independent of
  `--strict-conformer`, which governs the advisory axes above. It does not
  reintroduce the gameable bar because there is no bar to lower — a defect
  without a concrete case is dropped as non-actionable. When the diff is
  empty or unreadable the axis fails open.

  **The success criteria are not the ceiling of this attack.** The criteria
  are planner-authored, and a criterion can itself embed the defect: on one
  run a planner's criterion quoted a third-party API's human-readable error
  message as the success discriminator, the implementer matched that message
  with a regex, and the conformer — validating against the same criterion —
  reported no defects and wrote tests cementing the regex. Measured on that
  incident's inputs: the identical model flags the defect 3/3 when told the
  criteria are not the ceiling and asked for the two kinds above
  (`external_contract_assumption`, `unrevalidated_precondition`), and 0/3
  false-positives on a clean control diff. The same measurement grounded
  the sibling planner rule (a `success_criteria_seed` must state success in
  documented discriminators, never in an external interface's message
  wording): re-running the incident's implementer with the criterion
  rephrased flipped the output from the message regex to a code-only check
  in 3 of 3 samples, against 2 of 2 regexes under the original wording.
- **Evidence must be production-grounded: a fix that never fires is not a
  fix.** Every gate above asks whether the code matches its specification.
  None asks whether the specification matches reality, and a wrong
  specification propagates cleanly through implementer, criteria, conformer,
  and the final whole-tree pass. Measured on one run: four fixes shipped
  inert, six conformers reported zero defects, and the run exited 0 at
  confidence 8.5. The clearest instance resolved a repo's declared Node heap
  against a `.leerie/config.toml` fixture shape **0 of the 5 repos leerie
  manages use** — every criterion was met; the mechanism never ran once in
  production.

  The response is a `production_evidence` field on the implementer and
  conformer results: the worker must exercise the path it just wrote against
  the repo **as it actually is**, and record the command and what it
  observed. The requirement is not proof of correctness — a fixture can be
  right and a real repo still take a different branch — it is that *"I could
  not make this fire here"* becomes a recorded, gating outcome instead of
  silence. Absence of the field gates, matching *Findings carry a severity*
  above.

  Two adjacent prompt-level disciplines follow from the same measurement,
  because neither can be checked in general: **a new decision point logs
  which branch it took, including the branch that does nothing** (a
  mechanism with zero `log()` calls was found only by manual audit, while
  one that logged its own failure was caught from the log line); and **when
  a test forces a constant to be duplicated, the test is the defect** — an
  implementer that instead declared a second constant to keep a pin green
  produced two figures that then silently disagreed by 384 MiB.

  Two candidate gates were tested against the same run and **refused**.
  *Red-before-green* — requiring the new tests to fail on the base tree — is
  free and worthless: a new test against code that doesn't exist yet
  trivially fails, so all four findings already satisfied it. What has value
  is reproducing the reported *symptom*, a stronger requirement that would
  have caught the finding already fixed by an earlier PR. *Producer-branch
  coverage* — requiring tests to exercise both branches of the producer
  feeding the fix — also fails: instrumented, the defective branch executed
  under the defective fixture too, so the gate passes while the defect
  stands.
- **Self-reported risk is routed, not read.** The evidence contract above
  makes a worker *record* "I could not make this fire here" — but a recorded
  caveat that nothing consumes is still silence one hop downstream. Measured
  on a live run: an implementer disclosed, in its own structured output,
  both that its new path was never exercised (`exercised: false`, with a
  legitimate reason) and that its success hinged on an external API's exact
  message wording — and the run shipped the defect anyway, because the only
  consumer of `production_evidence` is a presence/shape check and the prose
  caveat lived in a `confidence.basis` string no code reads. Per the
  Language-to-JSON rule, the remedy is never to parse the prose: risk is
  surfaced as typed JSON and routed by code.

  Three mechanical consumers close the loop:

  1. **A `risk_register` in run state.** `_collect_subtask_risks` folds the
     already-typed tier (`production_evidence.exercised == false`, from the
     implementer and the conformer) together with an explicit typed
     `self_reported_risks` field on the implementer result, keyed by
     subtask, set and cleared on the same settle path as
     `symptom_findings`. (Measured across 2,627 implementer calls on three
     repos: the `exercised: false` tier fires on 3.2% of results; on the
     motivating run — a fourth, separate corpus — it flagged exactly the
     defect-bearing subtasks. A low-noise, high-recall signal.) Each typed
     entry says what is missing, where, and what would settle it, so code
     can route it: `gap` — `test_missing` (changed production code no test
     exercises), `test_weak` (a test exists but does not assert the
     change), `unverified_external` (depends on something outside the
     repository's own checks: a live service, real database, cloud
     resource, real device), or `none` (informational); `where_paths` —
     exact repository paths, which code keeps only when each is a file in
     the subtask's worktree; `settle_by` — `test`, `typecheck`, `install`
     or `build`; an optional `resource` naming what a human must supply,
     and `simulated_interleaving` for a race whose tests can only stub the
     interleaving. A note about the worker's own process ("typecheck was
     not run") is kind `process_note` and never enters the register: the
     orchestrator runs its own checks. (Bench Q7/G v5: of the 9 frozen
     late-chain subtasks, 8 of 9 first emissions carried only a
     process note.) **Only an entry naming an external resource is
     external.** "Needs human verification" is for a check no step inside
     the container can make: a live service, a real browser session, a
     cloud account, a device — named, so the reviewer knows what to bring.
     The `exercised: false` tier is typed `unverified_external` only when
     the worker names that resource in `production_evidence`'s
     `unexercisable_resource` (on the implementer and conformer schemas
     both; the conformer's room for it came from giving its three
     build/lint/test axes one `$defs` shape instead of three copies).
     Otherwise it is `test_missing`: the worker did not run the path, which
